A map with \(\det\mat F_0 \neq 0\) is therefore always one-to-one near \(P_0\). Let us test it on the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s, t + s^2)\) and the point \(P_0\) of figure 4.89. The matrix \(\mat F_0^{-1}\) has the largest element \(2\), so by lemma 4.46 on the bound for a matrix times a vector, item 2, \(m = 4\) will do, and the lemma gives the bound \(|PQ|/8\). The radius from step 1 of the proof: of the elements of the matrix of partial derivatives only \(2s\) varies, and the condition \(|2s - 2| < 1/24\) holds for \(|s - 1| < 1/48\), so \(r = 1/48\) will do, much less than the radius \(0{,}4\) with which the disc is drawn for clarity. NumPy shows that in the disc of radius \(1/48\) the smallest ratio \(|\Phi(P) - \Phi(Q)|/|PQ|\) is about \(0{,}408\), which is more than the bound \(0{,}125\). Distances in the direction that the linear part shrinks most shrink to about \(0{,}41\) times their length.

Now the idea of the theorem. Let \(Q_0 = \Phi(P_0)\) and let \(Q\) be a point near \(Q_0\). We look for a point \(P\) near \(P_0\) with \(\Phi(P) = Q\). Instead of solving the equation, we look for the point whose image is closest to \(Q\). The function

\[f(P) = |\Phi(P) - Q|^2\]

is continuous, so on a closed ball around \(P_0\) it attains a smallest value (theorem 1.79). The lower bound for stretching keeps the images of the points on the surface of the ball far from \(Q_0\) and therefore far from \(Q\), farther than \(Q_0\) itself. In the figure \(P\) is such a point of the surface and \(\Phi(P)\) its image: the orange segment from it to \(Q\) is longer than the blue segment from \(Q_0\) to \(Q\). The smallest value is therefore not on the surface but inside the ball, at the point \(P_*\), and there the partial derivatives of the function \(f\) are zero, because the value of \(f\) does not decrease when we move from \(P_*\) along one of the axes, as the derivative is zero at an interior extremum (lemma 1.83). By the chain rule this means \(\mat F_\Phi^\T\,(\Phi(P) - Q) = \vek 0\), and since the determinant is not zero, \(\Phi(P) = Q\). Why? A matrix with a nonzero determinant has an inverse matrix, so it sends the steps from \(P_*\) to steps of all directions. If the image of the point \(P_*\) were not \(Q\), one of them would be a step straight towards \(Q\), and a short such step would bring the image closer to \(Q\) and push the value of \(f\) below the smallest one. Figure 4.90 shows the idea for the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s, t + s^2)\). On the left is the disc \(K\) with centre \(P_0\) and radius \(r\) in the plane with the axes \(s\) and \(t\). On the right is the image of the disc with the axes \(x\) and \(y\), in it the point \(Q_0\), the blue disc around it and the bound \(2\rho\) to the image of the circle. The point \(Q\) in the blue disc has its \(P_*\) inside the disc \(K\).

For the second and third items of the theorem we look in the reverse direction (figure 4.91), again on the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s, t + s^2)\) and the point \(P_0\) with the coordinates \(s = 0{,}5\) and \(t = 0{,}5\). In the plane with the axes \(x\) and \(y\) is the point \(Q_0\) and around it the blue disc of radius \(\rho_0\), all of which lies in the image of the open disc \(B_0\) around \(P_0\). From \(Q_0\) we take the step \(h = 0{,}2\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) to the point \(Q\). The inverse map \(\Psi\) brings it back to the point \(P\) in the plane with the axes \(s\) and \(t\). What is the step \(\vek\Delta\) from \(P_0\) to \(P\) like? The lower bound for stretching says that it is no longer than \(2m\,h\), so it goes to zero as \(h\) goes to zero: \(\Psi\) is continuous. The same holds for a sequence of points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) that converges to \(Q_0\): the points \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = \Psi(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to \(P_0\). For the derivative we compare \(\vek\Delta\) with the step \(\mat A\,\overrightarrow{Q_0 Q}\) that the matrix \(\mat A = \mat F_0^{-1}\) makes of the step \(h\). They differ by the remainder \(\vek R'\), which here is \(0{,}04\) long, a fifth of the step \(h\). For \(h = 0{,}1\) it is \(0{,}01\) long, only a tenth of the step. The remainder is small compared with the step, and this is exactly the condition for \(\mat A\) to be the matrix of partial derivatives of the map \(\Psi\) at \(Q_0\).

Theorem 4.51 Inverse function theorem (izrek o inverzni preslikavi)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points of space, in figure 4.91 the open disc \(B_0\), and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 4.42), has points of space as images, is one-to-one on \(D\) (definition 4.45) and has at every point \(P\) of \(D\) the Jacobian \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\). Let \(\Psi\) be its inverse map on \(E = \Phi(D)\), in the figure the image of the disc \(B_0\). Then:

  1. Openness. For every open set \(U \subseteq D\) the image \(\Phi(U)\) is an open set: around \(Q_0\) there is a neighbourhood of radius \(\rho\) that stays in the image (figure 4.90). In particular \(E\) is open.
  2. Differentiability. The map \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable on \(E\): it returns the points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) that approach \(Q_0\) to the points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) that approach \(P_0\).
  3. Matrix of partial derivatives. For every point \(P\) of \(D\), in the figure \(P_0\),
    \[\mat F_\Psi\big(\Phi(P)\big) = \mat F_\Phi(P)^{-1} , \qquad J_\Psi\big(\Phi(P)\big) = \frac{1}{J_\Phi(P)} . \tag{4.29}\]

The same holds in the plane, like the planes \(s\), \(t\) and \(x\), \(y\) of the figure, for a map that assigns points of the plane to the points of an open set of the plane.

Proof

We have to show all three items. For the first we find the point whose image is closest to the given point \(Q\) and show that the image is exactly this point. For the second and the third we write the change of the map \(\Psi\), the step \(\vek\Delta\), with the theorem on the change of a field for \(\Phi\) and invert it with the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P)^{-1}\), which gives the linear step with the remainder, while the lower bound for stretching bounds the step in \(D\) by the step in \(E\).

1. Openness.

  1. Let \(U \subseteq D\) be an open set, \(Q_0\) a point of \(\Phi(U)\) and \(P_0\) a point of \(U\) with \(\Phi(P_0) = Q_0\). We have to show that there is \(\rho > 0\) such that every point closer to \(Q_0\) than \(\rho\) is in \(\Phi(U)\). In figure 4.90 these are \(Q_0\), \(P_0\) and the blue disc of radius \(\rho\).
  2. Let \(\mat F_0 = \mat F_\Phi(P_0)\). Since \(\det\mat F_0 = J_\Phi(P_0) \neq 0\), \(\mat F_0\) has an inverse matrix by theorem 2.76. Let \(g\) be the largest absolute value of its elements. Then \(g > 0\), because otherwise \(\mat F_0^{-1}\mat F_0\) would be the zero matrix, not \(\mat I\). By lemma 4.46 \(|\mat F_0^{-1}\vek w| \le m\,|\vek w|\) for every \(\vek w\), with \(m = 3g\). By lemma 4.50 there is \(r_0 > 0\) such that the ball with centre \(P_0\) and radius \(r_0\) lies in \(D\) and (4.28) holds in it. This is the ball of figure 4.89, there the disc around \(P_0\).
  3. The set \(U\) is open, so there is \(r_{\mathrm{U}} > 0\) such that all points closer to \(P_0\) than \(r_{\mathrm{U}}\) are in \(U\). Let \(r\) be half the smaller of the numbers \(r_0\) and \(r_{\mathrm{U}}\), and \(K\) the closed ball, the set of the points \(P\) with \(|P_0 P| \le r\). All points of \(K\) lie in \(U\) and in the ball of step 2. The set \(K\) is closed by lemma 1.76, because \(|P_0 P| \le r\) exactly when \(|P_0 P|^2 \le r^2\) (lemma 1.29), and \(|P_0 P|^2\) is a polynomial in the coordinates of the point \(P\). It is bounded, because by the triangle inequality for vectors (corollary 2.16) \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le |\overrightarrow{OP_0}| + r\). It is nonempty, because it contains \(P_0\). In the figure this is the disc \(K\) with radius \(r\).
  4. Let \(\rho = r/(4m)\), so that the bound \(r/(2m)\) of step 6 equals \(2\rho\), and let \(Q\) be a point with \(|Q_0 Q| < \rho\). Let \(f(P) = |\Phi(P) - Q|^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \big(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q)\big)^2\) for every \(P\) of \(D\), where \(x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q)\) is coordinate \(i\) of the point \(Q\). The components \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}\) are continuous (lemma 1.92), so by corollary 1.70, item 1, \(f\) is continuous on \(K\). By theorem 1.79, the extreme value theorem in space, there is a point \(P_* \in K\) at which \(f\) attains its smallest value on \(K\). In the figure these are the point \(Q\) in the blue disc and the point \(P_*\).
  5. At the centre \(f(P_0) = |Q_0 - Q|^2 < \rho^2\). This is the square of the length of the blue segment from \(Q_0\) to \(Q\).
  6. Let \(P\) be a point with \(|P_0 P| = r\), on the surface of the ball \(K\). The points \(P\) and \(P_0\) lie in the ball of step 2, so by (4.28) \(|\Phi(P) - Q_0| \ge r/(2m) = 2\rho\). By the triangle inequality for vectors \(|\Phi(P) - Q_0| \le |\Phi(P) - Q| + |Q - Q_0|\), so \(|\Phi(P) - Q| \ge 2\rho - |Q - Q_0| > \rho\), and \(f(P) > \rho^2 > f(P_0)\). In the figure \(P\) is a point of the surface, \(\Phi(P)\) its image, \(2\rho\) the bound for its distance from \(Q_0\) and the orange segment the distance \(|\Phi(P) - Q|\).
  7. By steps 4 to 6 the point \(P_*\) is not on the surface of the ball, because \(f(P_*) \le f(P_0)\). Hence \(|P_0 P_*| < r\). Let \(\varepsilon_* = r - |P_0 P_*| > 0\). In figure 4.90 \(P_*\) lies inside the disc \(K\), and \(\varepsilon_*\) is half the length of the blue segments through \(P_*\).
  8. Let \(j\) be one of the coordinates. For \(|h| < \varepsilon_*\) the point \(P_* + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\) is, by the triangle inequality for vectors, at most \(|P_0 P_*| + |h| < r\) away from \(P_0\), so it lies in \(K\). The function \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}(h) = f(P_* + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}})\) is therefore defined on the open interval \((-\varepsilon_*, \varepsilon_*)\) and attains its smallest value on it at \(h = 0\), because \(P_*\) is the point of the smallest value on \(K\). In the figure these are the two blue segments through \(P_*\), one along the axis \(s\) and one along the axis \(t\).
  9. The function \(f\) is composed of the map \(\Phi\) and the polynomial that assigns to a point \(Y\) the number \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} (x_{\mathrm{i}}(Y) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q))^2\) and has the partial derivatives \(2\,(x_{\mathrm{i}}(Y) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q))\). By the chain rule (lemma 4.43) \(f\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\) and
    \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P_*) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} 2\,\big(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P_*) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q)\big)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P_*) .\]
    By the definition of the partial derivative 1.26 this is the derivative \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'(0)\). In the figure \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the value of the function \(f\) along one of the blue segments.
  10. By lemma 1.83 on the derivative at an interior extremum \(\varphi_{\mathrm{j}}'(0) = 0\). Let \(\vek w = \Phi(P_*) - Q\) and \(\mat F_* = \mat F_\Phi(P_*)\). Since \((\mat F_*^\T)_{\mathrm{ji}} = (\mat F_*)_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 1.101), step 9 for \(j = x, y, z\) says \(\mat F_*^\T\,\vek w = \vek 0\). In the figure \(\vek w\) is the vector from the point \(Q\) to the image of the point \(P_*\).
  11. By lemma 2.73, item 6, \(\det\mat F_*^\T = \det\mat F_* = J_\Phi(P_*) \neq 0\), because \(P_*\) lies in \(D\). By theorem 2.76 \(\mat F_*^\T\) has an inverse matrix, so by lemma 1.100, item 1, and lemma 1.109 \(\vek w = (\mat F_*^\T)^{-1}(\mat F_*^\T\,\vek w) = (\mat F_*^\T)^{-1}\vek 0 = \vek 0\). Hence \(\Phi(P_*) = Q\). The image of the point \(P_*\) is exactly the point \(Q\).
  12. The point \(P_*\) lies in \(K\) and so in \(U\), hence \(Q\) lies in \(\Phi(U)\). This holds for every point \(Q\) closer to \(Q_0\) than \(\rho\), and \(Q_0\) was an arbitrary point of \(\Phi(U)\), so \(\Phi(U)\) is open. For \(U = D\) we get that \(E\) is open. In the figure the whole blue disc around \(Q_0\) lies in the image of the disc.

2. Continuity of the map \(\Psi\).

  1. Let \(Q_0\) be a point of \(E\), \(P_0 = \Psi(Q_0)\), and \(\mat F_0\), \(m\) and \(r_0\) as in step 2 of the first part. The ball \(B_0\) with centre \(P_0\) and radius \(r_0\) is an open set. For a point \(P\) of it, all points closer to \(P\) than \(r_0 - |P_0 P|\) are, by the triangle inequality for vectors, closer to \(P_0\) than \(r_0\). By the first part \(\Phi(B_0)\) is open and contains \(Q_0\), so there is \(\rho_0 > 0\) such that all points closer to \(Q_0\) than \(\rho_0\) are in \(\Phi(B_0)\). In figure 4.91 these are \(Q_0\), \(P_0\), the disc \(B_0\), its image and the blue disc of radius \(\rho_0\).
  2. Let \(|Q_0 Q| < \rho_0\), as for the point \(Q\) in the figure. Then \(Q = \Phi(P)\) for some point \(P\) of \(B_0\), and since \(\Phi\) is one-to-one, \(\Psi(Q) = P\), in the figure the point \(P\). The points \(P\) and \(P_0\) lie in \(B_0\), so by (4.28)
    \[|\Psi(Q) - \Psi(Q_0)| = |P_0 P| \le 2m\,|\Phi(P) - \Phi(P_0)| = 2m\,|Q_0 Q| .\]
  3. No component of a vector is longer than the vector (step 2 of the proof of lemma 1.67), so \(|\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q) - \Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q_0)| \le 2m\,|Q_0 Q|\). For the error \(\eta > 0\) a band smaller than the numbers \(\rho_0\) and \(\eta/(2m)\) will do. The components of the map \(\Psi\) are continuous at \(Q_0\) (definition 1.68). In figure 4.91 the step \(\vek\Delta\) is not longer than \(2m\) times the step \(h\).

3. The partial derivatives of the map \(\Psi\).

  1. Let \(\mat A = \mat F_0^{-1}\). For \(Q\) with \(|Q_0 Q| < \rho_0\) let \(P = \Psi(Q)\) and \(\vek\Delta = \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). By theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step, applied to every component \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}\) at the point \(P_0\), \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P) - \Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P_0) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\mat F_0)_{\mathrm{ij}}\,\Delta_{\mathrm{j}} + R_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\), written with vectors
    \[\overrightarrow{Q_0 Q} = \mat F_0\,\vek\Delta + \vek R , \qquad \vek R = (R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}}) .\]
  2. We multiply the equality by \(\mat A\). By lemma 1.98 on the linearity of the product with a matrix, lemma 1.100, item 1, and lemma 1.109 \(\mat A\,\overrightarrow{Q_0 Q} = \vek\Delta + \mat A\vek R\). In the figure \(\mat A\,\overrightarrow{Q_0 Q}\) is the grey vector, \(\vek\Delta\) the blue one, and the difference between them the orange remainder. Since \(\vek\Delta = \Psi(Q) - \Psi(Q_0)\), for every component \(k\)
    \[\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q) - \Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q_0) = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} A_{\mathrm{ki}}\,\big(x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q) - x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q_0)\big) + R'_{\mathrm{k}}(Q) , \qquad \vek R' = -\mat A\vek R .\]
  3. The remainder \(R'_{\mathrm{k}}\) is small compared with \(|Q_0 Q|\). We choose \(\eta > 0\) and let \(\eta' = \eta/(12m^2)\). Then the factors \(3m\) and \(2m\) of step 4 together with \(\eta'\) give \(\eta/2\). By the theorem on the change of a field there is for every \(i\) a band \(\delta_{\mathrm{i}} > 0\) such that \(|R_{\mathrm{i}}(P)| \le \eta'\,|P_0 P|\) for \(0 < |P_0 P| < \delta_{\mathrm{i}}\). Let \(\delta'\) be the smallest of the three bands. Let \(0 < |Q_0 Q|\), with \(|Q_0 Q|\) smaller than \(\rho_0\) and than \(\delta'/(2m)\). Then \(P \neq P_0\), because \(\Phi(P) = Q \neq Q_0 = \Phi(P_0)\), and by step 2 of the second part \(|P_0 P| \le 2m\,|Q_0 Q| < \delta'\). Hence \(|R_{\mathrm{i}}(P)| \le \eta'\,|P_0 P|\) for every \(i\). In the figure \(\vek R'\) is the orange remainder, and \(P\) the point to which \(\Psi\) returns \(Q\).
  4. The distance is not larger than the sum of the absolute values of the components (step 3 of the proof of lemma 1.67), so the remainder is \(|\vek R| \le 3\eta'\,|P_0 P|\), small against the step \(\vek\Delta\). By the assumption on the number \(m\) of step 2 of the first part and by step 2 of the second part
    \[|R'_{\mathrm{k}}(Q)| \le |\vek R'| = |\mat A\vek R| \le m\,|\vek R| \le 3m\,\eta'\,|P_0 P| \le 6m^2\,\eta'\,|Q_0 Q| = \tfrac{\eta}{2}\,|Q_0 Q| .\]
  5. Let \(i\) be one of the coordinates and \(h\) a number with \(0 < |h| < \min(\rho_0, \delta'/(2m))\). For \(Q = Q_0 + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\), in the figure the step \(h\) in the direction of the axis \(x\), \(x_{\mathrm{l}}(Q) - x_{\mathrm{l}}(Q_0)\) equals \(h\) for \(\ix{l} = \ix{i}\) and \(0\) otherwise, and \(|Q_0 Q| = |h|\). By step 2
    \[\frac{\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q_0 + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}) - \Psi_{\mathrm{k}}(Q_0)}{h} = A_{\mathrm{ki}} + \frac{R'_{\mathrm{k}}(Q)}{h} ,\]
    and by step 4 \(|R'_{\mathrm{k}}(Q)/h| \le \eta/2 < \eta\). We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily, so by the definition of the limit 1.5 and of the partial derivative 1.26 \(\partial\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q_0)\) exists and equals \(A_{\mathrm{ki}}\). Hence \(\mat F_\Psi(Q_0) = \mat F_\Phi(P_0)^{-1}\), which is the first equality of (4.29).

4. Continuity of the partial derivatives and the Jacobian.

  1. By step 5 of the third part, at every point \(Q\) of \(E\), in the figure \(Q_0\), the partial derivative \(\partial\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q)\) is the element \((k, i)\) of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(\Psi(Q))^{-1}\). By theorem 2.76 this element is a component of the vector product of two columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(\Psi(Q))\), divided by its determinant. The numerator \(p_{\mathrm{ki}}\) is the difference of two products of two elements of the matrix each, the denominator \(d\) the sum of six products of three elements each with signs ((2.70)).
  2. Let a sequence of points \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) of \(E\) converge to \(Q_0\), and let \(P_{\mathrm{n}} = \Psi(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\). By step 3 of the second part and lemma 1.69 on continuity through sequences of points the coordinates of the points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) converge to the coordinates of the point \(P_0\), and by lemma 1.67 \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) converges to \(P_0\). The partial derivatives \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) are continuous at \(P_0\), so by the same lemma on sequences the elements of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P_{\mathrm{n}})\) converge to the elements of the matrix \(\mat F_0\). In the figure these are the points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) and the points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\).
  3. By lemma 1.61 on limit laws for sequences, items 1 to 3, the numerators \(p_{\mathrm{ki}}\) at the points \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) therefore converge to the numerator at \(P_0\), and the determinants \(d_{\mathrm{n}} = J_\Phi(P_{\mathrm{n}})\) to \(d = J_\Phi(P_0) \neq 0\). In the figure the \(P_{\mathrm{n}}\) are the points that approach \(P_0\).
  4. The reciprocals of the determinants converge to \(1/d\). On the number line (figure 4.92) the numbers \(d_{\mathrm{n}}\) approach the number \(d\). By the definition of the limit of a sequence 1.39 with the error \(|d|/2\) there is a place \(N_1\) such that \(|d_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < |d|/2\) for \(n \ge N_1\), so \(d_{\mathrm{n}}\) lies in the band of radius \(|d|/2\) around \(d\), which does not reach zero, and by the triangle inequality for numbers then \(|d_{\mathrm{n}}| > |d|/2\). For \(n \ge N_1\) therefore
    \[\Big| \frac{1}{d_{\mathrm{n}}} - \frac{1}{d} \Big| = \frac{|d - d_{\mathrm{n}}|}{|d_{\mathrm{n}}|\,|d|} \le \frac{2}{d^2}\,|d_{\mathrm{n}} - d| .\]
    For an error \(\eta > 0\) there is by the same definition a place \(N_2\) such that \(|d_{\mathrm{n}} - d| < \eta\,d^2/2\) for \(n \ge N_2\), so \(d_{\mathrm{n}}\) lies in the narrower band. For \(n\) not smaller than \(N_1\) and \(N_2\) therefore \(|1/d_{\mathrm{n}} - 1/d| < \eta\), and \(1/d_{\mathrm{n}}\) converges to \(1/d\).
  5. By lemma 1.61, item 3, the product of the numerator and the reciprocal of the determinant, \(\partial\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q_{\mathrm{n}})\), converges to \(\partial\Psi_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{i}}(Q_0)\). We chose the sequence \((Q_{\mathrm{n}})\) arbitrarily, so by lemma 1.69, second direction, the partial derivative is continuous at \(Q_0\). The set \(E\) is open by the first part, so \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable on \(E\) (definition 4.42). In the figure: as the points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) approach \(Q_0\), the partial derivatives of the map \(\Psi\) at them approach those at \(Q_0\).
  6. By theorem 2.74 on the determinant of a product and lemma 2.73, item 5, \(\det\big(\mat F_\Phi(P)^{-1}\big)\det\mat F_\Phi(P) = \det\mat I = 1\), so \(J_\Psi(\Phi(P)) = 1/J_\Phi(P)\): \(\Phi\) stretches the area of the disc \(B_0\) to the area of its image by \(J_\Phi\), \(\Psi\) brings it back, which is the second equality of (4.29).

5. The plane.

  1. In the plane, like the planes in the figure, the steps are the same, with sums over two coordinates and with \(2 \times 2\) matrices. Lemma 4.46, item 2, gives \(m = 2g\), lemmas 4.50 and 4.47 hold in the plane, the theorem on the change of a field holds for functions of two variables, and in place of theorem 2.76 we use lemma 4.49, by which the elements of the inverse matrix are again elements divided by the determinant. For \(2 \times 2\) matrices \(\det\mat A^\T = A_{\mathrm{xx}} A_{\mathrm{yy}} - A_{\mathrm{yx}} A_{\mathrm{xy}} = \det\mat A\), and the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants by the argument after theorem 2.74.

Source: LEBL2 Thm. 8.5.1 (PDF pp. 51-54), where the theorem is proved with contractions for a neighbourhood of a point with invertible derivative, with the equality \(g'(y) = (f'(x))^{-1}\), and Cor. 8.5.2 (PDF p. 54), that the image of every open set is open. The proof of items 2 and 3 follows the idea of the source (PDF p. 53), the proof of item 1 with the smallest value is not from the sources.

The proof showed where each assumption is needed. Continuous differentiability and \(J_\Phi \neq 0\) gave the lower bound for stretching. The continuity of the derivatives entered in step 1 of lemma 4.50, where we used it to choose the disc around \(P_0\) in which the derivatives differ from those at \(P_0\) by less than \(1/(6m)\), in the example the disc with radius \(1/48\). Without it we could not choose such a disc, and there would be no bound. The condition \(J_\Phi \neq 0\) gave the matrix \(\mat F_0^{-1}\) and with it the number \(m\). The lower bound in the first part kept the images of the points on the surface of the ball far from \(Q_0\), at least \(2\rho\) away, and in the second and third parts bounded the step \(\vek\Delta\) in \(D\) by the step \(h\) in \(E\). The first part did not need the one-to-one property: the image of an open set is open also for a continuously differentiable map with \(J_\Phi \neq 0\) at every point that is not one-to-one. We needed it only for \(\Psi\) to be defined at all. The moves that will come back are finding the smallest value on a closed ball, the zero derivative at an interior extremum, and writing a change with a remainder that is small compared with the step.

What if we drop the one-to-one property? The map of the plane

\[\Phi(s, t) = (s^2 - t^2,\ 2st)\]

has the matrix of partial derivatives with the columns \((2s, 2t)\) and \((-2t, 2s)\) and the Jacobian \(4s^2 + 4t^2\), which is not zero at any point except the origin. On the plane without the origin, which is an open set, \(J_\Phi \neq 0\) therefore. But the map is not one-to-one, because \(\Phi(-s, -t) = \Phi(s, t)\): the points \(P\) and \(-P\), symmetric with respect to the origin, have the same image (figure 4.93). In the figure on the left are the disc around \(P\) and the disc around \(-P\) in the plane of the variables \(s\) and \(t\), and on the right their two images, which coincide. There is therefore no inverse map on the whole image. By lemma 4.50 on the lower bound for stretching, however, \(\Phi\) is one-to-one on a small disc around every point, and on this disc, which is an open set, the theorem holds. On a small disc around every point \(\Phi\) therefore has an inverse map, but not on the whole plane without the origin. For a deformation this would mean that two parts of the material come to the same place, although every small piece by itself deforms admissibly, with \(J > 0\). This is why for a deformation we require the one-to-one property for the whole body, not only for every piece. The example is from LEBL2 (Example 8.5.4, PDF p. 54).

Why do we need \(J_\Phi \neq 0\)? The function \(\Phi(t) = t^3\) is one-to-one on the number line (figure 4.94, left). The difference \(t'^3 - t^3 = (t' - t)(t'^2 + t' t + t^2)\) has the second factor equal to \((t' + t/2)^2 + \tfrac34\,t^2\), which is positive unless both numbers are zero, so \(t'^3 = t^3\) implies \(t' = t\). Its derivative \(3t^2\), however, is zero at \(t = 0\), and the graph is horizontal there. So it carries the piece of the axis \(t\) from \(-0{,}5\) to \(0{,}5\) of length \(1\) to the piece of the axis \(y\) from \(-0{,}125\) to \(0{,}125\) of length only \(0{,}25\). The inverse function \(\Psi\) assigns to the cube \(h^3\) the number \(h\). Its graph is on the right, with the axes exchanged. Between the points \(0\) and \(h^3\) its difference quotient, the slope of the blue secant, has the value

\[\frac{\Psi(h^3) - \Psi(0)}{h^3 - 0} = \frac{h}{h^3} = \frac{1}{h^2} ,\]

for \(h = 0{,}5\) thus \(4\). As \(h\) goes to zero the quotient grows beyond all bounds, so \(\Psi\) has no derivative at \(0\) (LEBL2, PDF p. 54). The function \(\Phi\) shrinks the piece from \(-h\) to \(h\) to \(h^2\) times its length, for \(h = 0{,}5\) to a quarter, for \(h = 0{,}01\) to a ten-thousandth. It thus squeezes a short piece of the line near \(0\) almost into a point, and the reverse rule must therefore stretch it beyond all bounds.

The same figure gives a second view of the equality (4.29), with one variable, where the matrix of partial derivatives is a single number, the slope of the graph. We get the graph of the inverse function from the graph of the function by swapping the axes. At the point \((1, 1)\) of the graph of the function \(\Phi\) the tangent has the slope \(3t^2 = 3\): a step \(0{,}2\) along the axis \(t\) raises it by \(0{,}6\). On the graph of the function \(\Psi\) this is again the point \((1, 1)\), and the same triangle lies on its side: a step \(0{,}6\) along the axis \(y\) raises the tangent by \(0{,}2\), so its slope is \(0{,}2/0{,}6 = 1/3\). Let us check with the difference quotient. Let \(t = \Psi(y)\), so \(y = t^3\). Then

\[\frac{\Psi(y) - \Psi(1)}{y - 1} = \frac{t - 1}{t^3 - 1} = \frac{1}{t^2 + t + 1} ,\]

because \(t^3 - 1 = (t - 1)(t^2 + t + 1)\). For \(y = 1{,}001\) we get \(t = 1{,}000333\) and the quotient \(0{,}3332\), close to \(1/3\). The slope of the inverse function is the reciprocal of the slope of the function, and the reciprocal of the number \(3\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix with the single element \(3\). This view adds what is hard to see at a glance with matrices: where the graph of the function is flat, the graph of the inverse function is steep, and where the slope is zero, as at the point \(0\), there is no reciprocal. This is the condition \(J_\Phi \neq 0\) of the theorem.

Let us test the theorem on the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s, t + s^2)\). It is one-to-one on the whole plane. From \((s, t + s^2) = (s', t' + s'^2)\) follows \(s = s'\) and then \(t = t'\). The Jacobian is \(1\) everywhere. The inverse map is

\[\Psi(x, y) = (x,\ y - x^2) ,\]

because \(\Psi(\Phi(s, t)) = (s, t + s^2 - s^2) = (s, t)\). Its matrix of partial derivatives at the point \(\Phi(s, t)\), where \(x = s\), is

\[\mat F_\Psi\big(\Phi(s, t)\big) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2s & 1 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

and by lemma 4.49, with the elements \(1\), \(0\), \(2s\) and \(1\) and the determinant \(1\), \(\mat F_\Phi(s, t)^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -2s & 1 \end{bmatrix}\), the same matrix, as (4.29) says. Also \(J_\Psi = 1 = 1/J_\Phi\). At the point of figure 4.91, where \(s = 0{,}5\), this matrix sends the step \(h = 0{,}2\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) to the vector with the components \(0{,}2\) and \(-0{,}2\), which we compared there with the true step \(\vek\Delta\).

Now the hanging bar, for which we do not know \(\Psi\). We have shown that \(\Phi\) is one-to-one on the set \(D\) of the interior points of the bar (figure 4.87). The Jacobian is positive on \(D\). All nine partial derivatives of the displacements are at most \(g = 2aL = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\) in absolute value, so by lemma 2.77 on the change of volume, item 2, \(J\) differs from \(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}} = 1 + 2a\,(L - x) - 2 \cdot 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) = 1 + 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\) by at most \(6g^2 + 6g^3 < 10^{-10}\), and \(J > 1 - 10^{-10} > 0\). The theorem therefore tells us that the image \(E = \Phi(D)\) is an open set, that the inverse map \(\Psi\), which assigns to a point after loading its place before loading, is continuously differentiable on \(E\), and that its matrix of partial derivatives at the point \(\Phi(P)\) is the matrix \(\mat F(P)^{-1}\). For the point \(P\) at the depth \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm from the axis in the plane \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) and hence \(1\) mm below the surface, by theorem 2.76, computed with SymPy,

\[\mat F(P)^{-1} - \mat I = \begin{bmatrix} -1{,}951996 \cdot 10^{-6} & 4{,}684794 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 \\ -4{,}684794 \cdot 10^{-10} & 5{,}856003 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5{,}856003 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

Let us check with a difference quotient. We found the point \(Q\) whose image is \(h\) lower than the image of the point \(P\), \(\Phi(Q) = \Phi(P) + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), numerically, by solving the three equations with a program to 40 decimal places. The quotient \((\Psi_{\mathrm{x}}(\Phi(P) + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) - \Psi_{\mathrm{x}}(\Phi(P)))/h - 1\) is \(-1{,}951801 \cdot 10^{-6}\) for \(h = 1\) mm and \(-1{,}951977 \cdot 10^{-6}\) for \(h = 0{,}1\) mm. The differences from the element \(-1{,}951996 \cdot 10^{-6}\) above are \(1{,}95 \cdot 10^{-10}\) and \(1{,}95 \cdot 10^{-11}\), ten times smaller for a ten times shorter step. The inverse matrix is almost \(\mat I - \mat H\), the identity matrix minus the displacement gradient: the element \(-H_{\mathrm{xx}} = -1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) differs from the element above by \(3{,}8 \cdot 10^{-12}\), which is \(H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\). This agrees with intuition: the displacement back is almost the opposite displacement, and for the sheared cube \(\mat I - \mat H\) was even exactly the inverse matrix.

With the inverse map and the chain rule we have everything we need about maps. The next step is the volume of an image, first under a map that is multiplication by a matrix.

4.3.3 Volume under a linear map

In section 2.10.2 we saw that a \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat A\) maps the unit cube onto the parallelepiped spanned by its columns, and that this parallelepiped has the volume \(|\det\mat A|\) (lemma 2.69). There we took the volume of a parallelepiped from school, as the area of the base times the height. Now we have an exact notion of volume for every set with volume (definition 4.27): the volume is the limit of the total volume of those cells of a grid that lie in the set. Two questions therefore arise. Does this notion give the same number for a parallelepiped as school does? And does a matrix with a nonzero determinant multiply the volume of every set with volume, for instance of the cross section of the round bar, by the same number \(|\det\mat A|\)?

We need the answer in section 4.3.4, where we will turn an integral over the image of a set into an integral over the set itself. There we will replace a map near each point by its linear part, just as in theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step we replaced the difference of displacements by the product of the displacement gradient and the step. A small cube then goes almost onto a parallelepiped, and we will compare its volume after the map with the volume of this parallelepiped. So we must know the volume of the image under a linear map exactly, as the volume of a set with volume.

The route is this. First we show that every matrix with a nonzero determinant is a product of matrices of three simple kinds. Then we show that the image of such a set has a volume too, and we do it at once for every continuously differentiable one-to-one map with a nonzero Jacobian, because we will need this in the next section as well. Finally we compute the volume of the image under a linear map: directly for the simple matrices, and through the product for the others.

In section 1.16.3 we met the matrices \(\mat D\) and \(\mat G\). The first doubles the component \(x\) of a vector, the second adds the component \(z\) to the component \(x\). Each of them does a single simple thing to a vector. There are three kinds of such simple things.

Definition 4.52 Elementary matrix (elementarna matrika)

Let \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) be two different indices among \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). An elementary matrix (elementarna matrika) of size \(3 \times 3\) is a matrix of one of three kinds:

  1. swap of the coordinates \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\): the matrix obtained from the identity matrix \(\mat I\) (definition 1.108) by swapping its rows \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\),
  2. multiplication of the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) by a number \(c \neq 0\): the matrix obtained from \(\mat I\) by replacing the element \(1\) in the place \(ii\) by \(c\),
  3. addition of \(k\) times the coordinate \(\ix{j}\) to the coordinate \(\ix{i}\), where \(k\) is any number: the matrix obtained from \(\mat I\) by replacing the element \(0\) in the place \(ij\) by \(k\).

An elementary matrix of size \(2 \times 2\) is a matrix of the same three kinds, with the indices \(x\) and \(y\).

Source: LEBL2 §8.2 (PDF pp. 30-31), for \(n \times n\) matrices.

The names say what the matrix does to a vector. For \(\ix{i} = x\) and \(\ix{j} = z\) the matrices of the three kinds are

\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \begin{bmatrix} c & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

and by (1.39) they map the vector \((v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) to the vectors \((v_{\mathrm{z}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{x}})\), \((c\,v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) and \((v_{\mathrm{x}} + k\,v_{\mathrm{z}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\). The matrix \(\mat D\) of section 1.16.3 is therefore an elementary matrix of the second kind with \(c = 2\), the matrix \(\mat G\) an elementary matrix of the third kind with \(k = 1\), and the deformation gradient of the sheared cube, which has the number \(0{,}001\) in the place \(xz\), is also an elementary matrix of the third kind. Geometrically the second kind stretches or compresses a body along one axis, and for \(c < 0\) also mirrors it, the third kind shears it like a deck of cards, and the first mirrors it in the plane in which the coordinates \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) are equal. All three are shown in figure 4.95. The next lemma says that these three kinds are enough for every matrix with a nonzero determinant.

The same is seen on the rows of a matrix \(\mat M\) with three rows (figure 4.96). In each panel the matrix \(\mat E\) is on the left, then the matrix \(\mat M\) with row \(x\) in blue, row \(z\) in orange and row \(y\) in grey, and on the right the product \(\mat E\mat M\). In a swap rows \(x\) and \(z\) change places, in a multiplication row \(x\) is multiplied by \(c\), in an addition \(k\) times row \(z\) is added to row \(x\), and row \(y\) stays. The bottom row shows how each of these operations is undone by an elementary matrix of the same kind.

For the fourth item of the lemma we need elimination, which turns a matrix into the identity matrix (figure 4.97). We bring column \(x\) to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), then column \(y\) to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and column \(z\) to \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), each time with a one on the diagonal and zeros in the other rows. If there is a zero on the diagonal, we swap rows. The procedure does not stop, because a nonzero determinant prevents it (figure 4.98): a zero column, two columns on one line or a third column in the plane of the first two give a flat parallelepiped with volume zero, so with determinant zero.

Lemma 4.53 Factorization into elementary matrices (razcep na preproste matrike)

Let \(\mat E\) be an elementary matrix of size \(3 \times 3\) (definition 4.52), with the indices \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\).

  1. For every matrix \(\mat M\) with three rows, \(\mat E\mat M\) is the matrix obtained from \(\mat M\) by the same operation on the rows: for a swap we swap the rows \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\), for a multiplication we multiply the row \(\ix{i}\) by \(c\), for an addition we add \(k\) times the row \(\ix{j}\) to the row \(\ix{i}\). In particular, for a vector \(\vek v\) written as a column, \(\mat E\vek v\) is the vector obtained from \(\vek v\) by swapping the components \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{j}}\), multiplying the component \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) by \(c\), or adding \(k\,v_{\mathrm{j}}\) to the component \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\), respectively.
  2. The determinant of a swap is \(-1\), the determinant of a multiplication of a coordinate by \(c\) is \(c\), the determinant of an addition is \(1\).
  3. The matrix \(\mat E\) has an inverse matrix, which is an elementary matrix of the same kind with the same indices: a swap, a multiplication by \(1/c\), or an addition of \((-k)\) times, respectively.
  4. Every \(3 \times 3\) matrix \(\mat A\) with \(\det\mat A \neq 0\) is a product of finitely many elementary matrices, \(\mat A = \mat E_1\,\mat E_2 \cdots \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\).

The same holds for matrices of size \(2 \times 2\).

Proof

We must show four items. The first three follow from the definition of the matrix product. We prove the fourth by elimination: step by step we turn the matrix \(\mat A\) into the identity matrix by multiplying it by elementary matrices from the left.

1. Action on the rows.

  1. By definition 1.99 the element in row \(\ix{l}\) and column \(\ix{q}\) of the matrix \(\mat E\mat M\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{m}} E_{\mathrm{lm}} M_{\mathrm{mq}}\). Row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is therefore the sum of the rows of \(\mat M\) multiplied by the elements of row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat E\): row \(\ix{m}\) of \(\mat M\) is multiplied by \(E_{\mathrm{lm}}\).
  2. A row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat E\) that equals row \(\ix{l}\) of the identity matrix has a single nonzero element, \(1\) in column \(\ix{l}\). By step 1 row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is therefore row \(\ix{l}\) of \(\mat M\). So it is, for a swap, with all rows except \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\), and for the other two kinds with all rows except \(\ix{i}\).
  3. Swap. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) is row \(\ix{j}\) of the identity matrix, with the element \(1\) in column \(\ix{j}\), so by step 1 row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is row \(\ix{j}\) of \(\mat M\). In the same way row \(\ix{j}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat M\).
  4. Multiplication. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) has a single nonzero element, \(c\) in column \(\ix{i}\), so row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat M\) multiplied by \(c\).
  5. Addition. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) has the nonzero elements \(1\) in column \(\ix{i}\) and \(k\) in column \(\ix{j}\), so row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\mat M\) is the sum of row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat M\) and \(k\) times its row \(\ix{j}\).
  6. A vector \(\vek v\) written as a column is a matrix with one column whose rows are its components. Steps 2 to 5 give for it the claim about the vector \(\mat E\vek v\).

2. Determinants.

  1. Swap. The identity matrix is symmetric, so swapping its rows \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) gives the same matrix as swapping its columns \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\): in both cases we get the matrix with ones in the places \(ij\) and \(ji\), with ones on the diagonal in the other rows and with zeros elsewhere. By items 4 and 5 of lemma 2.73 on the properties of the determinant, \(\det\mat E = -\det\mat I = -1\).
  2. Multiplication. Column \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) is \(c\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\), the other columns are columns of the identity matrix. By linearity in column \(\ix{i}\) (item 2 of the same lemma) and item 5, \(\det\mat E = c\det\mat I = c\).
  3. Addition. The element \(k\) in the place \(ij\) lies in column \(\ix{j}\), which is therefore \(\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} + k\,\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\), while the other columns are columns of the identity matrix. By linearity in column \(\ix{j}\), \(\det\mat E\) is the sum of the number \(\det\mat I = 1\) and \(k\) times the determinant of the matrix that has the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\) in column \(\ix{j}\). This matrix has equal columns \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\), so by item 3 of the same lemma its determinant is zero. Therefore \(\det\mat E = 1\).

3. Inverse matrix.

  1. Let \(\mat E'\) be the elementary matrix of the same kind with the same indices, a swap, a multiplication by \(1/c\), or an addition of \((-k)\) times, respectively. By the first item we get \(\mat E'\mat E\) by doing the operation of \(\mat E'\) on the rows of \(\mat E\).
  2. Swap. The matrix \(\mat E\) is the identity matrix with the rows \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) swapped. When we swap them back, we get \(\mat I\).
  3. Multiplication. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) has the element \(c\) on the diagonal. When we multiply it by \(1/c\), we get row \(\ix{i}\) of the identity matrix, and the other rows already are rows of the identity matrix.
  4. Addition. Row \(\ix{i}\) of \(\mat E\) is the sum of row \(\ix{i}\) of the identity matrix and \(k\) times row \(\ix{j}\) of the identity matrix, while row \(\ix{j}\) of \(\mat E\) is row \(\ix{j}\) of the identity matrix, because \(\ix{j} \neq \ix{i}\). When we add \((-k)\) times row \(\ix{j}\) to row \(\ix{i}\), we get row \(\ix{i}\) of the identity matrix.
  5. In all three cases therefore \(\mat E'\mat E = \mat I\). The matrix \(\mat E\) is the elementary matrix of the same kind for \(\mat E'\), with the reciprocal of the number \(1/c\) or with the opposite number of \(-k\), so by steps 2 to 4 with the roles exchanged also \(\mat E\mat E' = \mat I\). By definition 1.110, \(\mat E'\) is the inverse matrix of \(\mat E\).

4. Factorization.

  1. We will multiply the matrix \(\mat A\) by elementary matrices from the left, one after another. We denote the current matrix after each step by \(\mat B\). It has the form \(\mat E_{\mathrm{s}} \cdots \mat E_1\,\mat A\), so by theorem 2.74 on the determinant of a product and the second item, \(\det\mat B = \det\mat E_{\mathrm{s}} \cdots \det\mat E_1\,\det\mat A\), a product of nonzero numbers, which is not zero. What multiplication by an elementary matrix does to the rows of \(\mat B\) is said by the first item.
  2. Column \(x\). Column \(x\) of \(\mat B\) is not the zero vector. If it were, then by linearity in the first column (item 2 of lemma 2.73), used with the number \(0\), the determinant would be \(\det\mat B = \det(0 \cdot \vek 0, \vek b, \vek c) = 0 \cdot \det(\vek 0, \vek b, \vek c) = 0\), where \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) are the other two columns. So some element \(B_{\mathrm{lx}}\) is not zero. If \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0\), we multiply by the swap of the coordinates \(x\) and \(\ix{l}\), and then \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} \neq 0\).
  3. We multiply by the multiplication of the coordinate \(x\) by the number \(1/B_{\mathrm{xx}}\). Then \(B_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\).
  4. We multiply by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{yx}})\) times the coordinate \(x\) to the coordinate \(y\) and then by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{zx}})\) times the coordinate \(x\) to the coordinate \(z\). The rows \(y\) and \(z\) get \(-B_{\mathrm{yx}}\) times and \(-B_{\mathrm{zx}}\) times the row \(x\), which has the element \(1\) in column \(x\), so then \(B_{\mathrm{yx}} = B_{\mathrm{zx}} = 0\). Column \(x\) is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\).
  5. Column \(y\). The elements \(B_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(B_{\mathrm{zy}}\) are not both zero. If they were, column \(y\) would be \(B_{\mathrm{xy}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and by linearity in the second column and item 3 of lemma 2.73 we would have \(\det\mat B = B_{\mathrm{xy}}\det(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek c) = 0\). If \(B_{\mathrm{yy}} = 0\), we multiply by the swap of the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\). The rows \(y\) and \(z\) have zeros in column \(x\), so column \(x\) remains \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and then \(B_{\mathrm{yy}} \neq 0\).
  6. We multiply by the multiplication of the coordinate \(y\) by the number \(1/B_{\mathrm{yy}}\), then by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{xy}})\) times the coordinate \(y\) to the coordinate \(x\) and by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{zy}})\) times the coordinate \(y\) to the coordinate \(z\). Row \(y\) has a zero in column \(x\), so column \(x\) remains \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), while column \(y\) becomes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), as in steps 3 and 4.
  7. Column \(z\). We have \(B_{\mathrm{zz}} \neq 0\). Otherwise column \(z\) would be \(B_{\mathrm{xz}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + B_{\mathrm{yz}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), and by linearity in the third column and item 3 of the same lemma we would have \(\det\mat B = B_{\mathrm{xz}}\det(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) + B_{\mathrm{yz}}\det(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = 0\). We multiply by the multiplication of the coordinate \(z\) by the number \(1/B_{\mathrm{zz}}\), then by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{xz}})\) times the coordinate \(z\) to the coordinate \(x\) and by the addition of \((-B_{\mathrm{yz}})\) times the coordinate \(z\) to the coordinate \(y\). Row \(z\) has zeros in the columns \(x\) and \(y\), so these two columns remain, while column \(z\) becomes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). Now \(\mat B = \mat I\).
  8. We have obtained elementary matrices \(\mat E_1, \dots, \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\) with \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}} \cdots \mat E_1\,\mat A = \mat I\). By the third item \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\) has an inverse matrix \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\). We multiply both sides by it from the left. By item 2 of lemma 1.100 on the properties of the matrix product we may group the factors as we like, and \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\mat E_{\mathrm{m}} = \mat I\), so we get \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}-1} \cdots \mat E_1\,\mat A = \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\). In the same way we remove \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}-1}\), then \(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}-2}\), and finally \(\mat E_1\). We get \(\mat A = \mat E_1^{-1}\,\mat E_2^{-1} \cdots \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}^{-1}\), by the third item a product of elementary matrices.
  9. For matrices of size \(2 \times 2\) the steps are the same, with the columns \(x\) and \(y\), with two rows and with the determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, for which the same properties hold. The determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix is namely the determinant of the \(3 \times 3\) matrix that has the \(2 \times 2\) matrix in the rows and columns \(x\) and \(y\), the number \(1\) at the place \(zz\) and zeros elsewhere in the row and the column \(z\) (section 2.10.2), and row operations on the \(2 \times 2\) matrix are the same operations on the bigger matrix.

Source: LEBL2 §8.2 (PDF pp. 30-31): the kinds of elementary matrices, their determinants and Prop. 8.2.11, whose proof the source leaves to the reader. KREYSZIG §7.3 (PDF pp. 298-303) for elimination in systems of linear equations. The proof is not from the sources.

The proof is the elimination that KREYSZIG uses to solve systems of linear equations (Gauss elimination, Gaussovo izločanje, KREYSZIG §7.3, PDF p. 298). The nonzero determinant made sure that the procedure never gets stuck: in every column we found a nonzero element by which we divided. Let us try it on the turned plate of section 2.10.5. A thin square plate in the plane of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) turns as a whole about the axis \(z\) with the pair \(c = 0{,}6\), \(s = 0{,}8\), for which \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\), and in the plane of the plate its deformation gradient is the \(2 \times 2\) matrix

\[\mat R = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & -0{,}8 \\ 0{,}8 & 0{,}6 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The elimination has four steps, which figure 4.99 shows in reverse order.

  1. The element \(R_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}6\) is not zero. We multiply the row \(x\) by \(1/0{,}6 = 5/3\) and get the rows \((1, -\tfrac43)\) and \((0{,}8,\ 0{,}6)\).
  2. We add \((-0{,}8)\) times the row \(x\) to the row \(y\). We get \((0,\ 0{,}6 + 0{,}8 \cdot \tfrac43) = (0, \tfrac53)\).
  3. We multiply the row \(y\) by \(\tfrac35\) and get \((0, 1)\).
  4. We add \(\tfrac43\) times the row \(y\) to the row \(x\) and get \((1, 0)\).

The inverse matrices of these four steps, in the reverse order, give the factorization, which we checked with SymPy:

\[\mat R = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0{,}8 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac53 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\tfrac43 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

As a rule that assigns a vector to a vector, the rightmost factor acts first (figure 4.99). We first shear the square by adding \(-\tfrac43\) times the coordinate \(y\) to the coordinate \(x\), then stretch it along the axis \(y\) to \(\tfrac53\) times its height, then shear it by adding \(0{,}8\) times the coordinate \(x\) to the coordinate \(y\), and finally compress it along the axis \(x\) to \(0{,}6\) times its width. We start from the square. The areas are, in turn, \(1\), \(1\), \(\tfrac53\), \(\tfrac53\) and \(1\), and the determinants of the factors give \(0{,}6 \cdot 1 \cdot \tfrac53 \cdot 1 = 1 = \det\mat R\), as theorem 2.74 on the determinant of a product demands for \(2 \times 2\) matrices. A rotation, which stretches nothing, is thus made of two shears and two stretches that cancel. For the matrix \(\mat A\) of figure 2.150, with the columns \((1, 1, 2)\), \((2, 0, 0)\), \((1, 3, 0)\) and with the determinant \(12\), the elimination has eight steps, if we leave out the multiplication of a row by the number \(1\), which does not change the matrix. Two are multiplications of rows by \(-\tfrac12\) and by \(-\tfrac16\), six are additions. The inverse matrices of the multiplications have the determinants \(-2\) and \(-6\), those of the additions the determinant \(1\), and \((-2) \cdot (-6) = 12\).

Now to the volume of the image. Before we compute it, we must make sure that the image has a volume at all when the set we map has one. A set with volume is closed and bounded, and its boundary has zero volume (definition 4.27). Does its image have the same properties? The answer holds for every map that is continuously differentiable and one-to-one and has a nonzero Jacobian at every point, as described by theorem 4.51 on the inverse map, so we prove it at once for such maps. The idea has two parts. Every boundary point of the image is the image of a boundary point, because the map takes interior points to interior points and back. A set of zero volume stays such, because a map with bounded partial derivatives takes a small cube to a set that a cube with an edge proportional to the edge of the first covers. First the interior points. Let us draw them in the plane, with discs instead of balls (figure 4.100). At the top left is the set \(Y\) with an interior point \(P\) and the blue disc \(B\) around it, which lies entirely in \(Y\). The map \(\Phi\) takes the set \(Y\) to the set \(\Phi(Y)\) at the top right, the point \(P\) to the point \(\Phi(P)\), and the disc \(B\) to the orange set \(\Phi(B)\). This is no longer a disc, but it is open, and \(\Phi(P)\) lies in it, so \(\Phi(P)\) is an interior point of the image. Below is the same way back: the disc \(B'\) around \(\Phi(P)\) is taken by the inverse map \(\Psi\) to the orange open set \(\Psi(B')\) around \(P\). The boundary point \(P_{\mathrm{r}}\) goes to the point \(T\) on the boundary of the image: every disc around \(T\), the dashed one too, reaches out of \(\Phi(Y)\).

Item 3 of the lemma is shown in figure 4.101. At the top are three neighbouring cells in a row along the axis \(x\), the first two with a common side. At the bottom are their images, which touch only along the image of the common side. An interior point of the middle cell has its image only in the image of the middle cell, not in the image of the neighbour.

Lemma 4.54 Interior and boundary points of an image (notranje in robne točke slike)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(D\), with \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\) for every point \(P \in D\). Let \(Y\) be a set of points in \(D\).

  1. A point \(P \in Y\) is an interior point of the set \(Y\) if and only if \(\Phi(P)\) is an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\).
  2. If \(Y\) is closed and bounded (definition 1.75), every boundary point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\) (definition 4.23) is the image of some boundary point of the set \(Y\).
  3. If \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are sets of points in \(D\) and no interior point of either of them lies in the other, then also no interior point of either of the sets \(\Phi(Y_1)\) and \(\Phi(Y_2)\) lies in the other.

The same holds in the plane.

Proof

We must show three items. We get the first from theorem 4.51 on the inverse map, which says that \(\Phi\) and its inverse map \(\Psi\) take open sets to open sets. The other two follow from the first.

1. Interior points.

  1. Let \(P\) be an interior point of the set \(Y\). Then there is \(r > 0\) such that the ball \(B\) with centre \(P\) and radius \(r\), the set of points closer to \(P\) than \(r\) (section 1.12.6), lies in \(Y\).
  2. The ball \(B\) is open. For a point \(S \in B\) we have \(r - |PS| > 0\), and for every point \(T\) with \(|ST| < r - |PS|\) corollary 2.16 on the triangle inequality for vectors, item 2, gives \(|PT| \le |PS| + |ST| < r\), so \(T\) lies in \(B\).
  3. The ball \(B\) lies in \(Y \subseteq D\). By theorem 4.51, item 1, \(\Phi(B)\) is an open set. It contains \(\Phi(P)\) and lies in \(\Phi(Y)\), so all points close enough to \(\Phi(P)\) are in \(\Phi(Y)\). The point \(\Phi(P)\) is an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\).
  4. Conversely, let \(\Phi(P)\) be an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\), and let \(B'\) be a ball with centre \(\Phi(P)\) that lies in \(\Phi(Y)\). By step 2 it is open.
  5. Let \(E = \Phi(D)\) and let \(\Psi\) be the inverse map (definition 4.45), for which \(\Psi(\Phi(Q)) = Q\) for every \(Q \in D\) and \(\Phi(\Psi(T)) = T\) for every \(T \in E\). By theorem 4.51, \(E\) is open, \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable on \(E\) and \(J_\Psi(\Phi(Q)) = 1/J_\Phi(Q) \neq 0\). The map \(\Psi\) is one-to-one on \(E\): from \(\Psi(T_1) = \Psi(T_2)\) it follows that \(T_1 = \Phi(\Psi(T_1)) = \Phi(\Psi(T_2)) = T_2\).
  6. Theorem 4.51, item 1, applied to \(\Psi\) and the open set \(B' \subseteq \Phi(Y) \subseteq E\), says that \(\Psi(B')\) is an open set. It contains \(\Psi(\Phi(P)) = P\). Each of its points is \(\Psi(T)\) for some \(T \in B' \subseteq \Phi(Y)\), so \(T = \Phi(Q)\) with \(Q \in Y\), and \(\Psi(T) = Q\) lies in \(Y\). Around \(P\) there is therefore a ball that lies in \(\Psi(B') \subseteq Y\), and \(P\) is an interior point of the set \(Y\).

2. Boundary points.

  1. The map \(\Phi\) is continuous on \(Y\) (lemma 1.92 for each component), so by lemma 4.48 the set \(\Phi(Y)\) is closed and bounded.
  2. Let \(T\) be a boundary point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\). By lemma 4.24, item 1, it lies in \(\Phi(Y)\), so \(T = \Phi(P)\) for some point \(P \in Y\).
  3. If \(P\) were an interior point of the set \(Y\), then by the first item \(T\) would be an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y)\). Then some ball around \(T\) would lie in \(\Phi(Y)\) and would contain no point outside \(\Phi(Y)\), which contradicts \(T\) being a boundary point.
  4. The point \(P\) is therefore not an interior point of the set \(Y\). By lemma 4.24, item 2, it is therefore a boundary point of the set \(Y\), and \(T = \Phi(P)\).

3. Overlapping.

  1. Let \(T\) be an interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y_1)\) that lies in \(\Phi(Y_2)\). Then \(T = \Phi(P_1)\) with \(P_1 \in Y_1\) and \(T = \Phi(P_2)\) with \(P_2 \in Y_2\).
  2. The map \(\Phi\) is one-to-one, so \(P_1 = P_2\). This point lies in \(Y_2\), and by the first item it is an interior point of the set \(Y_1\). This contradicts the assumption.
  3. With the roles of the sets \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) exchanged we show that also no interior point of the set \(\Phi(Y_2)\) lies in \(\Phi(Y_1)\).
  4. In the plane the steps are the same, with discs instead of balls and with the inverse function theorem in the plane.

Source: LEBL2 proves item 2 in the proof of Prop. 10.5.9 (PDF pp. 126-127), with sequences and the inverse function theorem, and Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF p. 134) uses it where it needs that the image of a set with volume is again such a set. Items 1 and 3 and the proof with open images are not from the source.

The lemma says that a map that has an inverse map with the same properties keeps the difference between the inside and the boundary. An interior point stays interior, because a small ball around it goes to an open set, and a boundary point cannot become interior, because the inverse map would then return it to the inside. Without the one-to-one property the third item fails. A map that takes two separate discs to the same set, such as the one we met in section 4.3.2 (figure 4.93), turns two sets without common points into two sets that overlap.

For the second part of the idea we need bounds for the partial derivatives that hold also a little outside the set, since the cubes that cover the boundary reach beyond it. Figure 4.102 shows the idea, drawn in the plane, with squares instead of cubes. On the left is the curve \(Z\), a set of zero area, in a grid of squares with the edge \(h\). The light blue squares that contain a point of the curve cover it and reach to both sides of the curve. In one of them, the square \(C\), we choose a point \(P_{\mathrm{C}}\) of the curve. Every other point \(Q\) of the curve in \(C\) is at most the diagonal of the square, \(\sqrt2\,h\), away from it. In the middle, magnified, is what the map \(\Phi\), whose partial derivatives are at most \(M\) in absolute value, makes of the square \(C\): the orange image of the square with the image of the piece of the curve and the points \(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{C}})\) and \(\Phi(Q)\). The next lemma will show that such a map in the plane increases distances at most \(2M\) times. The point \(\Phi(Q)\) therefore lies in the dashed circle of radius \(2\sqrt2\,M h\) around \(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{C}})\) and so in the square \(C'\) with the edge \(4\sqrt2\,M h\). The area of the square \(C'\) is \(32\,M^2\) times the area of the square \(C\), the same for every \(h\). If the blue squares have a small total area, so do the squares \(C'\), which cover the image of the curve. We explain the right part of the figure before lemma 4.56.

The bounds for the cubes near the set \(K\) are shown in figure 4.103. The closed bounded set \(K\) is surrounded by the band \(K_\rho\) of width \(\rho\), and the band bounded by \(\delta_0\) is still wider. In the band the partial derivatives are bounded by \(M\). For a point \(P\) of the set and a point \(Q\) in the band on the segment between them the images are at most \(3M\,|PQ|\) apart.

Lemma 4.55 Bounded stretching near a closed bounded set (omejeno raztezanje ob zaprti omejeni množici)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 4.42), and \(K\) a nonempty closed and bounded set of points in \(D\). Then there are numbers \(\rho > 0\) and \(M > 0\) with the following properties.

  1. The set \(K_\rho\) of all points at a distance of at most \(\rho\) from some point of the set \(K\) is closed and bounded and lies in \(D\).
  2. For every point \(Q \in K_\rho\) and all indices \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\), \(|\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(Q)| \le M\).
  3. For every point \(P \in K\) and every point \(Q\) with \(|PQ| \le \rho\), \(|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| \le 3M\,|PQ|\).

The same holds in the plane, with \(2M\) instead of \(3M\).

Proof

We must show three items. We get the radius \(\rho\) from lemma 4.38 on the neighbourhood of a closed bounded set, the bound \(M\) from the extreme value theorem, and item 3 from the bound for stretching along a segment.

  1. By lemma 4.38 there is \(\delta_0 > 0\) such that every point at a distance less than \(\delta_0\) from some point of the set \(K\) lies in \(D\). Let \(\rho = \delta_0/2\). The points of the set \(K_\rho\) are at a distance of at most \(\rho < \delta_0\) from some point of \(K\), so they lie in \(D\).
  2. Boundedness. The set \(K\) is bounded, so there is \(R\) with \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\) for every \(P \in K\). For \(Q \in K_\rho\) and a point \(P \in K\) with \(|PQ| \le \rho\), corollary 2.16 on the triangle inequality for vectors, item 2, gives \(|\overrightarrow{OQ}| \le |\overrightarrow{OP}| + |PQ| \le R + \rho\).
  3. Closedness. Let a sequence of points \(Q_{\mathrm{n}}\) of \(K_\rho\) converge to a point \(Q\), and let \(P_{\mathrm{n}} \in K\) be a point with \(|P_{\mathrm{n}} Q_{\mathrm{n}}| \le \rho\). The set \(K\) is bounded, so by lemma 1.78 the sequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}})\) has a subsequence \((P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}})\) that converges to some point \(P\). The set \(K\) is closed, so \(P \in K\).
  4. By the same item of the same corollary, used twice,
    \[|PQ| \le |P P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}| + |P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}| + |Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} Q| \le |P P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}| + \rho + |Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} Q| .\]
    The sequences \(|P P_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}}|\) and \(|Q_{\mathrm{n}_\mathrm{k}} Q|\) converge to \(0\), the first by step 3, the second by lemma 1.55 on the limit of a subsequence. By lemma 1.61 on limit laws for sequences, item 1, the right side converges to \(\rho\), and by lemma 1.49, that limits preserve non-strict inequalities, item 1, with the constant sequence \(|PQ|\) on the left, \(|PQ| \le \rho\). The point \(Q\) lies in \(K_\rho\), which is therefore closed. 5. The bound \(M\). Each of the nine partial derivatives \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) is continuous on \(D\), so on \(K_\rho\). By theorem 1.79, the extreme value theorem in space, it attains on \(K_\rho\) a greatest value \(M_{\mathrm{ij}}\) and a least value \(m_{\mathrm{ij}}\), so \(|\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}| \le |M_{\mathrm{ij}}| + |m_{\mathrm{ij}}|\) on \(K_\rho\). Let \(M\) be \(1\) more than the largest of these nine numbers. Then \(M > 0\) and item 2 holds.
  5. Item 3. Let \(P \in K\) and \(|PQ| \le \rho\). The points of the segment from \(P\) to \(Q\) are \(P + t\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\) with \(t \in [0, 1]\), and they are at the distance \(t\,|PQ| \le \rho\) from \(P\), so they lie in \(K_\rho\), where all partial derivatives are at most \(M\) in absolute value. By lemma 4.47 on bounded derivatives and distances, \(|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| \le 3M\,|PQ|\).
  6. In the plane the steps are the same, with discs instead of balls, with lemma 4.38 in the plane, whose proof is the same, and with lemma 4.47 in the plane, which gives \(2M\).

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. LEBL2 in the proof of Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF p. 135) uses the same idea with the Lebesgue covering lemma and with a bound for the derivative.

To cover the boundary we need cubes, not just boxes. A box with the edges \(1\) mm, \(1\) mm and \(0{,}001\) mm goes, under a map that increases distances at most three times, to a set that perhaps only a cube with an edge of a few millimetres covers. The volume of such a cube is several thousand times the volume of the box, which is \(0{,}001\) mm³. The right part of figure 4.102 shows the same in the plane, less exaggerated. The thin rectangle with the sides \(2\) and \(0{,}14\) and the area \(0{,}28\) is turned by \(45^\circ\) and stretched to \(1{,}5\) times by the map. The smallest square with sides along the axes that covers the image has the edge \(2{,}27\) and the area \(5{,}15\), about \(18\) times the area of the rectangle. For a cube with the edge \(h\), however, the image lies in a cube with an edge proportional to \(h\), and the two volumes differ only by a constant factor. We get cubes from a grid in which all pieces of the partitions are equally long. Lemma 4.29, item 1, says that the cells of such a grid that contain a point of a set of zero volume cover this set, for a fine enough grid, with an arbitrarily small total volume.

Now let us show that the image has a volume too.

Lemma 4.56 Image of a set with volume (slika množice s prostornino)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 4.42).

  1. If \(Z\) is a set of zero volume (definition 4.25) that lies in some closed and bounded set \(K \subseteq D\), then \(\Phi(Z)\) is also a set of zero volume.
  2. If moreover \(\Phi\) is one-to-one on \(D\) and \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\) for every point \(P \in D\), then for every set with volume \(W \subseteq D\) (definition 4.27) also \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume.

The same holds in the plane, with area instead of volume.

Proof

We must show both items. In the first we replace every cube of the cover by a cube around the image of one of its points. In the second we use the first on the boundary of the set \(W\). Figure 4.102 shows the steps of the first item in the plane, where \(2\sqrt2\,M h\) and \(4\sqrt2\,M h\) stand in place of the distance \(3\sqrt3\,M h\) and the edge \(6\sqrt3\,M h\).

1. Set of zero volume.

  1. If \(Z\) is empty, so is \(\Phi(Z)\). Let it be nonempty. By lemma 4.55 for the set \(K\) there are \(\rho > 0\) and \(M > 0\) such that \(|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P)| \le 3M\,|PQ|\) for every \(P \in K\) and every \(Q\) with \(|PQ| \le \rho\).
  2. We choose \(\eta > 0\) and let \(\eta' = \eta/(648\sqrt3\,M^3)\). By lemma 4.29, item 1, there is \(\delta > 0\) such that for every grid of a box with pieces of the partitions shorter than \(\delta\) the cells that contain a point of the set \(Z\) have a total volume less than \(\eta'\). The set \(K\) is bounded, so it lies in the cube \([-R, R]^3\) for some \(R > 0\). By the Archimedean property 1.36 there is a natural number \(n\) such that \(h = 2R/n\) is less than \(\delta\) and than \(\rho/\sqrt3\). We divide every edge of the cube \([-R, R]^3\) into \(n\) equal pieces. The cells of this grid are cubes with the edge \(h\). We keep the cells that contain a point of the set \(Z\). They cover \(Z\), because every point of the set \(Z\) lies in the cube \([-R, R]^3\) and so in some cell, and they have a total volume less than \(\eta'\).
  3. For every kept cube \(C\) we choose a point \(P_{\mathrm{C}} \in Z \cap C\). For every point \(Q \in Z \cap C\) the coordinates of the points \(Q\) and \(P_{\mathrm{C}}\) differ by at most \(h\), so by (1.10) and lemma 1.29 \(|P_{\mathrm{C}} Q| \le \sqrt{3h^2} = \sqrt3\,h \le \rho\). Since \(P_{\mathrm{C}} \in Z \subseteq K\), step 1 gives for the distance of the images \(|\Phi(Q) - \Phi(P_{\mathrm{C}})| \le 3\sqrt3\,M h\).
  4. No difference of coordinates is larger than the distance, so every coordinate of the point \(\Phi(Q)\) differs from the same coordinate of the point \(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{C}})\) by at most \(3\sqrt3\,M h\). The point \(\Phi(Q)\) therefore lies in the cube \(C'\) with centre \(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{C}})\) and edge \(6\sqrt3\,M h\), with the volume \((6\sqrt3\,M)^3 h^3 = 648\sqrt3\,M^3\,h^3\).
  5. Every point of the set \(\Phi(Z)\) is \(\Phi(Q)\) for some \(Q \in Z\), which lies in some kept cube \(C\), and so by step 4 in the cube \(C'\). The cubes \(C'\) therefore cover \(\Phi(Z)\). Their total volume is \(648\sqrt3\,M^3\) times the total volume of the cubes \(C\), which is less than \(648\sqrt3\,M^3\,\eta' = \eta\).
  6. We chose the error \(\eta\) freely, so by definition 4.25 \(\Phi(Z)\) is a set of zero volume.

2. Set with volume.

  1. The set \(W\) is closed and bounded, and \(\Phi\) is continuous on it (lemma 1.92 for each component). By lemma 4.48, \(\Phi(W)\) is closed and bounded.
  2. The set \(W\) is closed, so by lemma 4.24, item 1, its boundary lies in \(W\). The boundary has zero volume (definition 4.27).
  3. By the first item with \(K = W\) and with \(Z\) the boundary of the set \(W\), the set of the images of the boundary points has zero volume.
  4. By lemma 4.54, item 2, every boundary point of the set \(\Phi(W)\) is the image of a boundary point of the set \(W\). The boundary of the set \(\Phi(W)\) therefore lies in the set of step 3, and by lemma 4.26, item 1, it has zero volume.
  5. By steps 1 and 4, \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume.
  6. In the plane the steps are the same, with squares instead of cubes and with the bound \(2M\) of lemma 4.55: a square with the edge \(h\) goes into a square with the edge \(4\sqrt2\,M h\) and the area \(32\,M^2 h^2\).

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 10.3.10 (PDF p. 114) for item 1 and Prop. 10.5.9 (PDF pp. 126-127) for item 2, which Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF p. 134) uses to know that \(g(S)\) is Jordan measurable. The proof is not from the source.

Now we need one more tool for computing with the volumes of images. When we add up over the cells of a grid, no interior point of the image of one cell lies in the image of another, so the integrals over the images add up. That a smaller set has a smaller volume is said by lemma 4.32, item 2.

Lemma 4.57 Integral over the images of cells (integral po slikah celic)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(D\), with \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\) for every \(P \in D\), and let \(C_1, \dots, C_{\mathrm{k}}\) be different cells of one grid (section 4.2.3), all lying in \(D\). Then \(Y = \Phi(C_1) \cup \dots \cup \Phi(C_{\mathrm{k}})\) is a set with volume, and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on \(Y\),

\[\int_{\mathrm{Y}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k} \int_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})} f\,\mathrm{d}V .\]

In particular \(V_{\mathrm{Y}} = V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_1)} + \dots + V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{k})}\). The same holds in the plane, with rectangles instead of boxes.

Proof

We must show that the images of the cells do not overlap in interior points, and then use the additivity of the integral over sets with volume.

  1. An interior point of a cell lies strictly between the planes that bound the cell in each direction. Let the cell be \([x_{\mathrm{i}-1}, x_{\mathrm{i}}] \times [y_{\mathrm{j}-1}, y_{\mathrm{j}}] \times [z_{\mathrm{n}-1}, z_{\mathrm{n}}]\) and \(P\) a point of it with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\). Every ball around \(P\) with radius \(r\) contains the point \(P - \tfrac{r}{2}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), whose coordinate \(x\) is less than \(x_{\mathrm{i}-1}\) and which is therefore not in the cell. Such a point \(P\) is therefore not interior. The same holds for \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = x_{\mathrm{i}}\) and for the other two coordinates.
  2. An interior point \(P\) of a cell \(C\) lies in no other cell \(C'\). The cell \(C'\) differs from \(C\) in at least one index, for instance in the index for \(x\), and has the interval \([x_{\mathrm{l}-1}, x_{\mathrm{l}}]\) with \(l \neq i\). The partition points increase, so for \(l < i\) we have \(x_{\mathrm{l}} \le x_{\mathrm{i}-1} < x_{\mathrm{P}}\), and for \(l > i\) we have \(x_{\mathrm{l}-1} \ge x_{\mathrm{i}} > x_{\mathrm{P}}\), and by step 1 \(P\) does not lie in \(C'\).
  3. Every cell is a box, so it is a set with volume (lemma 4.32, item 6), and it lies in \(D\). By lemma 4.56, item 2, \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\) is a set with volume.
  4. Let \(C_{\mathrm{l}}\) and \(C_{\mathrm{m}}\) be different cells. By step 2 no interior point of either of them lies in the other. By lemma 4.54, item 3, therefore no interior point of either of the sets \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\) and \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{m}})\) lies in the other.
  5. By lemma 4.32, item 4, \(Y\) is therefore a set with volume, and the integral of every function continuous on \(Y\) is the sum of the integrals over \(\Phi(C_1), \dots, \Phi(C_{\mathrm{k}})\).
  6. For \(f = 1\) we get the sum of volumes. In the plane the steps are the same, with rectangles and discs.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources. LEBL2 in the proof of Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF p. 137) uses that the images of rectangles overlap only in the images of their boundaries, which have measure zero.

Now we can compute the volume of the image under a linear map. For a matrix \(\mat A\) and points \(P_0\) and \(Q_0\) let us take the map that assigns to a point \(P\) the point

\[\Lambda(P) = Q_0 + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P} ,\]

where we write the vector \(\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\) as a column. It sends the point \(P_0\) to \(Q_0\) and multiplies the vector between two points by the matrix \(\mat A\): by the linearity of the product with a matrix (lemma 1.98), \(\overrightarrow{\Lambda(P)\Lambda(Q)} = \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 Q} - \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P} = \mat A\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\). We already know such maps. The sheared cube deformed by \(\Phi(P) = P + (0{,}001\,z_{\mathrm{P}}, 0, 0)\), which is \(\Lambda\) with \(P_0 = Q_0 = O\) and with the matrix \(\mat F\) that has the number \(0{,}001\) in the place \(xz\). The plate turned with the pair \(c = 0{,}6\), \(s = 0{,}8\) moved by a \(\Lambda\) whose matrix is \(\mat R\). For these two the deformation gradient was the same at all points, because the displacement field was linear. Mathematics, however, keeps the name linear map for maps that send the zero vector to the zero vector (section 1.16.2), so a \(\Lambda\) that does not send the origin to the origin is not linear in this narrower sense. Where it matters, we will say so.

How will we compute the volume of the image? For an elementary matrix the image of a box is again a box, or a box tilted by a shear (figure 4.95). In the figure the rectangle \([1, 3] \times [1, 2]\) is grey and dashed, on the left is its image under the swap of the coordinates, in the middle under the multiplication of the coordinate \(x\) by \(2\), on the right under a shear, everywhere in the plane with the axes \(x\) and \(y\). We compute the volume of the tilted box with a single iterated integral, because it is a body between the graphs of two linear functions. Then we fill a set with volume with the cells of a grid, which are boxes (figure 4.106 at the end of the section), and for other matrices we use the factorization of lemma 4.53.

The two basic maps on which the proof rests are shown in figure 4.105 on a rectangle \(K\). A shift carries it without changing the lengths of the sides, a stretch of the coordinate \(x\) multiplies the length of one side by \(c\). Each of them is undone by a shift in the opposite direction and by a stretch by the number \(1/c\).

Theorem 4.58 Volume under a linear map (prostornina pri linearni preslikavi)

Let \(\mat A\) be a \(3 \times 3\) matrix with \(\det\mat A \neq 0\), let \(P_0\) and \(Q_0\) be points, and let the map \(\Lambda\) assign to a point \(P\) the point \(\Lambda(P) = Q_0 + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). If \(W\) is a set with volume (definition 4.27), then \(\Lambda(W)\) is also a set with volume, and

\[V_{\Lambda(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat A|\,V_{\mathrm{W}} . \tag{4.30}\]

The same holds in the plane, for a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, with area instead of volume.

Proof

We must show that \(\Lambda(W)\) has a volume and that it is \(|\det\mat A|\) times the volume of the set \(W\). We compute the volume first for elementary matrices and shifts on boxes, then for every set with volume, and finally for every matrix with the factorization. Figure 4.95 shows the second part in the plane, figure 4.106 the third, there with a matrix that is not elementary, but the argument is the same.

1. The map \(\Lambda\) has the properties of the inverse function theorem.

  1. Let \(P\) have the coordinates \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\), the point \(P_0\) the coordinates \(p_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(p_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(Q_0\) the coordinates \(q_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(q_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(q_{\mathrm{z}}\). By (1.39) the components of the map are \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = q_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{j}} A_{\mathrm{ij}}\,(x_{\mathrm{j}} - p_{\mathrm{j}})\), polynomials of degree one. Their partial derivatives are the constant numbers \(\partial\Lambda_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = A_{\mathrm{ij}}\), which are continuous. The map \(\Lambda\) is therefore continuously differentiable in the whole space, with the matrix of partial derivatives \(\mat F_\Lambda = \mat A\) and with the Jacobian \(J_\Lambda = \det\mat A \neq 0\) (definition 4.42).
  2. The map \(\Lambda\) is one-to-one. If \(\Lambda(P) = \Lambda(Q)\), then \(\mat A\,\overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{\Lambda(P)\Lambda(Q)} = \vek 0\), and since \(\det\mat A \neq 0\), lemma 2.75 on a zero determinant gives \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \vek 0\), so \(P = Q\).
  3. The whole space is an open set. By lemma 4.56, item 2, \(\Lambda(W)\) is therefore a set with volume.

2. Basic maps on a box.

  1. The basic maps are of two kinds. For an elementary matrix \(\mat E\) (definition 4.52), \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}}(P) = O + \mat E\,\overrightarrow{OP}\), the point whose coordinates are \(\mat E\) times the coordinates of the point \(P\). Its factor is \(|\det\mat E|\). For a vector \(\vek w\), the shift is \(T_{\vek{w}}(P) = P + \vek w\). Its factor is \(1\). Both kinds have the form \(\Lambda\) of the theorem, the first with \(P_0 = Q_0 = O\), the second with the matrix \(\mat I\), \(P_0 = O\) and \(Q_0 = O + \vek w\), so the first part holds for them.
  2. Let \(K = [a_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{x}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{y}}, b_{\mathrm{y}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{z}}, b_{\mathrm{z}}]\) be a box. Its volume as a set with volume is the school one, \(V_{\mathrm{K}} = (b_{\mathrm{x}} - a_{\mathrm{x}})(b_{\mathrm{y}} - a_{\mathrm{y}})(b_{\mathrm{z}} - a_{\mathrm{z}})\), by lemma 4.32, item 6.
  3. Shift. The image \(T_{\vek{w}}(K)\) is the box \([a_{\mathrm{x}} + w_{\mathrm{x}}, b_{\mathrm{x}} + w_{\mathrm{x}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{y}} + w_{\mathrm{y}}, b_{\mathrm{y}} + w_{\mathrm{y}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{z}} + w_{\mathrm{z}}, b_{\mathrm{z}} + w_{\mathrm{z}}]\) with the same lengths of the edges, so it has the volume \(V_{\mathrm{K}}\).
  4. Swap of the coordinates \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\). By lemma 4.53, item 1, the point \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}}(P)\) has the coordinates \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) of the point \(P\) swapped. The image of the box is therefore the box with the intervals in the directions \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) swapped, with the same product of the lengths of the edges. The volume is \(V_{\mathrm{K}} = |{-1}|\,V_{\mathrm{K}} = |\det\mat E|\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\) (lemma 4.53, item 2).
  5. Multiplication of the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) by \(c\). The point \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}}(P)\) has the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) equal to \(c\,x_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the other two stay. When \(x_{\mathrm{i}}\) runs over \([a_{\mathrm{i}}, b_{\mathrm{i}}]\), \(c\,x_{\mathrm{i}}\) runs over the interval \([c\,a_{\mathrm{i}}, c\,b_{\mathrm{i}}]\) for \(c > 0\), or \([c\,b_{\mathrm{i}}, c\,a_{\mathrm{i}}]\) for \(c < 0\), whose length is \(|c|\,(b_{\mathrm{i}} - a_{\mathrm{i}})\). The image of the box is therefore a box with the volume \(|c|\,V_{\mathrm{K}} = |\det\mat E|\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).
  6. Addition of \(k\) times the coordinate \(\ix{j}\) to the coordinate \(\ix{i}\). Let \(\ix{l}\) be the third index.
