The point \(Q = \Lambda_{\mat{E}}(P)\) has the coordinates \(y_{\mathrm{j}} = x_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(y_{\mathrm{l}} = x_{\mathrm{l}}\) and \(y_{\mathrm{i}} = x_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,x_{\mathrm{j}}\). The point \(Q\) lies in the image of the box if and only if \(a_{\mathrm{j}} \le y_{\mathrm{j}} \le b_{\mathrm{j}}\), \(a_{\mathrm{l}} \le y_{\mathrm{l}} \le b_{\mathrm{l}}\) and \(a_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}} \le y_{\mathrm{i}} \le b_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}}\). The image is therefore the body between the graphs of the functions \(a_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}}\) over the rectangle \([a_{\mathrm{j}}, b_{\mathrm{j}}] \times [a_{\mathrm{l}}, b_{\mathrm{l}}]\), in which the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) runs between the graphs (definition 4.15). The functions are polynomials, continuously differentiable in the whole plane, and the first is smaller than the second. By theorem 4.33 the volume equals the iterated integral whose inner integral is \(\int_{\mathrm{a}_\mathrm{i} + \mathrm{k}\,\mathrm{y}_\mathrm{j}}^{b_{\mathrm{i}} + k\,y_{\mathrm{j}}} 1\,\mathrm{d}y_{\mathrm{i}} = b_{\mathrm{i}} - a_{\mathrm{i}}\), and the middle and outer integrals multiply this constant number by \(b_{\mathrm{j}} - a_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(b_{\mathrm{l}} - a_{\mathrm{l}}\). The volume is \(V_{\mathrm{K}} = |\det\mat E|\,V_{\mathrm{K}}\).

3. Basic maps on a set with volume.

  1. Let \(\Lambda'\) be a basic map with the factor \(\gamma\). Its inverse map \(\Lambda''\) is basic with the factor \(1/\gamma\): for \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}}\) it is \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}^{-1}}\), because \(O + \mat E^{-1}\mat E\,\overrightarrow{OP} = P\), where \(\mat E^{-1}\) is elementary (lemma 4.53, item 3) with the determinant \(1/\det\mat E\) (theorem 2.74, because \(\det\mat E\,\det\mat E^{-1} = \det\mat I = 1\)), and for \(T_{\vek{w}}\) it is \(T_{-\vek{w}}\).
  2. Let \(W\) be a set with volume and \(\eta > 0\). By definition 4.30 with the function \(1\) there is a band \(\delta\) such that for every grid of a box containing \(W\) with pieces of the partitions shorter than \(\delta\) the total volume \(S\) of the cells that lie in \(W\) is larger than \(V_{\mathrm{W}} - \eta\). We take such a grid.
  3. Let \(C_1, \dots, C_{\mathrm{k}}\) be the cells that lie in \(W\). By the second part, \(\Lambda'(C_{\mathrm{l}})\) has the volume \(\gamma\,V_{\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l}}\). By the first part, \(\Lambda'\) has the properties of lemma 4.57 with \(D\) the whole space, so the union of their images \(Y = \Lambda'(C_1) \cup \dots \cup \Lambda'(C_{\mathrm{k}})\) is a set with the volume \(\gamma\,(V_{\mathrm{C}_1} + \dots + V_{\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{k}}) = \gamma\,S\).
  4. The cells \(C_{\mathrm{l}}\) lie in \(W\), so \(Y\) lies in \(\Lambda'(W)\), which by the first part is a set with volume. By lemma 4.32, item 2, \(V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} \ge \gamma\,S > \gamma\,(V_{\mathrm{W}} - \eta)\). If no cell lies in \(W\), then \(S = 0\), and the inequality holds because a volume is not negative (lemma 4.32, item 2, with the functions \(0 \le 1\)).
  5. Therefore \(\gamma\,V_{\mathrm{W}} - V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} < \gamma\,\eta\) for every \(\eta > 0\). By lemma 1.35, \(V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} \ge \gamma\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  6. We use steps 2 to 5 for the inverse map \(\Lambda''\) with the factor \(1/\gamma\) and for the set with volume \(\Lambda'(W)\). Since \(\Lambda''(\Lambda'(W)) = W\), we get \(V_{\mathrm{W}} \ge V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})}/\gamma\). Together with step 5, \(V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} = \gamma\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).

4. Any matrix.

  1. By lemma 4.53, item 4, \(\mat A = \mat E_1 \cdots \mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\) with elementary matrices \(\mat E_{\mathrm{l}}\). By item 1 of lemma 1.100 on the properties of the matrix product, used \((m - 1)\) times, \(\mat A\vek v = \mat E_1\big(\mat E_2(\cdots(\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}\vek v))\big)\), so \(\Lambda_{\mat{A}}\) is the map \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}_\mathrm{m}}\) followed by \(\Lambda_{\mat{E}_{\mathrm{m}-1}}, \dots, \Lambda_{\mat{E}_1}\).
  2. By the third part, used \(m\) times, every intermediate image is a set with volume, and \(V_{\Lambda_{\mat{A}}(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat E_1| \cdots |\det\mat E_{\mathrm{m}}|\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  3. By theorem 2.74, used \((m - 1)\) times, \(\det\mat E_1 \cdots \det\mat E_{\mathrm{m}} = \det\mat A\), and the absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values. Therefore \(V_{\Lambda_{\mat{A}}(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat A|\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  4. The map \(\Lambda\) is the shift \(T_{-\overrightarrow{OP_0}}\) followed by \(\Lambda_{\mat{A}}\) and the shift \(T_{\overrightarrow{OQ_0}}\). The shift \(T_{-\overrightarrow{OP_0}}\) sends \(P\) to the point \(O + \overrightarrow{P_0 P}\), \(\Lambda_{\mat{A}}\) sends this point to \(O + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\), and the second shift to \(Q_0 + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). The shifts keep the volume (third part with the factor \(1\)), so \(V_{\Lambda(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat A|\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\).
  5. In the plane the steps are the same, with \(2 \times 2\) matrices, rectangles and areas. We use lemma 2.75 and theorem 2.74 on \(3 \times 3\) matrices into which we put the \(2 \times 2\) matrices with \(1\) at the place \(zz\), as in section 2.10.2. In step 6 of the second part the image of a rectangle is a region between the graphs of two linear functions, whose area theorem 4.33 in the plane gives.

Source: LEBL2 Prop. 10.7.1 (PDF p. 134) for rectangles, whose proof the source leaves to the reader (Exercise 10.7.1, PDF p. 137) with the hint that the proof for elementary matrices is enough. The proof is not from the source.

The proof used the same idea twice. Since for the volume we only have an inequality from the cells that lie in the set, we only got \(V_{\Lambda'(\mathrm{W})} \ge \gamma\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\). The reverse inequality came from the same inequality for the inverse map. We will take the same route in section 4.3.4.

Let us now answer the two questions from the beginning of the section. The parallelepiped spanned from a point \(P\) by the vectors \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\) and \(\vek c\) with \(\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c) \neq 0\) is the image of the unit cube \([0, 1]^3\) under \(\Lambda(Q) = P + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{OQ}\), where the matrix \(\mat A\) has the columns \(\vek a\), \(\vek b\), \(\vek c\). The point \((s, t, w)\) of the cube goes to \(P + s\,\vek a + t\,\vek b + w\,\vek c\), as in section 2.10.2. By the theorem the parallelepiped is a set with volume, and its volume is \(|\det\mat A| \cdot 1 = |\vek a\cdot(\vek b\times\vek c)|\), exactly the school volume of lemma 2.69. The two volumes therefore agree, and what we took from school in chapter 2 now holds as a theorem. A flattened parallelepiped with determinant zero is not covered by the theorem, and we will not need it.

The second test is a set with a curved boundary. Let us take the cross section of the round hanging bar, a disc with the radius \(5\) mm and the area \(78{,}54\) mm², and the \(2 \times 2\) matrix with the columns \((3, 1)\) and \((1, 2)\) and the determinant \(5\) of figure 2.152. The image of the disc is an ellipse, which should have the area \(5 \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 392{,}70\ \text{mm}^2\) (figure 4.106). On the left is the disc with a grid of squares of edge \(1\) mm and the blue squares that lie in the disc, in the plane with the axes \(y\) and \(z\), on the right the ellipse with their images, parallelograms of area \(5\) mm², and with the axes at a different scale. There are \(60\) blue squares, with the total area \(60\) mm² of \(78{,}54\) mm², and their images have \(300\) mm² of \(392{,}70\) mm² in total. The share is the same on both sides, because every parallelogram is \(5\) times as large as its square. Let us check with the definition of area: with NumPy we added up, for grids with square cells of edge \(h\) whose division points are the multiples of \(h\), the areas of the cells that lie in the ellipse.

\(h\) in mm \(1\) \(0{,}5\) \(0{,}25\) \(0{,}1\) \(0{,}05\)
area of the cells in the ellipse in mm² \(348{,}0\) \(368{,}5\) \(379{,}9\) \(387{,}2\) \(390{,}0\)

The sums approach \(392{,}70\) mm², as the theorem says. Why so slowly? The cells in the ellipse do not cover a narrow band along the boundary of the ellipse. We see such a band in figure 4.106 between the blue parallelograms and the boundary of the ellipse, and on the left between the blue squares and the circle. A point of the ellipse that is farther from the boundary than the diagonal of a cell, \(h\sqrt2\), lies in a cell that is entirely in the ellipse, so the band is narrower than \(h\sqrt2\). For half the \(h\) the band is half as wide, and the missing area roughly halves: for \(h = 0{,}1\) mm \(5{,}5\) mm² is missing, for \(h = 0{,}05\) mm \(2{,}7\) mm².

For the sheared cube the matrix is elementary, with determinant \(1\), and the theorem says that the volume of the cube after the shear is exactly \(1000\) mm³, as we found for small pieces in section 2.10.5. For the turned plate the determinant of the matrix \(\mat R\) is \(1\), and every shape on the plate has the same area after the rotation as before it, whatever its form.

4.3.4 Change of variables in an integral

Now we can write down the rule we need. Let \(\Phi\) be a map that is continuously differentiable and one-to-one on an open set \(D\) and has a nonzero Jacobian at every point, and let \(W\) be a set with volume in \(D\). What is the volume of the set \(\Phi(W)\), and how do we integrate a function over it if we know how to integrate over \(W\)? For the deformation of a body, \(W\) is a part of the body before loading, \(\Phi(W)\) the same part after it, and the question is what its volume after loading is.

Let us first look at the question where everything is seen at one glance, on a line (figure 4.107). We divide the segment from \(0\) to \(1\) into four pieces of length \(h = 0{,}25\). The map \(\Phi(s) = s + 0{,}5\,s^2\) stretches it into the segment from \(0\) to \(1{,}5\), but not equally everywhere: the division points go to \(0\), \(0{,}28\), \(0{,}63\), \(1{,}03\) and \(1{,}5\), and the pieces of the image grow longer towards the right. The piece that starts at \(s_0 = 0{,}5\) goes to a piece of length \(\Phi(0{,}75) - \Phi(0{,}5) = 0{,}41\). The derivative \(\Phi'(s) = 1 + s\) tells how many times longer a short piece at the point \(s\) becomes. At \(s_0\) this is \(1{,}5\), and the estimate \(\Phi'(s_0)\,h = 0{,}375\) misses the true length \(0{,}41\) by \(0{,}03\), because the derivative is not constant on the piece. The sum of the four estimates is \(1{,}375\), for \(h = 0{,}125\) the sum of the eight estimates is \(1{,}44\), and for \(h = 0{,}0625\) it is \(1{,}47\) (NumPy). The sums approach the integral \(\int_0^1 (1 + s)\,\mathrm{d}s = 1{,}5\), and this is the length of the image. The theorem that follows says the same in the plane and in space. The piece becomes a cube, the length a volume, and in place of the derivative \(\Phi'\) stands \(|J_\Phi|\), the number that tells how many times larger the volume of a small cube at the point becomes. Two things the line cannot show: there a piece has no boundary for the grid to cut, and the image of a piece is again a piece, not a curved shape. These two things are what makes the proof long.

The idea is old, and let us draw it in the plane, where cubes are squares and volumes are areas (figure 4.108). We cut the set \(W\) with a grid into small cubes with the edge \(h\). The map \(\Phi\) sends the straight lines of the grid to curved lines, and the set \(W\) to \(\Phi(W)\). Take one of the cubes, \(C\), and a point \(P_0\) in it. Its image \(\Phi(C)\) at this size already looks like a parallelogram, and that is the whole idea. Near a point \(P_0\) of a cube, theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step, applied to each component, gives \(\Phi(P) \approx \Phi(P_0) + \mat F_\Phi(P_0)\,\overrightarrow{P_0 P}\). On the cube \(\Phi\) therefore behaves almost like the map \(\Lambda\) of theorem 4.58 with the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(P_0)\), which sends the cube to a parallelepiped with the volume \(|J_\Phi(P_0)|\,h^3\). The integral of a function \(f\) over \(\Phi(W)\) is therefore roughly the sum of the numbers \(f(\Phi(P_0))\,|J_\Phi(P_0)|\,h^3\) over the cubes that lie in \(W\), and this is a sum that approaches the integral of the function \(f(\Phi(P))\,|J_\Phi(P)|\) over \(W\).

The proof must handle two things that the idea passes over. First, the cubes at the boundary of the set \(W\) do not lie entirely in \(W\). These are the boundary cells, and their total volume is small by lemma 4.29 when \(h\) is small. In figure 4.108 it is not yet: at \(h = 0{,}125\) the boundary cells have the total area \(0{,}69\), more than half of the area \(1{,}18\) of the set \(W\). With every halving of \(h\), however, their area roughly halves, because they lie in a band along the boundary whose width is proportional to \(h\) (counted with NumPy):

\[\begin{array}{l|cccc} h & 0{,}125 & 0{,}0625 & 0{,}03125 & 0{,}015625 \\ \hline \text{area of the boundary cells} & 0{,}69 & 0{,}33 & 0{,}16 & 0{,}08 \end{array}\]

This is why the proof makes the error at the boundary smaller than any given number \(\eta\). The lemma holds for sets with volume, and this is why the theorem demands that \(W\) be one.

Second, the image of a cube is not a parallelepiped. It lies, however, in a slightly enlarged parallelepiped, because the partial derivatives change only a little on a small cube (figure 4.109). In the figure, on the left is the square \(C\) with the edge \(h\) and the point \(P_0\). The map \(G\), which the proof builds from \(\Phi\), moves every point of the square only a little. It moves the upper right corner by \(0{,}064\) to the right and by \(0{,}037\) upwards, the other three corners by just as much, and all other points by less. So the image \(G(C)\) lies in the square \(\tilde C\), widened by \(\kappa h = 0{,}08\) on every side. On the right is \(\Phi(C)\) inside the parallelogram \(\Lambda(\tilde C)\), with the point \(\Phi(P_0)\) and the parallelogram \(\Lambda(C)\) grey and dashed, and between the planes the map \(\Phi\). This enlarges the area by the factor \((1 + 2\kappa)^2 = 1{,}16^2 \approx 1{,}35\), in space by \((1 + 2\kappa)^3\). In the proof \(\kappa\) is as small as we like, because the cube is small, and the factor tends to \(1\). This gives only an inequality: the integral over \(\Phi(W)\) is not larger than the integral over \(W\). We get the reverse inequality from the same inequality for the inverse map \(\Psi\), just as for theorem 4.58 we got the reverse inequality with the inverse map. This is the route of LEBL2 (Theorem 10.7.2, PDF pp. 134-137).

Theorem 4.59 Change of variables theorem (izrek o zamenjavi spremenljivk)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(\Phi\) a map that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(D\), with \(J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\) for every point \(P \in D\). Let \(W \subseteq D\) be a set with volume (definition 4.27). Then \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume, and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on \(\Phi(W)\),

\[\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{W}} f\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\big|J_\Phi(P)\big|\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{4.31}\]

In particular \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} |J_\Phi|\,\mathrm{d}V\). The same holds in the plane, for a map that has a point of the plane as input and as output, with a set with area \(W\), with areas and with \(\mathrm{d}A\) instead of \(\mathrm{d}V\).

Proof

We must show that \(\Phi(W)\) has a volume and that both inequalities between the sides of (4.31) hold. First we bound the volume of the image of a small cube, then we prove the inequality \(\le\) for nonnegative functions, the reverse inequality with the inverse map, and finally we pass to any function.

1. The set \(\Phi(W)\) and the integral on the right.

  1. By lemma 4.56, item 2, \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume.
  2. The function \(J_\Phi\) is a sum of products of partial derivatives of the components of the map \(\Phi\) ((2.70)), which are continuous on \(D\), so by corollary 1.70, item 1, it is continuous on \(D\). Also \(|J_\Phi|\) is continuous. By lemma 1.6 on the triangle inequality, item 1, we have \(|a| \le |a - b| + |b|\) and \(|b| \le |b - a| + |a|\), so \(\big||a| - |b|\big| \le |a - b|\) for any two numbers \(a\) and \(b\). The function \(P \mapsto f(\Phi(P))\) is continuous on \(W\) by lemma 4.35. The integrand on the right is a product of continuous functions and is continuous on \(W\), so the integral on the right exists (theorem 4.31).
  3. If \(W\) is empty, so is \(\Phi(W)\), and both sides are zero, because no cell lies in the empty set. Let \(W\) be nonempty.

2. Constants.

  1. By lemma 4.55 for \(K = W\) there are \(\rho > 0\) and \(M > 0\) such that the set \(W_\rho\) of points at a distance of at most \(\rho\) from some point of the set \(W\) is closed, bounded and in \(D\), and that on it all partial derivatives \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\) are at most \(M\) in absolute value.
  2. The function \(|J_\Phi|\) is continuous and positive on \(W_\rho\). By theorem 1.79, the extreme value theorem in space, it attains on \(W_\rho\) a least value \(m_{\mathrm{J}} > 0\) and a greatest value \(M_{\mathrm{J}}\).
  3. By theorem 2.76 the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(Q)\) for \(Q \in\) \(W_\rho\) has an inverse matrix whose rows are vector products of the columns divided by \(J_\Phi(Q)\). Every element of a vector product is a difference of two products of two elements of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(Q)\), so it is at most \(2M^2\) in absolute value. Every element of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi(Q)^{-1}\) is therefore at most \(N = 2M^2/m_{\mathrm{J}}\) in absolute value.
  4. By theorem 4.6, applied to each of the nine partial derivatives on \(W_\rho\), for every \(\omega > 0\) there is \(\delta_\omega > 0\) such that \(|\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(Q) - \partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(Q')| < \omega\) for all \(\ix{i}\), \(\ix{j}\) and for any two points \(Q, Q' \in W_\rho\) with \(|QQ'| < \delta_\omega\). For \(\delta_\omega\) we take the smallest of the nine bands. The same \(\delta_\omega\) holds everywhere on \(W_\rho\), so in the third part the same bound will hold for every cube of the grid at once.

3. The image of a small cube.

Let \(\omega > 0\) and \(\kappa = 9\sqrt3\,N\omega\). Let \(C\) be a cube with edges parallel to the axes, of length \(h\), where \(\sqrt3\,h\) is less than \(\rho\) and than \(\delta_\omega\), that contains some point of the set \(W\), and let \(P_0\) be any point of the cube \(C\). Let us show that \(C\) lies in \(D\) and that

\[V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C})} \le |J_\Phi(P_0)|\,(1 + 2\kappa)^3\,h^3 .\]
  1. Two points of the cube differ by at most \(h\) in each coordinate, so by (1.10) they are at a distance of at most \(\sqrt3\,h\). Every point of the cube is therefore at a distance of at most \(\sqrt3\,h < \rho\) from the point of the set \(W\) in the cube and lies in \(W_\rho\) \(\subseteq D\). The cube is a set with volume (lemma 4.32, item 6), so by lemma 4.56 also \(\Phi(C)\) is a set with volume.
  2. Let \(\mat A = \mat F_\Phi(P_0)\) and \(\mat B = \mat A^{-1}\), whose elements are at most \(N\) in absolute value. Let \(\Lambda(Q) = \Phi(P_0) + \mat A\,\overrightarrow{P_0 Q}\), the map of theorem 4.58, which sends the square \(C\) to the parallelogram \(\Lambda(C)\), and \(G(P) = P_0 + \mat B\,\overrightarrow{\Phi(P_0)\Phi(P)}\) for \(P \in D\). Then
    \[\Lambda\big(G(P)\big) = \Phi(P_0) + \mat A\mat B\,\overrightarrow{\Phi(P_0)\Phi(P)} = \Phi(P) ,\]
    because \(\overrightarrow{P_0 G(P)} = \mat B\,\overrightarrow{\Phi(P_0)\Phi(P)}\) and \(\mat A\mat B = \mat I\). Therefore \(\Phi(C) = \Lambda(G(C))\): we get the image \(\Phi(C)\) by mapping the set \(G(C)\) with \(\Lambda\).
  3. The components of the map \(G\) are \(G_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = x_{\mathrm{P}_0, \mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\big(\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}(P) - \Phi_{\mathrm{l}}(P_0)\big)\), where \(x_{\mathrm{P}_0, \mathrm{i}}\) is the coordinate \(\ix{i}\) of the point \(P_0\). By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82, items 1 and 2), applied to a partial derivative as to a derivative with respect to one variable, \(\partial G_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)\), and these derivatives are continuous on \(D\).
  4. Let \(H(P) = \overrightarrow{P\,G(P)}\), a vector field with the components \(H_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = G_{\mathrm{i}}(P) - x_{\mathrm{i}}\). Since \(\sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P_0) = (\mat B\mat A)_{\mathrm{ij}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\),
    \[\frac{\partial H_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) - \delta_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} B_{\mathrm{il}}\,\Big(\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P) - \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{l}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P_0)\Big) .\]
  5. For \(P \in C\) the points \(P\) and \(P_0\) are in \(W_\rho\) and at a distance of at most \(\sqrt3\,h < \delta_\omega\), so every bracket in step 4 is less than \(\omega\) in absolute value, and \(|\partial H_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}(P)| \le 3N\omega\).
  6. The cube contains the segment between any two of its points, because the coordinates of the points of the segment lie between the coordinates of the endpoints. By lemma 4.47 on bounded derivatives and distances, applied to the map \(P \mapsto O + H(P)\), whose components are \(H_{\mathrm{i}}\), on the segment from \(P_0\) to \(P \in C\), \(|H(P) - H(P_0)| \le 9N\omega\,|P_0 P| \le 9\sqrt3\,N\omega\,h = \kappa h\). Since \(G(P_0) = P_0\), we have \(H(P_0) = \vek 0\), so \(|\overrightarrow{P\,G(P)}| \le \kappa h\): the displacement of the point \(P\) to \(G(P)\) is not longer than \(\kappa h\).
  7. Every coordinate of the point \(G(P)\) therefore differs from the same coordinate of the point \(P\) by at most \(\kappa h\). Let \(\tilde C\) be the cube obtained from \(C\) by extending each of its intervals by \(\kappa h\) on both sides. Its edge is \((1 + 2\kappa)\,h\), and \(G(C)\) \(\subseteq \tilde C\).
  8. By step 2, \(\Phi(C) = \Lambda(G(C)) \subseteq \Lambda(\tilde C)\). By theorem 4.58, \(\Lambda(\tilde C)\) is a set with the volume \(|\det\mat A|\,(1 + 2\kappa)^3 h^3 = |J_\Phi(P_0)|\,(1 + 2\kappa)^3 h^3\), and by lemma 4.32, item 2, \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C})}\) is at most that.

4. The inequality \(\le\) for a nonnegative function.

Let \(f \ge 0\) be continuous on \(\Phi(W)\) and \(g(P) = f(\Phi(P))\,|J_\Phi(P)|\) for \(P \in\) \(W\). Let us show that \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\).

  1. The set \(\Phi(W)\) is closed, bounded and nonempty, so by theorem 1.79 \(f\) attains on it a greatest value \(\mu\).
  2. We choose \(\eta\) with \(0 < \eta \le 1\) and take \(\omega = \eta/(9\sqrt3\,N)\), so that \(\kappa = \eta\). By definition 4.30 for \(g\) on \(W\) there is a band \(\delta_1\), and by lemma 4.29, item 3, a band \(\delta_2\) such that for every grid of a box containing \(W\) with pieces of the partitions shorter than \(\delta_2\) the total volume of the boundary cells is less than \(\eta\).
  3. The set \(W\) is bounded, so it lies in the cube \([-R, R]^3\) for some \(R > 0\). By the Archimedean property 1.36 there is a natural number \(n\) such that \(h = 2R/n\) is less than \(\delta_1\) and than \(\delta_2\) and that \(\sqrt3\,h\) is less than \(\rho\) and than \(\delta_\omega\). We divide every edge of the cube \([-R, R]^3\) into \(n\) equal pieces. The cells of this grid are cubes with the edge \(h\).
  4. We denote the cells that lie in \(W\) by \(C_1, \dots, C_{\mathrm{k}}\), and the boundary cells, which contain a point of the set \(W\) and a point outside it, by \(C'_1, \dots, C'_{\mathrm{k}'}\). Every point of the set \(W\) lies in some cell, which therefore contains a point of the set \(W\) and is of one of these two kinds. So \(W\) lies in the union \(U\) of all these cells. By the first step of the third part they all lie in \(D\).
  5. The function \(P \mapsto f(\Phi(P))\) is continuous on \(C_{\mathrm{l}} \subseteq W\), so by theorem 1.79 it attains its greatest value on \(C_{\mathrm{l}}\) at some point \(P_{\mathrm{l}} \in C_{\mathrm{l}}\). This is also the greatest value of the function \(f\) on \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\). The sum \(S = \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k} g(P_{\mathrm{l}})\,h^3\) is a sum of definition 4.30, so \(S < \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V + \eta\).
  6. By lemma 4.57, \(\Phi(U)\) is a set with the volume \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{U})} = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})} + \sum_{\mathrm{l}} V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}'_\mathrm{l})}\), and the set \(Y\) \(= \Phi(C_1) \cup \dots \cup \Phi(C_{\mathrm{k}})\) is a set with the volume \(V_{\mathrm{Y}} = \sum_{\mathrm{l}} V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})}\), over which the integral of the function \(f\) is the sum of the integrals over \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\). If no cell lies in \(W\), \(Y\) is empty, and \(V_{\mathrm{Y}}\), the integral over \(Y\) and the sum \(S\) are zero.
  7. The set \(\Phi(W)\) lies in \(\Phi(U)\), so by lemma 4.32, item 2, \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} \le V_{\Phi(\mathrm{U})}\), and
    \[V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} - V_{\mathrm{Y}} \le \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k'} V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}'_\mathrm{l})} .\]
    The part of the set \(\Phi(W)\) outside the set \(Y\) is covered by the images of the boundary cells.
  8. The cells \(C_{\mathrm{l}}\) lie in \(W\), so \(Y\) lies in \(\Phi(W)\). The function \(\mu - f\) is continuous and nowhere negative on \(\Phi(W)\), so by the same item of the same lemma \(\int_{\mathrm{Y}} (\mu - f)\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} (\mu - f)\,\mathrm{d}V\). By linearity (lemma 4.32, item 1), with \(\int \mu\,\mathrm{d}V = \mu\) times the volume, we rearrange this into
    \[\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le \mu\,\big(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} - V_{\mathrm{Y}}\big) + \int_{\mathrm{Y}} f\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  9. The first term. By step 7 and the third part with the point \(P_0\) in the cell \(C'_{\mathrm{l}}\),
    \[\mu\,\big(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} - V_{\mathrm{Y}}\big) \le \mu\,M_{\mathrm{J}}\,(1 + 2\eta)^3 \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k'} h^3 \le \mu\,M_{\mathrm{J}}\,(1 + 2\eta)^3\,\eta ,\]
    because the total volume of the boundary cells is less than \(\eta\).
  10. The second term. On \(\Phi(C_{\mathrm{l}})\) we have \(f \le f(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{l}}))\), so by lemma 4.32, item 2, \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le f(\Phi(P_{\mathrm{l}}))\,V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})}\). By the third part with \(P_0 = P_{\mathrm{l}}\), \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{C}_\mathrm{l})} \le |J_\Phi(P_{\mathrm{l}})|\,(1 + 2\eta)^3 h^3\). By step 6 and step 5 therefore
    \[\int_{\mathrm{Y}} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le (1 + 2\eta)^3 \sum_{\mathrm{l}=1}^{k} g(P_{\mathrm{l}})\,h^3 = (1 + 2\eta)^3 S < (1 + 2\eta)^3\Big(\int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V + \eta\Big) .\]
  11. Let \(I = \int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V\), which is not negative (lemma 4.32, item 2), and \(c = 1 + \mu M_{\mathrm{J}}\). From steps 8 to 10, \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V < (1 + 2\eta)^3\,(I + c\,\eta)\). Since \(\eta \le 1\), \((1 + 2\eta)^3 = 1 + 6\eta + 12\eta^2 + 8\eta^3 \le 1 + 26\eta\), and
    \[\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V - I < (1 + 26\eta)(I + c\,\eta) - I = \eta\,\big(26 I + c + 26\,c\,\eta\big) \le \eta\,(26 I + 27 c) .\]
  12. This holds for every \(\eta \le 1\), so the difference \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V - I\) is less than every positive number. On the number line (figure 4.110) the difference lies in the band up to \(\eta\,(26 I + 27 c)\), which narrows towards \(0\) as \(\eta\) gets smaller, and the difference stays in every band. For a given number \(\varepsilon' > 0\) we take \(\eta\) smaller than \(1\) and than \(\varepsilon'/(26 I + 27 c)\). By lemma 1.35, \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V \le I\).

5. The reverse inequality.

  1. Let \(E = \Phi(D)\) and \(\Psi\) the inverse map, which sends \(\Phi(W)\) back to \(W\). By theorem 4.51, \(E\) is open, \(\Psi\) is continuously differentiable on \(E\), and \(J_\Psi(\Phi(P)) = 1/J_\Phi(P) \neq 0\). As in step 5 of the proof of lemma 4.54, \(\Psi\) is one-to-one on \(E\). The set \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume in \(E\), and \(\Psi(\Phi(W)) = W\).
  2. The function \(g\) of the fourth part is continuous and nowhere negative on \(W = \Psi(\Phi(W))\). The fourth part, applied to the map \(\Psi\), the set \(\Phi(W)\) and the function \(g\), gives
    \[\int_{\mathrm{W}} g\,\mathrm{d}V \le \int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} g\big(\Psi(Q)\big)\,\big|J_\Psi(Q)\big|\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  3. For \(Q = \Phi(P)\) we have \(g(\Psi(Q))\,|J_\Psi(Q)| = f(Q)\,|J_\Phi(P)| \cdot 1/|J_\Phi(P)| = f(Q)\). The right side is therefore \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V\). Together with the fourth part, (4.31) holds for every continuous function \(f \ge 0\).

6. Any continuous function.

  1. By theorem 1.79, \(f\) has a least value \(m\) on \(\Phi(W)\). The function \(f - m\) is continuous and nowhere negative, so by the fifth part (4.31) holds for \(f - m\), and for the constant function \(1\) we get \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} |J_\Phi|\,\mathrm{d}V\).
  2. By the linearity of the integral on both sides, \(\int_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} f\,\mathrm{d}V - m\,V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} f(\Phi(P))\,|J_\Phi(P)|\,\mathrm{d}V - m\int_{\mathrm{W}} |J_\Phi|\,\mathrm{d}V\). The subtracted terms are equal by step 1, so (4.31) holds.
  3. In the plane (figure 4.108) the steps are the same, with squares instead of cubes, with \(\sqrt2\) instead of \(\sqrt3\), with areas and with the power \(2\) instead of \(3\). In the second part \(N = M/m_{\mathrm{J}}\), because by lemma 4.49 the elements of the inverse of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix are elements of the matrix or their opposites, divided by the determinant, the partial derivatives of the field \(H\) are at most \(2N\omega\) in absolute value, lemma 4.47 in the plane gives \(|H(P) - H(P_0)| \le 4N\omega\,|P_0 P|\), and \(\kappa = 4\sqrt2\,N\omega\).

Source: LEBL2 Theorem 10.7.2 (PDF pp. 134-137), with the integral from lower and upper sums and with a function \(f\) that is only integrable. KREYSZIG §10.3, (6) and (7) (PDF pp. 455-456), in the plane, without proof. The proof follows LEBL2: the image of a small rectangle in an enlarged rectangle, the inequality for \(g\), and the reverse inequality with the inverse map. The work with boundary cells instead of extending the function \(f\) by zero is not from the source.

The proof showed where the absolute value of the Jacobian comes from. On a small cube the map behaves almost like its linear part, and by theorem 4.58 this multiplies volume by \(|J_\Phi|\). Everything else was careful counting of errors: the uniform continuity of the partial derivatives gave an enlarged parallelepiped that is the same for all cubes, the lemma on boundary cells bounded the part at the boundary, and the inverse map gave the reverse inequality. For a linear map \(\Lambda\) the value \(|J_\Lambda| = |\det\mat A|\) is constant, and (4.31) with the function \(1\) gives \(V_{\Lambda(\mathrm{W})} = |\det\mat A|\,V_{\mathrm{W}}\), theorem 4.58.

Every hypothesis of the theorem entered the proof at its own place, and there we see what it is for.

  • Continuous partial derivatives. In the third part they change by less than \(\omega\) on a small cube, so \(G(C)\) stays in \(\tilde C\). The effect on the result is the factor \((1 + 2\kappa)^3\), which tends to \(1\).
  • \(J_\Phi \neq 0\). In the second part, step 3, it gives the inverse matrix with elements bounded by \(N = 2M^2/m_{\mathrm{J}}\), and in the fifth part the differentiable inverse map \(\Psi\). Where \(J_\Phi\) comes close to zero, \(m_{\mathrm{J}}\) tends to zero and the bound \(N\) grows beyond all bounds, so the estimate of the third part needs smaller and smaller cubes.
  • Injectivity. In the fourth part, step 6, the volumes of the images of the cells add up by lemma 4.57, and in the fifth part \(\Psi\) exists. Without it the right side counts the overlapped parts of the image several times, as the second of the examples below shows.
  • \(W\) is a set with volume. In the fourth part, step 2, the total volume of the boundary cells is less than \(\eta\).
  • \(f\) is continuous. In the first part the two integrals, over \(\Phi(W)\) and over \(W\), exist, in the fourth part \(f\) attains its greatest value \(\mu\) and its greatest value on every cell.

Let us test the theorem in the plane on the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s,\ t + s^2)\) of section 4.3.2, on the square \(W\), which is \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\), and with the function \(f(x, y) = y\) (figure 4.77). The matrix of partial derivatives has the rows \((1, 0)\) and \((2s, 1)\), so \(J_\Phi = 1\). The image of the square is the region between the graphs of the functions \(x^2\) and \(x^2 + 1\) over the interval \([0, 1]\). The vertical segments of the square only move up by \(s^2\), so the area does not change. The left side of (4.31) is, by theorem 4.33, the iterated integral

\[\int_0^1 \int_{\mathrm{x}^2}^{x^2 + 1} y\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^1 \frac{(x^2 + 1)^2 - x^4}{2}\,\mathrm{d}x = \int_0^1 \Big(x^2 + \frac12\Big)\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac56 ,\]

and the right side is

\[\int_0^1 \int_0^1 (t + s^2) \cdot 1\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s = \int_0^1 \Big(\frac12 + s^2\Big)\,\mathrm{d}s = \frac56 .\]

We checked both with SymPy. The function \(f(x, y) = y\) is the height of a point, and the integral is the area times the mean height. Every vertical segment of the square rises by \(s^2\), so the mean height grows from \(\tfrac12\) by the mean of the number \(s^2\) on \([0, 1]\), which is \(\tfrac13\).

The theorem demands injectivity, and its absence would go unnoticed if we computed only with the right side. Take the map \(\Phi(s, t) = (s^2, t)\) on the rectangle \(W\), which is \([-1, 1] \times [0, 1]\) and has area \(2\) (figure 4.111). It is continuously differentiable, with the rows \((2s, 0)\) and \((0, 1)\) of the derivative matrix, so \(J_\Phi = 2s\). The map is not injective: the points \((s, t)\) and \((-s, t)\) both map to the same point \((s^2, t)\). The rectangle folds along the segment \(s = 0\), and the left half falls onto the same square as the right half. The image is the square with area \(1\), which is \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) and is covered by two sheets. The right side of (4.31) with the function \(1\) is \(\int_{-1}^1 \int_0^1 |2s|\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s = \int_{-1}^1 2|s|\,\mathrm{d}s = 2\) (SymPy). The equality fails, \(1 \neq 2\), and the difference is no accident: every point of the image with \(x > 0\) is the image of two points of \(W\), so the integral on the right counts it twice, once for the blue sheet and once for the orange one. The same square as the image of the right half \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\), on which \(\Phi\) is injective, gives \(\int_0^1\int_0^1 2s\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s = 1\), which is the true area. The Jacobian determinant is also zero at \(s = 0\), which the theorem also forbids, but the segment \(s = 0\) has area zero and does not affect the integral. The double counting is caused by the missing injectivity.

We will first use the theorem in the next two subsections. In the first we answer with it the question of chapter 2 of how the volume of a piece of a body near a point changes. In the second we use its plane version to show that the surface integral does not depend on how we describe the surface, when a suitable map joins the two descriptions. Then in section 4.3.7 we prove with it the divergence theorem for bodies that we get when we bend a box continuously.

4.3.5 The volume of a small piece after loading

In chapter 2, section 2.10.5, we drew three short fibres with the vectors \(h\,\vek a\), \(h\,\vek b\) and \(h\,\vek c\) from a point \(P\) of a body and showed that the ratio of the volume of the parallelepiped of the vectors \(\mat F(h\,\vek a)\), \(\mat F(h\,\vek b)\), \(\mat F(h\,\vek c)\) to the volume of the piece before loading is exactly the Jacobian \(J = \det\mat F\) at the point \(P\). The true piece after loading, however, is not this parallelepiped, because its edges curve slightly. On the hanging bar we saw with numbers that the ratio of volumes approaches \(J\) for ever shorter fibres, but we did not prove a general statement, because it needs the volume of a body with curved faces and the rule for a change of variables. Now we have both.

Let us set up the model (figure 4.112, left). Before loading the body is a set of points contained in an open set \(D\) on which the displacement field \(\vek u\) is continuously differentiable (definition 1.91). A point \(P\) moves by the displacement vector \(\vek u(P)\) and goes after loading to the point \(\Phi(P) = P + \vek u(P)\). We call the map \(\Phi\) the deformation. A piece \(W\) around \(P\), drawn grey and dashed, goes with it to the set \(\Phi(W)\), drawn orange, and we ask for the ratio of their volumes. The components of the deformation are \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = x_{\mathrm{i}} + u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\), with the indices \(\ix{i}\) running over \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) as in section 1.18.4, so \(\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\). The matrix of partial derivatives of the map \(\Phi\) is the deformation gradient \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) (definition 1.113), and its Jacobian is \(J = \det\mat F\) of lemma 2.77 on the change of volume.

We assume three things. For each assumption let us say why it is justified, when it fails and what it does to the result (figure 4.114).

  1. The displacement field is continuously differentiable on \(D\). This is justified in a body without cracks, where two neighbouring points move almost equally. It fails at a crack or at a surface along which two parts slip: there the displacement jumps, the matrix \(\mat H\) does not exist and \(J\) has no value. Then we take each side of the crack as its own \(D\).
  2. The deformation is one-to-one: two different points of the material are not at the same point after loading. This is justified because the material does not pass through itself. The model alone does not guarantee it. Take the cubes \(W_1\) and \(W_2\) with the volume \(1\ \text{cm}^3\) and a displacement field that is zero on \(W_1\) and a constant vector \(\vek u\) on \(W_2\), which carries the second cube to the place of the first. On both cubes \(\mat H = \mat 0\) and \(J = 1\), but after loading both lie at the same place. The integral of \(J\) over both cubes is \(2\ \text{cm}^3\), while the space they occupy measures \(1\ \text{cm}^3\). Without a one-to-one deformation the integral counts the covered place twice.
  3. \(J > 0\) at every point of \(D\). This is justified by corollary 2.80 on the positive Jacobian: for gradual loading in which the material nowhere collapses to nothing, \(J\) is positive. It fails for a reflection. The field \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = -2x\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) carries a piece with the corners \(1\), \(2\), \(3\) across the plane \(x = 0\) to its mirror image, in which the corners follow each other the other way round. The deformation is one-to-one, but \(J = -1\). We cannot reach the mirror image gradually without the piece being squeezed into the plane on the way, where \(J = 0\). For a piece with the volume \(1\ \text{cm}^3\) the integral of \(J\) would give \(-1\ \text{cm}^3\), while the true volume is \(1\ \text{cm}^3\). This is why the change of variables theorem has \(|J|\), and the assumption \(J > 0\) lets us write \(J\) without the absolute value.
Corollary 4.60 Volume of a small piece after loading (prostornina majhnega koščka po obremenitvi)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points, the displacement field \(\vek u\) continuously differentiable on \(D\), the deformation \(\Phi(P) = P + \vek u(P)\) one-to-one on \(D\) (definition 4.45), and \(J(P) = \det\big(\mat I + \mat H(P)\big) > 0\) for every point \(P \in D\).

  1. For every set with volume \(W \subseteq D\), \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume and
    \[V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} J\,\mathrm{d}V . \tag{4.32}\]
  2. Let \(P \in D\). For every \(\eta > 0\) there is \(r > 0\) such that for every set with volume \(W\) with \(V_{\mathrm{W}} > 0\) all of whose points are closer to \(P\) than \(r\),
    \[\Big| \frac{V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})}}{V_{\mathrm{W}}} - J(P) \Big| < \eta .\]
  3. In particular, for the cube \(K_{\mathrm{h}}\) with centre \(P\) and edge \(h\), with edges parallel to the axes, for every \(\eta > 0\) there is \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|V_{\Phi(\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{h})}/h^3 - J(P)| < \eta\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < h < \delta\).
Proof

We must show three items. The first is the change of variables theorem with the function \(1\), the other two follow from the continuity of the function \(J\) at \(P\).

  1. The components of the deformation \(\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = x_{\mathrm{i}} + u_{\mathrm{i}}(P)\) have the partial derivatives \(\delta_{\mathrm{ij}} + \partial u_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}\), which are continuous on \(D\). The map \(\Phi\), which takes the point \(P\) to \(\Phi(P)\), is therefore continuously differentiable on \(D\), with the matrix of partial derivatives \(\mat F_\Phi = \mat I + \mat H\) and with the Jacobian \(J_\Phi = J\) (definition 4.42).
  2. By assumption \(\Phi\) is one-to-one and \(J_\Phi = J > 0\). By theorem 4.59, the change of variables theorem, with the function \(f = 1\), \(\Phi(W)\) is a set with volume and \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})} = \int_{\mathrm{W}} |J|\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{W}} J\,\mathrm{d}V\). This is item 1.
  3. The function \(J\) is a sum of products of continuous partial derivatives ((2.70)), and by corollary 1.70, item 1, it is continuous at \(P\). For \(\eta > 0\) there is therefore \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|J(Q) - J(P)| < \eta/2\) for every point \(Q\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\): closer to \(P\) than \(\delta\) the curve of \(J\) stays in the band between the horizontal lines \(J(P) - \eta/2\) and \(J(P) + \eta/2\) around the value \(J(P)\). Since \(D\) is open, there is \(r_0 > 0\) such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r_0\) are in \(D\). Let \(r\) be smaller than the numbers \(\delta\) and \(r_0\), the radius of the ball around \(P\).
  4. Let \(W\) be a set with volume with \(V_{\mathrm{W}} > 0\) all of whose points are closer to \(P\) than \(r\), so that it lies in the ball. Then \(W\) lies in \(D\), and above \(W\) we have \(J(P) - \eta/2 < J < J(P) + \eta/2\). The figure shows \(J\) along one line through \(P\), where the integral is the area under the curve, and this lies between the areas of the lower and the higher rectangle on the same base. In space the volume \(V_{\mathrm{W}}\) stands in place of the length of the base. By lemma 4.32, items 1 and 2,
    \[\Big(J(P) - \frac\eta2\Big)\,V_{\mathrm{W}} \le \int_{\mathrm{W}} J\,\mathrm{d}V \le \Big(J(P) + \frac\eta2\Big)\,V_{\mathrm{W}} .\]
  5. By item 1 the middle term is \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})}\). We divide by the positive number \(V_{\mathrm{W}}\) and get \(|V_{\Phi(\mathrm{W})}/V_{\mathrm{W}} - J(P)| \le \eta/2 < \eta\). This is item 2.
  6. The cube \(K_{\mathrm{h}}\) is a set with the volume \(h^3 > 0\) (lemma 4.32, item 6). Its points differ from the centre \(P\) in each coordinate by at most \(h/2\), so they are at a distance of at most \(\sqrt{(h/2)^2 + (h/2)^2 + (h/2)^2} = \sqrt3\,h/2\) from \(P\), as far as a corner. Let \(\delta = r\) of step 3. For \(0 < h < \delta\) we have \(\sqrt3\,h/2 < h < r\), the cube is all inside the ball of radius \(r\), and by item 2, \(|V_{\Phi(\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{h})}/h^3 - J(P)| < \eta\). This is item 3.

Source: CM (3.3.18)-(3.3.20) (PDF pp. 125-126), where \(\mathrm{d}v = J\,\mathrm{d}V\) is written for a parallelepiped of the vectors \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf X\), and CM (5.2.34), (5.2.35) (PDF p. 220), where the integral of the density over the body after loading is written, with \(\mathrm{d}\mathbf x = J\,\mathrm{d}\mathbf X\), as an integral over the body before loading. BOWER §2.1.4 (PDF pp. 46-47): \(\mathrm{d}V/\mathrm{d}V_0 = \det\mathbf F = J\). The proof is not from the sources.

The corollary says what in chapter 2 we saw only on an example, now for every piece and every continuously differentiable displacement field with a one-to-one deformation and a positive Jacobian. Which pieces? Every set with volume that lies close enough to the point \(P\): a cube with centre \(P\), a cube with a corner at \(P\), and also the parallelepiped spanned from \(P\) by the fibres \(h\,\vek a\), \(h\,\vek b\) and \(h\,\vek c\), which by theorem 4.58 is a set with the volume \(h^3\,|\det(\vek a, \vek b, \vek c)|\). The same holds for a ball around \(P\), once we have shown in section 4.3.7 that it is a set with volume. When the piece shrinks to the point \(P\), the ratio of the volumes after and before loading approaches \(J(P)\), whatever the shape of the piece. The first item says even more: the volume of every part of the body after loading is the integral of the Jacobian over this part before loading. The Jacobian is the density with which volumes add up.

Let us test this on the hanging bar of section 2.10.5. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with the radius of the cross section \(r = 5\) mm hangs under its own weight and is held in an idealized way: only the centre \(O\) of the top face is fixed, and the face is pulled up evenly by a force that carries the weight (section 1.7.1). The axis \(x\) points from \(O\) vertically down. The displacement field (1.19) is

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). Let us first check the assumptions of the corollary. For \(D\) we take the open box \((-1\ \text{m}, 11\ \text{m}) \times (-1\ \text{m}, 1\ \text{m}) \times (-1\ \text{m}, 1\ \text{m})\), which contains the bar. The components of the field are polynomials, so they are continuously differentiable. The partial derivatives are \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 2a\,(L - x)\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,y\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,y\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial z = -0{,}6\,a\,z\), \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial x = 0{,}6\,a\,z\), and the others are zero. In \(D\) we have \(|L - x| < 11\) m and \(|y|, |z| < 1\) m, so all of them are less than \(g = 2a \cdot 11\ \text{m} = 4{,}294 \cdot 10^{-6}\) in absolute value.

  1. The deformation is one-to-one on \(D\). The box \(D\) contains the segment between any two of its points. By lemma 4.47 on bounded derivatives and distances, applied to the map \(P \mapsto O + \vek u(P)\), whose components are \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(|\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)| \le 3g\,|PQ|\). Since \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{\Phi(P)\Phi(Q)} - \big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big)\), corollary 2.16 on the triangle inequality for vectors gives \(|PQ| \le |\Phi(P)\Phi(Q)| + 3g\,|PQ|\), so \(|\Phi(P)\Phi(Q)| \ge (1 - 3g)\,|PQ|\). For \(P \neq Q\) this is positive, so \(\Phi(P) \neq \Phi(Q)\).
  2. \(J > 0\) on \(D\). By lemma 2.77, item 2, \(J\) differs from \(1 + H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zz}}\) by at most \(6g^2 + 6g^3\), and the sum of the diagonal elements is at most \(3g\) in absolute value. Therefore \(J \ge 1 - 3g - 6g^2 - 6g^3 = 0{,}9999871\dots > 0\).

Now let us take the point \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\), where \(J(P) - 1 = 7{,}80798 \cdot 10^{-7}\), and the cube with a corner at \(P\) and edges of length \(h\) along the axes, as spanned by the fibres in section 2.10.5. We computed its volume after loading by (4.32) with SymPy, as the integral of the polynomial \(J\) over the cube. The table gives the ratios of the volumes after and before loading, reduced by \(1\), exactly and by the estimates of chapter 2:

\(h = 1\) mm \(h = 0{,}1\) mm
exact ratio \(V_{\Phi(\mathrm{K})}/h^3\), reduced by \(1\) \(7{,}80720 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(7{,}80790 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
difference from \(J(P) - 1 = 7{,}80798 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(-7{,}81 \cdot 10^{-11}\) \(-7{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\)
parallelepiped of the fibres after loading, reduced by \(1\) \(7{,}80603 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(7{,}80779 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
difference from \(J(P) - 1\) \(-1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-10}\) \(-1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-11}\)

The exact ratio approaches \(J(P)\), as item 2 of the corollary says, and the difference becomes ten times smaller with a ten times smaller edge (figure 4.116). On the left is the cube with edge \(1\) mm before loading (grey, dashed) and after it, with the corner \(P\) and the axes \(x\) and \(y\), and below it the difference between the ratio and \(J(P)\). On the right is the cube with edge \(0{,}1\) mm, which in the left figure is the small blackwhite frame at \(P\), drawn enlarged, and below it the ten times smaller difference.

What does the number \(J(P) - 1 = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\) mean in the figure? The edge of the cube along the axis \(x\) gets longer by \(1{,}95 \cdot 10^{-6}\) of its length \(h\), because at \(P\) the derivative is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = 2a\,(L - x_{\mathrm{P}}) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\). The edge along the axis \(y\) gets shorter by \(0{,}59 \cdot 10^{-6}\) of its length, because \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x_{\mathrm{P}}) = -0{,}5856 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and so does the edge along the axis \(z\), which is perpendicular to the plane of the figure. The volume is the product of the three edges, so relative changes this small add up:

\[1{,}9520 \cdot 10^{-6} - 0{,}5856 \cdot 10^{-6} - 0{,}5856 \cdot 10^{-6} = 0{,}7808 \cdot 10^{-6} .\]

This sum differs from \(J(P) - 1\) only by the products of two and three derivatives, together \(-1{,}9 \cdot 10^{-12}\) (lemma 2.77, item 2). So the piece stretches in the direction of the weight, gets thinner across it, and the stretching wins.

And where does the difference between the ratio and \(J(P)\) come from (figure 4.116)? By (4.32) the ratio is the mean of the function \(J\) over the cube. Its main part is \(J - 1 \approx 0{,}8\,a\,(L - x)\), the divergence of the field, which we computed in section 4.2.5, and it decreases with depth. The cube with a corner at \(P\) lies below \(P\), between the depths \(5\) m and \(5\ \text{m} + h\), so the mean equals the value at the depth \(5\ \text{m} + h/2\), the middle of the cube, which is \(0{,}8\,a\,h/2\) less than the value at \(P\). For \(h = 1\) mm this is \(0{,}8 \cdot 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 0{,}0005 = 7{,}81 \cdot 10^{-11}\), exactly the difference in the table. For the cube with centre \(P\) and edge \(1\) mm SymPy gave a difference of only \(-4 \cdot 10^{-21}\), because \(J\) is almost a linear function, and the mean of a linear function over a cube is its value at the centre, since the excess on one side of the centre cancels the deficit on the other. The parallelepiped of the fibres of chapter 2 is a different set: it is not the image of the cube but the parallelepiped spanned by the vectors of the fibres after loading. Its difference is different, but it also goes to zero.

Finally the whole bar. It is cut into the pieces \(C\), \(D\) and \(E\), so it is a set with volume (corollary 4.34, item 2). Its volume before loading is \(L A = 785\,400\ \text{mm}^3\), with the area of the cross section \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\) of section 4.2.8. The volume after loading is \(\int_{\mathrm{V}} J\,\mathrm{d}V\) by (4.32), so by linearity the change of volume is the integral of the function \(J - 1\) over the bar. SymPy gave

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} (J - 1)\,\mathrm{d}V = 0{,}6132369\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

Where do these \(0{,}613\ \text{mm}^3\) come from (figure 4.117)? The bar before loading is drawn grey and dashed, after it orange, the point \(O\) stays in place, the axis \(x\) points down. The lower end moves down by \(a L^2 = 0{,}0195\) mm. With an unchanged cross section such an elongation would add \(A \cdot 0{,}0195\ \text{mm} = 1{,}533\ \text{mm}^3\). At the same time the bar gets narrower: at the top, where it carries all the weight, the radius decreases by \(0{,}6\,a L r = 5{,}86\) nm, and at the bottom, below which there is no weight left, by nothing. The narrowing takes away \(0{,}920\ \text{mm}^3\), exactly \(0{,}6\) of the first contribution, and \(0{,}613\ \text{mm}^3\) remain. This breakdown adds only the first derivatives of the displacements, which is the divergence.

In section 4.2.12 we computed the change of volume of the bar with the divergence theorem as the flux of the displacements through the surface and got \(0{,}6132\ \text{mm}^3\), with SymPy to more digits \(0{,}6132389\ \text{mm}^3\), which is the integral of the divergence \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\). That computation was an approximation for small displacements: the flux \(\vek u\cdot\vek n\,\Delta A\) is only approximately the volume swept by a patch. The difference between the two numbers is \(0{,}6132369\ \text{mm}^3 - 0{,}6132389\ \text{mm}^3 = -2{,}0 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{mm}^3\). By (2.75), \(J - 1\) differs from the divergence by the second bracket and the term \(\det\mat H\), the terms with products of two and three partial derivatives, so \(-2{,}0 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{mm}^3\) is the integral of these terms. These are of the size \(a^2 L^2 \approx 4 \cdot 10^{-12}\), so the difference is smaller than the change itself by a factor of the order \(10^{-6}\). The exact change of volume is \(J - 1\) integrated over the body, and the divergence is its main part for small displacements.

4.3.6 Surfaces described by two parameters

In section 4.2.11 we integrated over the pieces of the surface of a body between two graphs. We described each piece with the two variables given by the description of the body: the top lid by the points \((x, y, h(x, y))\), the side piece in the plane \(x = a\) by the points \((a, y, z)\). The question remained whether the surface integral does not depend on how we describe the same surface. The part of the plane \(y = 3\) mm between the pieces \(C\) and \(D\) of the round bar is a side piece for the piece \(C\) and the bottom lid for the piece \(D\). In section 4.2.12 we checked the agreement of the two descriptions of this cut directly, because they gave the same iterated integral. In section 4.3.7, however, we will need surfaces that are not graphs over a rectangle, the surfaces of curved bodies, and there such a direct comparison will not be possible.

So we describe a surface more generally. A point of the surface is fixed by two numbers \(s\) and \(t\), which we call parameters (parametra), as the numbers \(x\) and \(y\) fix a point of a lid. The pair \((s, t)\) is a point of the plane of parameters, and the map \(\vek r\) assigns to it the position vector \(\vek r(s, t)\) of a point of the surface, the vector from the origin \(O\) to it, with the components \(r_{\mathrm{x}}(s, t)\), \(r_{\mathrm{y}}(s, t)\) and \(r_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t)\). We get the area of a small patch as for a lid (figure 4.118). On the left is the set \(M\) in the plane of parameters with the axes \(s\) and \(t\), on the right the surface with a mesh of the images of lines with constant \(s\) or \(t\). A small rectangle of the plane of parameters with the sides \(\Delta s\) and \(\Delta t\) goes to a patch that is almost a parallelogram spanned by the vectors \(\frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial s}\,\Delta s\) and \(\frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial t}\,\Delta t\), where \(\partial\vek r/\partial s\) is the vector of the partial derivatives of the components with respect to \(s\). By section 2.8.1 the area of the parallelogram is the length of the vector product of the sides, \(|\vek N|\,\Delta s\,\Delta t\) with \(\vek N\)\( = \frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial s}\times\frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial t}\), and this vector is perpendicular to both sides, so to the patch.

That the patch is almost a parallelogram is an assumption, and it enters here. It is right because \(\vek r\) is continuously differentiable: when \(s\) grows by \(\Delta s\), the point of the surface moves by \(\frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial s}\,\Delta s\) and by a correction that, for small enough \(\Delta s\), is an arbitrarily small part of this move. It fails at a crease of the surface, where the derivatives jump, which is why the definition below demands continuous derivatives. What the assumption costs is shown by a circle of radius \(5\) mm: the arc between the points \((3, 4)\) and \((4, 3)\) is \(1{,}41897\) mm long, and the straight chord between them \(1{,}41421\) mm, which is \(0{,}34\ \%\) less. For an arc half as long the difference is \(0{,}084\ \%\), a quarter of the previous one. So when we make the patches finer, the error of the sum of the parallelogram areas goes to zero, and the integral of the definition remains.

Definition 4.61 Surface described by two parameters (ploskev, opisana s parametroma)

Let \(M\) be a set with area (definition 4.27) in the plane whose points we write with the coordinates \(s\) and \(t\), and \(U\) an open set of this plane that contains \(M\). Let \(\vek r\) be a map that has as input a point \((s, t)\) of \(U\) and as output the vector \(\vek r(s, t) = \big(r_{\mathrm{x}}(s, t), r_{\mathrm{y}}(s, t), r_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t)\big)\), and that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(U\). At every point of the set \(M\) let

\[\vek N = \frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial s}\times\frac{\partial\vek r}{\partial t} \neq \vek 0 . \tag{4.33}\]

The set \(S\) of the points with the position vectors \(\vek r(s, t)\), \((s, t) \in M\), is a surface described by two parameters (ploskev, opisana s parametroma), the map \(\vek r\) on \(M\) is its description, and \(\vek N\) its normal vector (normalni vektor). For a function \(f\) that is continuous on \(S\), the surface integral (ploskovni integral) over \(S\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{S}} f\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{M}} f\big(\vek r(s, t)\big)\,\big|\vek N(s, t)\big|\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.34}\]

where \(f(\vek r(s, t))\) means the value of the function \(f\) at the point with the position vector \(\vek r(s, t)\). For a vector field \(\vek v\) that is continuous on \(S\), the flux (pretok) through \(S\) in the direction of the vector \(\vek N\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{M}} \vek v\big(\vek r(s, t)\big)\cdot\vek N(s, t)\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.35}\]

Source: KREYSZIG §10.5, (2), (4) (PDF pp. 466-467) for the description of a surface and the normal vector, §10.6, (3) (PDF p. 469) for the flux and (6), (8) (PDF p. 474) for the surface integral of a function and the area of a surface. KREYSZIG does not demand that the map be one-to-one and integrates only over a rectangle or a region of the plane.

The definition says what goes in. The set \(M\) is a part of the plane of parameters, and the map \(\vek r\) sends it onto the surface. Why do we demand that the map be one-to-one? So that the map covers no part of the surface twice. The map \(\vek r(s, t) = (s^2, t, 0)\) on the rectangle \([-1, 1] \times [0, 1]\) sends the points \((s, t)\) and \((-s, t)\) to the same point, and covers the square \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) in the plane \(z = 0\) twice. The integral (4.34) would then count every point twice. For the area of the square, which is \(1\), it would give \(2\): here \(\vek N = (2s, 0, 0)\times(0, 1, 0) = (0, 0, 2s)\) and \(\int_{-1}^{1} 2\,|s|\,\mathrm{d}s = 2\). Why \(\vek N \neq \vek 0\)? So that the surface has at every point a normal \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\), as a lid has in definition 4.36. The flux (4.35) is the integral of the function \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\) by (4.34), since \((\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N| = \vek v\cdot\vek N\), as we saw for a lid in lemma 4.37. The direction of the vector \(\vek N\) depends on the order of the parameters. When we exchange \(s\) and \(t\), the vector \(\vek N\) turns around by item 1 of lemma 2.34, and the flux changes sign.

Figure 4.119 shows both examples. On the left is the plane of parameters with the rectangle \([-1, 1] \times [0, 1]\), in it the points \((s, t)\) and \((-s, t)\), which the map \(\vek r(s, t) = (s^2, t, 0)\) sends to the same point of the square in the plane \(z = 0\). So the square is covered twice. On the right is the same plane of parameters with the line \(s = 0\), where the map \((s^3, t, 0)\) has no normal.

The condition \(\vek N \neq \vek 0\) rejects a map that differs from a suitable one in a single exponent. The map \(\vek r(s, t) = (s^3, t, 0)\) on \([-1, 1] \times [0, 1]\) describes the same rectangle of the plane \(z = 0\) as \(\vek r(s, t) = (s, t, 0)\). It is continuously differentiable and injective, because the cube increases. The derivatives are \(\partial\vek r/\partial s = (3s^2, 0, 0)\) and \(\partial\vek r/\partial t = (0, 1, 0)\), so \(\vek N = (0, 0, 3s^2)\). On the line \(s = 0\) we have \(\vek N = \vek 0\), and the normal \(\vek N/|\vek N|\) does not exist there. For \(\vek r(s, t) = (s, t, 0)\) we have \(\vek N = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}} \times \vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) everywhere. The condition therefore does not reject the surface but its description, since the plane itself has a normal. What would breaking the condition cost? The area comes out right even with the rejected description, \(\int_{-1}^{1} 3s^2\,\mathrm{d}s = 2\), the area of the rectangle \([-1, 1] \times [0, 1]\). So the condition does not protect the area but the unit normal \(\vek n\) at every point, with which we read the flux as the integral of the function \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\). On the right of figure 4.119 are the vectors \(\vek N = (0, 0, 3s^2)\), which shrink toward the line to zero, while the description \((s, t, 0)\) has the same vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) everywhere.

Let us state exactly that the integrals exist.

Figure 4.120 says what the proof shows. In the plane of parameters lies a point \((s, t)\) with a neighbourhood, and on the surface the normal vectors at this point and at a nearby point have a small difference. So the graph stays in the band when the point stays in the neighbourhood.

Lemma 4.62 Existence of the surface integral (obstoj ploskovnega integrala)

Let \(S\) be a surface with the description \(\vek r\) on the set \(M\) (definition 4.61), \(f\) a function continuous on \(S\), and \(\vek v\) a field continuous on \(S\). Then the functions under the integrals in (4.34) and (4.35) are continuous on \(M\), and both integrals exist. In figure 4.120 this means that the graph of the function stays inside an arbitrarily narrow band when the point stays in the neighbourhood.

Proof

We must show that the integrands are continuous and use the theorem on the existence of the integral. Continuity means that a neighbourhood of the point keeps the value in the band.

  1. The components of the map \(\vek r\) are continuously differentiable on \(U\), so they are continuous (lemma 1.92 in the plane). By lemma 4.35 the function \((s, t) \mapsto f(\vek r(s, t))\) is continuous on \(M\), and so are the components of the field \(\vek v\) at the points of the surface. The map \(\vek r\) sends the neighbourhood of the point to a small part of the surface, where \(f\) and \(\vek v\) stay in the band.
  2. The components of the vector \(\vek N\) are differences of products of the partial derivatives of the components of the map \(\vek r\), which are continuous, so by corollary 1.70, item 1, they are continuous. Each component falls in the band around its value at \((s, t)\) in the neighbourhood.
  3. The length \(|\vek N|\) is continuous. By corollary 2.16 on the triangle inequality for vectors, item 3, \(\big||\vek N(s, t)| - |\vek N(s_1, t_1)|\big| \le |\vek N(s, t) - \vek N(s_1, t_1)|\). The length of a vector is not larger than the sum of the absolute values of its components (step 3 of the proof of lemma 1.67), and by step 2 these are arbitrarily small when the point \((s_1, t_1)\) is close enough to the point \((s, t)\). The difference of the lengths is at most the length of the difference of the vectors.
  4. The integrands are products and sums of continuous functions and are continuous on \(M\). The set \(M\) has an area, so by theorem 4.31 the integrals exist. The integrand is continuous on the set \(M\), which has an area, and the graph does not jump anywhere.

Source: The lemma is not from the sources.

Figure 4.121 shows the body between the graphs over the rectangle \(R\) with the six pieces of its surface: the top lid \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\), the bottom lid \(S_{\mathrm{g}}\), the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\) at \(x = b\) and \(x = a\), and the side pieces \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) and \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\) at \(y = d\) and \(y = c\). From each piece an outward normal points out.

The pieces of the surface of a body between two graphs are special cases. Let the body lie between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15). We describe the top lid with the parameters \(s = x\) and \(t = y\), with the map \(\vek r(s, t) = (s, t, h(s, t))\) on \(M = R\). Its partial derivatives are \(\partial\vek r/\partial s = (1, 0, \partial h/\partial x)\) and \(\partial\vek r/\partial t = (0, 1, \partial h/\partial y)\), and by definition 2.33

\[\vek N = \Big( 0 \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \cdot 1,\ \ \frac{\partial h}{\partial x} \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot \frac{\partial h}{\partial y},\ \ 1 \cdot 1 - 0 \cdot 0 \Big) = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}} ,\]

the vector of definition 4.36. For the other five pieces we must choose the parameters in the right order, so that \(\vek N\) points out of the body, as the next lemma says. In the figure this is the lid \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) over the rectangle \(R\) with the normal \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\).

Lemma 4.63 Pieces of the surface of a body between two graphs as surfaces described by two parameters (kosi površine telesa med grafoma kot ploskve s parametroma)

Let \(V\) be a body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15). Each of the six pieces of its surface (definition 4.36) is a surface described by two parameters (definition 4.61), with the description: These are the six pieces of the body over the rectangle \(R\).

  1. the top lid \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (s, t, h(s, t))\) on \(M = [a, b] \times [c, d]\), with \(\vek N = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\), This is the top lid with the normal \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\).
  2. the bottom lid \(S_{\mathrm{g}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (t, s, g(t, s))\) on \(M = [c, d] \times [a, b]\), with \(\vek N = \vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\), This is the bottom lid with the normal \(\vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\).
  3. the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (b, s, t)\) on the set \(M\) of the points with \(c \le s \le d\) and \(g(b, s) \le t \le h(b, s)\), with \(\vek N = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), and the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{a}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (a, t, s)\) on the set of the points with \(c \le t \le d\) and \(g(a, t) \le s \le h(a, t)\), with \(\vek N = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), These are the side pieces, and the set \(M\) of the piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) is the region between the graphs.
  4. the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (t, d, s)\) on the set of the points with \(a \le t \le b\) and \(g(t, d) \le s \le h(t, d)\), with \(\vek N = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), and the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{c}}\): \(\vek r(s, t) = (s, c, t)\) on the set of the points with \(a \le s \le b\) and \(g(s, c) \le t \le h(s, c)\), with \(\vek N = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). These are the side pieces at the other two sides.

For a body in which the coordinate \(y\) runs between the graphs and whose rectangle lies in the plane of the variables \(z\) and \(x\), we read the first coordinate in these descriptions and in the vectors \(\vek N\) as \(z\), the second as \(x\) and the third as \(y\). For a body in which \(x\) runs between the graphs and whose rectangle lies in the plane of the variables \(y\) and \(z\), we read them as \(y\), \(z\) and \(x\). Renaming is a cyclic shift of the labels.

The surface integral (4.34) of every function continuous on a piece equals the integral over this piece as the definition of the integral over the surface of a body between graphs gives it, and the flux (4.35) equals the flux through the piece with the outward normal of the body. This is the integral over each of the six pieces, with the normals out of the body.

Proof

We must show that the descriptions really are descriptions by the definition, that the vectors \(\vek N\) are as the lemma says, and that the integrals agree. We check them on all six pieces.

  1. All the maps are defined on open sets of the plane. For the lids it is the open set \(U\) of definition 4.15, or the set of the points \((s, t)\) for which \((t, s) \in U\), which is open because swapping the coordinates keeps distances. For the side pieces it is the whole plane, where the components are polynomials of degree one. The components are continuously differentiable. For the lids this is a neighbourhood of the rectangle \(R\), for the side pieces a neighbourhood of the set \(M\).
  2. The maps are one-to-one, because the parameters can be read off the point \(\vek r(s, t)\) as two of its coordinates: for the top lid as \(x\) and \(y\), for the bottom one as \(y\) and \(x\), for \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) as \(y\) and \(z\), and similarly for the other pieces. A point of the lid \(S_{\mathrm{h}}\) is fixed by the point of the rectangle below it.
  3. The vectors \(\vek N\). For the top lid \(\vek N = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\), as we computed before the lemma. For the bottom one \(\partial\vek r/\partial s = (0, 1, \partial g/\partial y)\) and \(\partial\vek r/\partial t = (1, 0, \partial g/\partial x)\), and by definition 2.33 \(\vek N = \big(\frac{\partial g}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial y},\ -1\big) = \vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). For the side pieces the two partial derivatives are unit vectors of the axes, and by items 1 and 6 of lemma 2.34, \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). None of these vectors is the zero vector. The results are the normals of the figure.
  4. The sets \(M\). The rectangles have an area by lemma 4.32, item 6. For the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\), \(M\) is the region between the graphs of the functions \(s \mapsto g(b, s)\) and \(s \mapsto h(b, s)\) over the interval \([c, d]\). These functions are continuously differentiable on an open interval that contains \([c, d]\). By lemma 4.38, whose proof works the same way in the plane, there is \(\delta_0 > 0\) such that the points \((b, s)\) with \(c - \delta_0 < s < d + \delta_0\) lie in \(U\), where \(g\) and \(h\) have continuous partial derivatives with respect to \(y\). By theorem 4.33 in the plane, \(M\) has an area, and the integral of a continuous function over \(M\) is the iterated integral, first over \(t\) from \(g(b, s)\) to \(h(b, s)\) and then over \(s\) from \(c\) to \(d\). For the other side pieces it is the same. For the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) the set \(M\) is the region between the graphs.
  5. The integrals. For the lids the integral over the rectangle \(M\) is, by lemma 4.32, item 6, the iterated integral of definition 4.8, for the top lid \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d f(s, t, h(s, t))\,|\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}|\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s\), which is (4.18). For the bottom lid theorem 4.9 on the order of integration gives the same iterated integral, only with the names of the variables exchanged. For the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) we have \(|\vek N| = 1\), and by step 4 the integral is \(\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_{\mathrm{g}(\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{s})}^{h(b, s)} f(b, s, t)\,\mathrm{d}t\,\mathrm{d}s\), the integral of definition 4.36 with \(y = s\) and \(z = t\). For the other side pieces it is the same. Over a lid we integrate over the rectangle, over a side piece over the region \(M\).
  6. The fluxes. By step 3 the vectors \(\vek N\) are the vectors of definition 4.36, which point out of the body, so \(\vek v\cdot\vek N = (\vek v\cdot\vek n)\,|\vek N|\) with the outward unit normal \(\vek n\), and by step 5 the flux (4.35) is the integral of the function \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\) over the piece of definition 4.36. The normals of all pieces point out of the body.
  7. Renamed coordinates. When \(y\) runs between the graphs, a point or a vector with the components \((n_1, n_2, n_3)\) in the names of the lemma has the components \((n_2, n_3, n_1)\) along the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). For vectors \(\vek a\) and \(\vek b\) the vector product of the vectors \((a_2, a_3, a_1)\) and \((b_2, b_3, b_1)\) has, by definition 2.33, the components \((a_3 b_1 - a_1 b_3,\ a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1,\ a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2)\), which are the second, third and first components of the vector \(\vek a\times\vek b\). The vector product is therefore renamed in the same way as both factors, steps 1 to 6 hold with the renamed coordinates, and the vectors \(\vek N\) are the vectors of definition 4.36 with renamed coordinates, which point out of the body. When \(x\) runs between the graphs it is the same, with the same shift of the components once more. The labels shift cyclically.

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6 (PDF p. 470), where for a surface \(z = h(x, y)\) he gets \(\vek N = (-h_{\mathrm{x}}, -h_{\mathrm{y}}, 1)\). The lemma and the proof are not from the source.

Now the answer to the question from the beginning. Let a surface \(S\) have two descriptions, \(\vek r_1\) on \(M_1\) and \(\vek r_2\) on \(M_2\), and let there be a map \(\tau\) of the plane of parameters between them that assigns to a point \((s, t)\) of \(M_2\) the point \(\tau(s, t)\) of \(M_1\) that describes the same point of the surface: \(\vek r_2(s, t) = \vek r_1(\tau(s, t))\). We denote the components of the map \(\tau\) by \(\tau_{\mathrm{s}}\) and \(\tau_{\mathrm{t}}\), because they are the coordinates \(s\) and \(t\) in the plane of parameters of the first description. By the chain rule the vectors of partial derivatives of the second description, \(\partial\vek r_2/\partial s\) and \(\partial\vek r_2/\partial t\), are expressed by the vectors of partial derivatives of the first, and the vector product gives the first normal vector multiplied by the Jacobian of the map \(\tau\). This is exactly the factor that the change of variables theorem in the plane brings into the integral. Figure 4.122 shows it. On the left is the plane of parameters of the second description, in the middle that of the first and the map \(\tau\) between them, on the right the surface, to which \(\vek r_2\) and \(\vek r_1\) send them.

Figure 4.118 says the same without a calculation. The map \(\tau\) sends a small rectangle of the plane of parameters of the second description, with the sides \(\Delta s\) and \(\Delta t\), to a region of the plane of parameters of the first description with the area almost \(|J_\tau|\,\Delta s\,\Delta t\), and both describe the same patch of the surface. Its area is almost \(|\vek N_2|\,\Delta s\,\Delta t\) by the second description and almost \(|\vek N_1|\,|J_\tau|\,\Delta s\,\Delta t\) by the first, so \(|\vek N_2| = |J_\tau|\,|\vek N_1|\) must hold. This view adds the reason why the two factors agree: both measure how many times the area grows on the way from the plane of parameters to the surface.

Corollary 4.64 The surface integral does not depend on the description (ploskovni integral ni odvisen od opisa)

Let \(\vek r_1\) be a description of a surface \(S\) on the set \(M_1\) with the open set \(U_1 \supseteq M_1\) (definition 4.61), with the normal vector \(\vek N_1\). Let \(M_2\) be a set with area in the plane, \(U_2 \supseteq M_2\) an open set and \(\tau\) a map that has as input a point \((s, t)\) of \(U_2\) and as output the point \(\tau(s, t) = \big(\tau_{\mathrm{s}}(s, t), \tau_{\mathrm{t}}(s, t)\big)\) of \(U_1\), that is continuously differentiable (definition 4.42) and one-to-one (definition 4.45) on \(U_2\), with \(J_\tau \neq 0\) on \(U_2\), and let \(\tau(M_2) = M_1\). Let \(\vek r_2(s, t) = \vek r_1(\tau(s, t))\) for \((s, t) \in U_2\). Then:

  1. \(\vek r_2\) on \(M_2\) is a description of the same surface \(S\), and its normal vector is
    \[\vek N_2(s, t) = J_\tau(s, t)\,\vek N_1\big(\tau(s, t)\big) . \tag{4.36}\]
  2. For every function \(f\) continuous on \(S\) the surface integrals (4.34) with the two descriptions are equal. The sum over the patches is the same, only that the rectangles of the second description give regions with \(|J_\tau|\) times larger area.
  3. For every field \(\vek v\) continuous on \(S\) the fluxes (4.35) with the two descriptions are equal if \(J_\tau > 0\) on \(M_2\), and opposite if \(J_\tau < 0\) on \(M_2\). The normals \(\vek N_1\) and \(\vek N_2\) point to the same side of the surface for \(J_\tau > 0\) and to opposite sides for \(J_\tau < 0\).
Proof

We must show that the normal vector gets multiplied by \(J_\tau\), and then use the change of variables theorem in the plane. This is \(\vek N_2\) as a \(J_\tau\)-multiple of \(\vek N_1\).

  1. The map \(\vek r_2\) is continuously differentiable on \(U_2\) by lemma 4.43 on the chain rule, applied to each component of the map \(\vek r_1\) composed with \(\tau\). It is one-to-one, because each of the maps \(\tau\) and \(\vek r_1\) is one-to-one: from \(\vek r_1(\tau(P)) = \vek r_1(\tau(Q))\) it follows that \(\tau(P) = \tau(Q)\) and then \(P = Q\). Since \(\tau(M_2) = M_1\), the set of the points with the position vectors \(\vek r_2(s, t)\), \((s, t) \in M_2\), is \(S\). The composed map goes from \(M_2\) by \(\tau\) to \(M_1\) and by \(\vek r_1\) onto the surface.
  2. Let \((s, t) \in U_2\) and \(\vek p = \frac{\partial\vek r_1}{\partial s}(\tau(s, t))\), \(\vek q = \frac{\partial\vek r_1}{\partial t}(\tau(s, t))\). These are the vectors that span the parallelogram of the first description, without the factors \(\Delta s\) and \(\Delta t\). By lemma 4.43 on the chain rule
    \[\frac{\partial\vek r_2}{\partial s} = \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial s}\,\vek p + \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{t}}}{\partial s}\,\vek q , \qquad \frac{\partial\vek r_2}{\partial t} = \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial t}\,\vek p + \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{t}}}{\partial t}\,\vek q ,\]
    with the derivatives of the components of the map \(\tau\) at the point \((s, t)\).
  3. We expand the vector product by items 2 and 3 of lemma 2.34. We get four terms, with \(\vek p\times\vek p\), \(\vek p\times\vek q\), \(\vek q\times\vek p\) and \(\vek q\times\vek q\). By item 1 of the same lemma the first and the last are zero, and \(\vek q\times\vek p = -\vek p\times\vek q\). Therefore
