    \[\vek N_2 = \Big( \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial s}\,\frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{t}}}{\partial t} - \frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{t}}}{\partial s}\,\frac{\partial\tau_{\mathrm{s}}}{\partial t} \Big)\,\vek p\times\vek q = J_\tau\,\vek N_1(\tau(s, t)) ,\]
    because the bracket is the determinant of the matrix of partial derivatives of the map \(\tau\) (definition 4.42, definition 2.72 for \(2 \times 2\) matrices). This is (4.36): the vector \(\vek N_2\) lies on the same line as \(\vek N_1 = \vek p\times\vek q\), is \(|J_\tau|\) times as long, and is turned around when \(J_\tau < 0\). Since \(J_\tau\) and \(\vek N_1(\tau(s, t))\) are nonzero for \((s, t) \in M_2\), we have \(\vek N_2 \neq \vek 0\), and \(\vek r_2\) meets all the requirements of a description. So the first item of the corollary holds.
  4. By (4.36), \(|\vek N_2| = |J_\tau|\,|\vek N_1 \circ \tau|\), so the integrand of the second description is \(f(\vek r_2)\,|\vek N_2| = \big(f(\vek r_1)\,|\vek N_1|\big)(\tau(s, t))\,|J_\tau(s, t)|\). The area of the patch is by the second description \(|\vek N_2|\) times the area of the rectangle, by the first \(|\vek N_1|\) times the area of the region, which is \(|J_\tau|\) times larger.
  5. The function \(F = f(\vek r_1)\,|\vek N_1|\) is continuous on \(M_1 = \tau(M_2)\) by lemma 4.62. By theorem 4.59, the change of variables theorem in the plane, with the map \(\tau\), the open set \(U_2\) and the set with area \(M_2\),
    \[\int_{\mathrm{M}_1} F\,\mathrm{d}A = \int_{\mathrm{M}_2} F\big(\tau(s, t)\big)\,\big|J_\tau(s, t)\big|\,\mathrm{d}A .\]
    The left side is the surface integral with the first description, the right side by step 4 the one with the second. This is item 2.
  6. The flux. By (4.36), \(\vek v(\vek r_2)\cdot\vek N_2 = J_\tau\,\big(\vek v(\vek r_1)\cdot\vek N_1\big)(\tau)\). For \(J_\tau > 0\) on \(M_2\) we have \(J_\tau = |J_\tau|\), and as in step 5 the fluxes are equal. For \(J_\tau < 0\) we have \(J_\tau = -|J_\tau|\), and by the linearity of the integral (lemma 4.32, item 1) the flux with the second description is opposite to the flux with the first. This is item 3. For \(J_\tau < 0\) the vector \(\vek N_2\) is reversed relative to \(\vek N_1\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.6, Theorem 1 (PDF p. 472): replacing the vector \(\vek N\) by \(-\vek N\) multiplies the flux by \(-1\). KREYSZIG does not prove the independence of the description for surfaces. The proof with the change of variables theorem is not from the source.

For the flux only the direction of the normal vector counts. The flux through a surface is the sum of \(\vek v\cdot\vek n\,\Delta A\), and two descriptions with \(J_\tau > 0\) give the same direction of the normal, two with \(J_\tau < 0\) opposite ones. The surface integral of a function, however, does not know the direction, because it has only \(|\vek N|\). In the figure this is the direction of \(\vek N_1\) and \(\vek N_2\), which lie on the same line.

Let us test the corollary on the cut \(y = 3\) mm between the pieces \(C\) and \(D\) of the round hanging bar (section 4.2.6, figure 4.123, left), in the plane with the axes \(y\) and \(z\), where the disc also has the cut \(y = -3\) mm and the left piece \(E\). We write the coordinates \(y\) and \(z\) in millimetres. For the piece \(C\) the cut is the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{d}}\) with \(d = 3\), and by lemma 4.63 we describe it by \(\vek r_1(s, t) = (t, 3, s)\) on \(M_1 = [-4, 4] \times [0, L]\), where \(s\) is the coordinate \(z\) and \(t\) the coordinate \(x\), with \(\vek N_1\)\( = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). For the piece \(D\), in which \(y\) runs between the graphs, the cut is the bottom lid, the graph of the constant function \(3\) over the rectangle \([0, L] \times [-4, 4]\) in the variables \(x\) and \(z\). By lemma 4.63, item 2, with the first coordinate \(z\), the second \(x\) and the third \(y\), we describe it by \(\vek r_2(s, t) = (s, 3, t)\) on \(M_2 = [0, L] \times [-4, 4]\), with \(\vek N_2\)\( = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). We have \(\vek r_2(s, t) = \vek r_1(t, s)\), so \(\tau(s, t) = (t, s)\), with the matrix of partial derivatives with the rows \((0, 1)\) and \((1, 0)\) and with \(J_\tau = -1\). By the corollary the surface integrals are equal, both are the area \(8\ \text{mm} \cdot L\), because the cut reaches from \(z = -4\) to \(z = 4\), while the fluxes are opposite. This is exactly the condition on the pairs of corollary 4.40.

The second test is curved. On the mantle of the bar let us take the strip between the points \((y, z) = (3, 4)\) and \((4, 3)\) of the cross section, along the whole length of the bar (figure 4.123, right), in the plane with the axes \(y\) and \(z\). The strip lies on the top lid of the piece \(D\), which is the graph \(y = q(z)\) with \(q(t) = \sqrt{25 - t^2}\), for \(z\) between \(3\) and \(4\). But we can also describe it as the graph \(z = q(y)\) for \(y\) between \(3\) and \(4\), like the top lid of the piece \(C\), only over another interval.

  1. The first description, as for the piece \(D\): \(\vek r_1(s, t) = (t, q(s), s)\) on \(M_1 = [3, 4] \times [0, L]\), with \(s = z\) and \(t = x\). By lemma 4.16, \(q'(s) = -s/q(s)\), so \(\partial\vek r_1/\partial s = (0, q'(s), 1)\), \(\partial\vek r_1/\partial t = (1, 0, 0)\) and \(\vek N_1\)\( = \big(0,\ 1,\ s/q(s)\big)\).
  2. The second description, as for the piece \(C\): \(\vek r_2(s, t) = (s, t, q(t))\) on \(M_2 = [0, L] \times [3, 4]\), with \(s = x\) and \(t = y\), and \(\vek N_2\)\( = \big(0,\ t/q(t),\ 1\big)\).
  3. For \(t\) between \(0\) and \(5\) we have \(q(q(t)) = \sqrt{25 - (25 - t^2)} = t\), so \(\vek r_2(s, t) = \vek r_1(q(t), s)\) and \(\tau(s, t) = (q(t), s)\). The matrix of partial derivatives has the rows \((0, q'(t))\) and \((1, 0)\), so \(J_\tau = -q'(t) = t/q(t)\), for \(t\) between \(3\) and \(4\) between \(\tfrac34\) and \(\tfrac43\), positive. The map \(\tau\) is continuously differentiable and one-to-one on the open set of the points with \(0 < t < 5\), because \(q\) decreases on \((0, 5)\). In the figure \(\tau\) is the map between the intervals that the arc gets as \(z\) and as \(y\), and \(J_\tau\) is the ratio of the lengths of the two normals.
  4. Let us check (4.36): \(J_\tau\,\vek N_1(\tau(s, t)) = \frac{t}{q(t)}\,\big(0,\ 1,\ q(t)/t\big) = \big(0,\ t/q(t),\ 1\big) = \vek N_2\). In the figure at the point of the arc \(\vek N_2\) is shorter than \(\vek N_1\) exactly by \(J_\tau\).

The area of the strip is, with both descriptions, \(L \cdot 1{,}41897\) mm, where \(1{,}41897\) mm is the length of the circular arc between the two points, computed by SymPy. The flux of the displacement field of the hanging bar, with \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\), \(L = 10\) m and the radius \(r = 5\) mm, is \(-0{,}041547\ \text{mm}^3\) with both descriptions. The figure shows what this number is. As the bar gets thinner, the strip moves towards the axis, from its place before loading to its place after it, by \(\delta = 0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,r\). At the top of the bar, at \(x = 0\), this is \(5{,}856\) nm, at the lower end zero, so on average \(2{,}928\) nm, and the figure exaggerates the move strongly. The strip sweeps a volume that is the length of the arc times the length of the bar times the average move, \(1{,}41897\ \text{mm} \cdot 10^4\ \text{mm} \cdot 2{,}928 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{mm} = 0{,}041547\ \text{mm}^3\). The minus sign says that it sweeps it inwards. The integrands differ. In the first description the point of the surface is \((t, q(s), s)\), so \(x = t\) and \(\vek u\cdot\vek N_1 = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - t)\,\big(q(s) + s^2/q(s)\big) = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - t) \cdot 25/q(s)\), because \(q(s)^2 + s^2 = 25\). In the second the point is \((s, t, q(t))\), so \(x = s\) and \(\vek u\cdot\vek N_2 = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - s) \cdot 25/q(t)\). We integrate the first integrand over \(M_1\), the second over \(M_2\), and the integrals are equal, as the change of variables theorem says. Since \(J_\tau > 0\), both descriptions give the normal that points out of the bar.

With this we have answered the question from the beginning of the subsection: when two descriptions of the same surface are joined by a map \(\tau\) with the assumptions of the corollary, the surface integral does not depend on the description, and the flux depends only on the side to which the normal vector points. That any two descriptions of the same surface have such a map we do not prove in the book. We do not need it, because in every case we meet we write the map \(\tau\) down explicitly, as in the two tests. In section 4.3.7 we will use surfaces described by two parameters to describe the surface of bodies that are images of boxes, and prove the divergence theorem for them. In figure 4.122 this is the map \(\tau\) between the planes of parameters, which both go to the same surface.

4.3.7 Curved boxes and the divergence theorem

So far we have proved the divergence theorem for a box and a body made of boxes (theorem 4.14), for a body between two graphs (theorem 4.39) and for a body cut into pieces between graphs (corollary 4.40). We cut the round bar into three pieces, because it is curved only in its cross section and straight along its axis. A ball is curved in all directions. Each of its pieces that reaches the surface would need a graph over a rectangle as its lid, and the pieces would have to meet in whole pieces of their surfaces. We will not look for such a cut. We will, however, need a ball and a thick spherical shell, the body between two spheres with a common centre, in chapter 11, and in chapter 15 bodies that the finite element method cuts into small six-faced pieces with curved faces. For them we need the divergence theorem in a form that does not rely on graphs.

The idea is simple. We know the box. If we bend and stretch a box continuously, without tearing it or folding it over itself, we get a body with curved faces. For instance, the deformation \(P \mapsto P + \vek u(P)\) of chapter 1 maps a box of material before loading into the body that this material occupies after loading. We will build the ball from a cube in the middle and six bent boxes, one over each face of the cube (figure 4.129). For a bent box we get the divergence theorem from the theorem for a box. A change of variables carries the integral over the bent box to the box, there we use theorem 4.14, and the faces of the box are mapped onto the curved faces of the body.

The route is this. First we say exactly what a bent box is, define the vectors of its faces and show that they point out of the body. Then we prove an identity for the second derivatives of the map, with it the divergence theorem for a bent box, and a corollary for a body made of such boxes and of bodies between graphs. At the end we cut a ball of radius 10 mm, a thick spherical shell and a ring into such pieces and test the theorem with numbers.

Definition 4.65 Curved box (ukrivljen kvader)

Let \(K = [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\) be a box, \(D\) an open set of points that contains \(K\), and \(\Phi\) a map on \(D\) (definition 4.42) whose input is a point \(P = (x, y, z)\) of \(D\) and whose output is the point \(\Phi(P) = \big(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}(P), \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}(P), \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(P)\big)\). Let:

  1. the components \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) of the map have at every point of \(D\) partial derivatives of the first and second order (definition 1.130), continuous at every point of \(D\),
  2. \(\Phi\) be one-to-one on \(D\) (definition 4.45): it maps two different points of \(D\) to two different points (not like the points \(P\) and \(Q\) with the same image, which we exclude),
  3. the Jacobian \(J_\Phi = \det\mat F_\Phi\) be positive at every point of \(D\), otherwise the map would turn the image over like the flag.

The set \(V = \Phi(K)\), the image of the box \(K\), is a curved box (ukrivljen kvader). The columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\), the vectors \(\partial\Phi/\partial x\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial y\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\) of the partial derivatives of the components, are multiplied two at a time by the vector product:

\[\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} = \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y}\times\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z} , \qquad \vek N_{\mathrm{y}} = \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}\times\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial x} , \qquad \vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial x}\times\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y} . \tag{4.37}\]

The surface (površina) \(S\) of the curved box has six faces, which are the images of the faces of the box \(K\):

  • the faces \(z = b_3\) and \(z = a_3\) are the sets of the points \(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\) and \(\Phi(x, y, a_3)\) with \((x, y) \in [a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2]\), with the face vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, b_3)\) and \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, a_3)\),
  • the faces \(x = b_1\) and \(x = a_1\) are the sets of the points \(\Phi(b_1, y, z)\) and \(\Phi(a_1, y, z)\) with \((y, z) \in [a_2, b_2] \times [a_3, b_3]\), with the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}(b_1, y, z)\) and \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}(a_1, y, z)\),
  • the faces \(y = b_2\) and \(y = a_2\) are the sets of the points \(\Phi(x, b_2, z)\) and \(\Phi(x, a_2, z)\) with \((x, z) \in [a_1, b_1] \times [a_3, b_3]\), with the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}(x, b_2, z)\) and \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}(x, a_2, z)\), which point out of the body like the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\).

On a face with the vector \(\vek N\) the outward unit normal is \(\vek n = \vek N/|\vek N|\), the face vector with length 1. The flux (pretok) of a field \(\vek v\) through the face \(z = b_3\) is the number

\[\int_{\mathrm{a}_1}^{b_1}\int_{\mathrm{a}_2}^{b_2} \vek v\big(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\big)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, b_3)\,\mathrm{d}y\,\mathrm{d}x , \tag{4.38}\]

and through the other faces likewise, with the face vector and the iterated integral over the rectangle on which the face is described (definition 4.8). The integral of a function \(f\) over a face is the same iterated integral of the function \(f(\Phi)\,|\vek N|\). The flux through the surface \(S\), \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\), is the sum of the fluxes through the six faces.

Source: The definition is not from the sources. KREYSZIG §10.6, (2) (PDF p. 469) describes a surface by two parameters and its normal as the vector product of the derivatives with respect to the parameters. COOK §6.5 (PDF p. 231) describes six-faced isoparametric finite elements as images of a cube whose faces are the images of the faces of the cube.

The definition says what goes in. The box \(K\) and the map \(\Phi\) are given, and the curved box \(V\) is the set of points to which \(\Phi\) maps the points of the box (figure 4.124). In the figure, on the left is the box with its top face and the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) pointing out of it, in space with the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\), and on the right its image with the edges that we cannot see. At a point of the top face of the image are the tangent vectors \(\partial\Phi/\partial x\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial y\), a third vector \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\) and a vector perpendicular to the first two, and on the front face a similar vector perpendicular to the face. This is the exact form of the bent box from the start of the section.

Each of the three conditions has its task, and for each let us say why we may demand it, when it fails and what then happens to the theorem. The second derivatives will be needed in the proof of the divergence theorem, where we will differentiate the face vectors, which are built from the first derivatives. In our examples this condition costs nothing, because the maps with which we will cut the ball, the shell and the ring are built from polynomials and the root of a positive polynomial and have continuous derivatives of all orders. It fails for a box bent with a sharp crease, where the first derivatives jump and the second do not exist. We cut such a piece along the crease into two curved boxes, when on each side of the crease the map is a part of a map that satisfies the conditions. The one-to-one property, the condition that \(\Phi\) maps two different points to two different points, ensures that the box does not overlap itself when it is bent, and the change of variables theorem 4.59 needs it. When it fails, the change of variables counts the part of the body that is covered twice twice (figure 4.125, bottom, an example with numbers follows). A positive Jacobian says that no small cube in \(K\) is flattened, which the change of variables theorem also needs, and that none is mirrored, which will make the face vectors point out of the body. When it is negative, the face vector points into the body and the flux gets the opposite sign (the same figure, top). For the deformation of a body the last two conditions are physical. Material does not penetrate itself, and the Jacobian is the ratio of the volumes of a small piece after and before loading, which is positive (corollary 2.80).

The face vectors are vector products of columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\), just as the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\) in section 4.2.11 was the vector product of the sides of a patch on a lid. On the face \(z = b_3\) the point \(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\) moves by about \(\Delta x\,\partial\Phi/\partial x\) for a small step \(\Delta x\) and by about \(\Delta y\,\partial\Phi/\partial y\) for a step \(\Delta y\), that is, along the two vectors that lie in the face. The theorem 1.89 on the change of a field over a short step says so, applied to each component. A small patch of the face is therefore nearly a parallelogram with the sides \(\Delta x\,\partial\Phi/\partial x\) and \(\Delta y\,\partial\Phi/\partial y\), and the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\), multiplied by \(\Delta x\,\Delta y\), is perpendicular to it and as long as the area of the parallelogram. The approximation here only explains why \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) stands in the flux (4.38). The flux itself is an exact integral, so the approximation brings no error into the theorem. The columns are \(\partial\Phi/\partial x = \mat F_\Phi\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial y = \mat F_\Phi\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), so by Nanson's formula (2.138) \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = J_\Phi\,\mat F_\Phi^{-\T}(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}) = J_\Phi\,\mat F_\Phi^{-\T}\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The face vector is therefore the vector of Nanson's formula for the face of the box with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Where does the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) point? We take its scalar product with the third column. By the definition of the determinant 2.72 and the cyclic exchange of the columns (lemma 2.73, item 1)

\[\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = \det\Big(\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}, \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y}\Big) = \det\Big(\frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial\Phi}{\partial z}\Big) = J_\Phi > 0 .\]

The vector \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\) says where the point \(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\) moves when \(z\) is increased a little. The points \(\Phi(x, y, b_3 + h)\) with a small \(h > 0\) do not lie in \(V\), because the point \((x, y, b_3 + h)\) is not in \(K\) and \(\Phi\) does not map two different points to the same point. The vector \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\) therefore points from the face out of the body, and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) points to the same side of the face, because their scalar product is positive. The same holds on the other faces, on the face \(z = a_3\) for instance with the vectors \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(-\partial\Phi/\partial z\). With a negative Jacobian all face vectors would point into the body.

Let us look at this on the reflection \(\Phi(x, y, z) = (x, y, 1 - z)\) of the cube \(K = [0, 1]^3\) (figure 4.125, top, a section in the plane with the axes \(x\) and \(z\)). Into the cube \(K\) we draw a flag, to see what the map does with it, we thicken the top face \(z = 1\) and put its outward normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) on it. The map is smooth and injective, the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\) has the columns \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), so \(J_\Phi = -1 < 0\). The image is again the cube \([0, 1]^3\), only the flag is upside down. It differs from the true cube only in the sign of \(J_\Phi\). The face vector of the face \(z = 1\) is \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}} \times \vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The face \(z = 1\) maps to \(\Phi(x, y, 1) = (x, y, 0)\), the bottom face of the cube, whose outward normal is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) therefore points into the body, and the scalar product with the third column is \(-\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} \cdot \vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = -1 = J_\Phi\), exactly as in the equation above. Likewise the face \(z = 0\) maps to the top face, where the outward normal is \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), while the face vector \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = -\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) points inward. For the field \(\vek v = (0, 0, z)\) with \(\mathrm{div}\,\vek v = 1\) the true flux through the surface of the cube is \(1\), since \(1\) flows through the top face and \(0\) through the bottom. With the face vectors, however, we get \(\vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) on the image of the face \(z = 1\) and \(\vek v\cdot(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}) = -1\) on the image of the face \(z = 0\), together \(-1\). The flux has lost its sign, and this is exactly \(\int_{\mathrm{K}} (\mathrm{div}\,\vek v)(\Phi)\,J_\Phi\,\mathrm{d}V = -1\). The condition \(J_\Phi > 0\) rejects the reflection, not smoothness or injectivity.

We test the one-to-one property in the same way, on a map that has a positive Jacobian and still maps two points to the same point. Take the box \(K = [-1, 1] \times [0, 1] \times [\tfrac14, 1]\) and the map

\[\Phi(x, y, z) = \big(x^3 - 3xz^2,\ y,\ 3x^2 z - z^3\big) ,\]

which does not change the coordinate \(y\), so we draw it in the section by the plane \(y = 0\) (figure 4.125, bottom). The components are polynomials, and the Jacobian is \(J_\Phi = 9\,(x^2 + z^2)^2\) (SymPy). It is positive everywhere except on the \(y\) axis, which is at the distance \(\tfrac14\) from the box. So the first and the third condition hold. The points \(P = (1, 0, \tfrac12)\) and \(Q = (-\tfrac12 - \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4},\ 0,\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} - \tfrac14)\), about \((-0{,}933, 0, 0{,}616)\), both lie in \(K\). They are equally far from the \(y\) axis, and the grey dashed segments to them enclose a third of a full turn. When we insert them into \(\Phi\), we get both times the same point \((\tfrac14, 0, \tfrac{11}{8})\) (SymPy). For the map winds the image of the box around the \(y\) axis by more than one turn, and covers one part twice. Two parts of the box map onto it, one with the point \(P\) and the other with the point \(Q\). What does this do to the theorem? The integral of the Jacobian over \(K\) is \(\tfrac{26199}{2560} = 10{,}23\) (SymPy), but the volume of the image is only \(9{,}04\), because the part covered twice, of volume \(1{,}20\), is counted twice (NumPy). The change of variables, on which the proof of the divergence theorem will rest, would give a wrong number for this body. A cut helps. The plane \(x = 0\) divides \(K\) into two boxes, on each the map is one-to-one, and each half is a curved box.

Each face is a surface described by two parameters (definition 4.61). The face \(z = b_3\) is described by the function \(\vek r(x, y) = \Phi(x, y, b_3)\) on the rectangle \([a_1, b_1] \times [a_2, b_2]\), which has an area. The function is continuously differentiable on the set of the points \((x, y)\) of the plane for which \((x, y, b_3)\) is in \(D\). This set is open, because \(D\) is open, and it contains the rectangle. On it \(\vek r\) does not map two different points to the same point, and its normal vector \(\partial\vek r/\partial x\times\partial\vek r/\partial y = \vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) is not the zero vector, because its scalar product with \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\) is positive. The integral over a rectangle is the iterated integral (lemma 4.32, item 6), so (4.38) is the flux of definition 4.61. For the face \(z = a_3\) we take the parameters in the reverse order, \(\vek r(y, x) = \Phi(x, y, a_3)\), so that \(\partial\vek r/\partial y\times\partial\vek r/\partial x = -\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) by item 1 of lemma 2.34. For the faces \(x = b_1\) and \(x = a_1\) the parameters are \((y, z)\) and \((z, y)\), for the faces \(y = b_2\) and \(y = a_2\) they are \((z, x)\) and \((x, z)\).

Let us try the definition on bodies we already know. For the map \(\Phi(P) = P\) we have \(\mat F_\Phi = \mat I\) with the columns \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and by item 6 of lemma 2.34 \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\). The curved box is then the box \(K\) itself, the face vectors are the outward normals of figure 4.31, and the flux is the sum of the integrals over the outer faces of a body made of boxes (definition 4.11, item 3).

The second is the body between the graphs of the functions \(g\) and \(h\) over the rectangle \(R = [a, b] \times [c, d]\) (definition 4.15) for which \(g < h\) at every point of \(R\) and \(g\) and \(h\) have continuous partial derivatives of the first and second order on an open set \(U\). The set \(U'\) of the points of \(U\) at which \(h > g\) is open, because the continuity of the function \(h - g\) at such a point, written with an error equal to half the value of \(h - g\) there, gives a disc in which \(h - g > 0\). It contains \(R\). On the open set \(D\) of the points \((x, y, z)\) with \((x, y) \in U'\) let the map \(\Phi\) and the box \(K\) be

\[\Phi(x, y, z) = \Big(x,\ y,\ g(x, y) + z\,\big(h(x, y) - g(x, y)\big)\Big) , \qquad K = [a, b] \times [c, d] \times [0, 1] .\]

At \(z = 0\) the point \(\Phi(x, y, z)\) lies on the bottom lid, at \(z = 1\) on the top lid, and in between \(z\) divides the vertical segment between the lids evenly. The first two rows of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\) are \((1, 0, 0)\) and \((0, 1, 0)\), and the third has \(h - g\) in its last place, so by (2.70) \(J_\Phi = h - g > 0\). Two points with the same image have the same \(x\) and \(y\), and \(g + z\,(h - g) = g + z'\,(h - g)\) gives \(z = z'\), because \(h - g \neq 0\). On the face \(z = 1\) we have \(\partial\Phi/\partial x = (1, 0, \partial h/\partial x)\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial y = (0, 1, \partial h/\partial y)\), so \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = (-\partial h/\partial x, -\partial h/\partial y, 1) = \vek N_{\mathrm{h}}\), the vector of the top lid of definition 4.36. On the face \(z = 0\) likewise \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek N_{\mathrm{g}}\). On the face \(x = b\) we have \(\partial\Phi/\partial y = (0, 1, \cdot)\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial z = (0, 0, h - g)\), so \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} = (h - g, 0, 0)\), and the flux is

\[\int_{\mathrm{c}}^d \int_0^1 v_{\mathrm{x}}\big(b, y, g + z\,(h - g)\big)\,(h - g)\,\mathrm{d}z\,\mathrm{d}y ,\]

where \(g\) and \(h\) are taken at the point \((b, y)\). The inner integral is \(\int_{\mathrm{g}}^h v_{\mathrm{x}}(b, y, w)\,\mathrm{d}w\). Indeed, the function \(G(w) = \int_{\mathrm{g}}^w v_{\mathrm{x}}(b, y, \omega)\,\mathrm{d}\omega\) has by the fundamental theorem of calculus 3.55, item 2, the derivative \(v_{\mathrm{x}}(b, y, w)\), and the function \(z \mapsto G\big(g + z\,(h - g)\big)\) has the derivative \(v_{\mathrm{x}}\big(b, y, g + z\,(h - g)\big)\,(h - g)\), because its difference quotient with the step \(k\) is \((h - g)\) times the difference quotient of the function \(G\) with the step \(k\,(h - g)\) (definition 1.9), so by item 1 of the same theorem the integral of this derivative from \(0\) to \(1\) is \(G(h) - G(g)\). The flux through the face \(x = b\) is therefore the flux through the side piece \(S_{\mathrm{b}}\) of definition 4.36, and the same holds for the other side faces. A body between two graphs with \(g < h\) and continuous second derivatives is a curved box with the same surface and the same fluxes.

How do we show that the divergence theorem holds for a curved box too? Let us draw the box \(K\) and the curved box \(V\) in section (figure 4.127) and think of \(\vek v\) as a displacement field, as in section 4.2.5. The flux through a patch is then the volume that the patch sweeps when it moves. In \(K\) take a small cell with the sides \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\), \(\Delta z\) at the top face. The map \(\Phi\) carries it to a curved cell at the top face of the body. The top side of the curved cell has the face vector of about \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\), so under the displacement \(\vek v\) it sweeps a volume of about \(\vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\), where \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) is the face vector. The number \(\vek v(\Phi)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) is therefore the flux through the image of the side, divided by the area \(\Delta x\,\Delta y\) of the side in \(K\). Let us draw it on the cell in \(K\) as the arrow \(G_{\mathrm{z}}\) and do the same in the other two directions. We get a field \(\vek G\) on \(K\) with the components \(G_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(G_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\), which carries through each side of a cell in \(K\) as much as the field \(\vek v\) carries through its image. This is a second view of the theorem: the field \(\vek G\) is the field \(\vek v\) counted in the coordinates of the box, and the theorem for \(V\) is the theorem for \(K\) applied to \(\vek G\).

Now the same with equations. By the change of variables theorem 4.59 the integral of the divergence of a field \(\vek v\) over \(V\) equals the integral of the function \((\mathrm{div}\,\vek v)(\Phi)\,J_\Phi\) over the box \(K\), where \(\mathrm{div}\,\vek v\) is short for the divergence (definition 4.13). On the face \(z = b_3\) of the box the theorem for a box integrates the component \(G_{\mathrm{z}}\), and with our choice this is the flux (4.38) through the face of the body. Is the divergence of the field \(\vek G\) really \((\mathrm{div}\,\vek v)(\Phi)\,J_\Phi\)? For a cell this is a balance. Out of the curved cell a volume of about \(\mathrm{div}\,\vek v\) times its volume is swept, and that volume is about \(J_\Phi\) times the volume \(\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z\) of the cell in \(K\). The computation shows it exactly. The product rule splits the divergence of the field \(\vek G\) into two parts. In the first the components of the field \(\vek v(\Phi)\) are differentiated, and the chain rule and the inverse matrix will turn it into \((\mathrm{div}\,\vek v)(\Phi)\,J_\Phi\). In the second the face vectors are differentiated, and this part must be zero. The next lemma says so.

Lemma 4.66 Piola identity (Piolova identiteta)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(\Phi\) a map on \(D\) whose components have at every point of \(D\) partial derivatives of the first and second order, continuous at every point of \(D\). Let \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) be the vectors (4.37). Then at every point of \(D\) (in the plane the edge vectors fold into a closed figure)

\[\frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = \vek 0 , \tag{4.39}\]

where the partial derivative of a vector means the vector of the partial derivatives of its components.

Proof

We must show that after differentiation all terms cancel. We differentiate each vector product by the product rule, then use the symmetry of mixed derivatives and the exchange of the order in the vector product. For short we write \(\vek f_{\mathrm{x}} = \partial\Phi/\partial x\), \(\vek f_{\mathrm{y}} = \partial\Phi/\partial y\) and \(\vek f_{\mathrm{z}} = \partial\Phi/\partial z\) for the columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\), the vectors of figure 4.124, of which two lie in the face and the third points out of the body. The steps are pure computation, so we do not draw them.

  1. Derivative of a vector product. The \(x\) component of \(\vek p\times\vek q\) is \(p_{\mathrm{y}} q_{\mathrm{z}} - p_{\mathrm{z}} q_{\mathrm{y}}\) (definition 2.33). By the product rule (lemma 1.82, items 1 and 3) its \(x\)-derivative is
    \[\Big(\frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\,q_{\mathrm{z}} - \frac{\partial p_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\,q_{\mathrm{y}}\Big) + \Big(p_{\mathrm{y}}\,\frac{\partial q_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x} - p_{\mathrm{z}}\,\frac{\partial q_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) ,\]
    the \(x\) component of \(\partial\vek p/\partial x\times\vek q + \vek p\times\partial\vek q/\partial x\), likewise for the rest. Hence
    \[\frac{\partial(\vek p\times\vek q)}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial\vek p}{\partial x}\times\vek q + \vek p\times\frac{\partial\vek q}{\partial x} .\]
  2. By step 1
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} &= \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{z}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{y}}\times\frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x} , \\ \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} &= \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{x}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{z}}\times\frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} , \\ \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} &= \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{y}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{x}}\times\frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} . \end{aligned}\]
    The components of the vector \(\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial x\) are the mixed derivatives \(\partial^2\Phi_{\mathrm{i}}/\partial x\,\partial y\), first with respect to \(y\) and then with respect to \(x\) (definition 1.130).
  3. Since \(D\) is open and the mixed derivatives are continuous at the point \(P\), by the theorem 1.131 we have at \(P\)
    \[\frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} , \qquad \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x} = \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} , \qquad \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} .\]
    We denote them by \(\vek g_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\vek g_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\vek g_{\mathrm{yz}}\). Without continuous second derivatives these equalities fail.
  4. We insert them into step 2 and group the terms into three pairs:
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = {} & \big(\vek g_{\mathrm{xy}}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{z}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{z}}\times\vek g_{\mathrm{xy}}\big) + \big(\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}\times\vek g_{\mathrm{xz}} + \vek g_{\mathrm{xz}}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{y}}\big) \\ & + \big(\vek g_{\mathrm{yz}}\times\vek f_{\mathrm{x}} + \vek f_{\mathrm{x}}\times\vek g_{\mathrm{yz}}\big) . \end{aligned}\]
  5. By item 1 of lemma 2.34 \(\vek q\times\vek p = -(\vek p\times\vek q)\), so each bracket is the zero vector. The sum is \(\vek 0\).

Source: The proof is not from the sources. We have not found the identity in the sources of the library. Writing it with the columns of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\) and the connection with Nanson's formula (CM (3.3.25), PDF p. 127) are ours.

What does the identity say? By theorem 2.76 the vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\), divided by \(J_\Phi\), are the rows of the inverse matrix \(\mat F_\Phi^{-1}\). The lemma therefore says that the sum of the derivatives of the rows of the matrix \(J_\Phi\,\mat F_\Phi^{-1}\), each with respect to its own coordinate, is zero. We see the geometric meaning on a very small curved box with the sides \(\Delta x\), \(\Delta y\), \(\Delta z\). On the faces \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) the face vectors, multiplied by the area \(\Delta y\,\Delta z\) of the face of the box, are about \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}(x)\,\Delta y\,\Delta z\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}(x + \Delta x)\,\Delta y\,\Delta z\), and their sum is about \(\frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\,\Delta z\). The same holds for the other two pairs of faces. The lemma therefore says that the face vectors, multiplied by the areas, add up to the zero vector, just as the sides of a closed polygon add up to the zero vector (figure 4.128). In the figure, on the left is a curved quadrilateral, the image of a rectangle, with its edges and their chords (grey, dashed). At the middle of an edge is the chord turned by a quarter turn, numbered from \(1\) to \(4\). On the right are the same four vectors placed one after another from the blackwhite dot, to which they return. Why do they return? Whoever walks along the chords from corner to corner and comes back to the first corner has not moved in total, so the sum of the chords is the zero vector. When we turn each chord by a quarter turn, the sum turns by a quarter turn too, and the zero vector stays the zero vector. Why the turned chord? In the plane an edge plays the role of a face. Its vector at each point is perpendicular to the edge, and when we add such vectors along an edge, we get the chord turned by a quarter turn, however the edge is curved between its two corners. We will show this exactly after the theorem.

Theorem 4.67 Divergence theorem for a curved box (izrek o divergenci za ukrivljen kvader)

Let \(V = \Phi(K)\) be a curved box with the surface \(S\) and the outward unit normal \(\vek n\) (definition 4.65), \(E\) an open set of points that contains \(V\), and \(\vek v = (v_{\mathrm{x}}, v_{\mathrm{y}}, v_{\mathrm{z}})\) a field that is continuously differentiable on \(E\) (definition 1.91). Then \(V\) is a set with volume (definition 4.27), and

\[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A , \tag{4.40}\]

where the left side is the integral over a set with volume (definition 4.30) and the right side the flux through the six faces of the curved box.

Proof

We must show that the integral of the divergence over \(V\) is the sum of the fluxes through the six faces. The change of variables theorem carries the integral from the body \(V\) to the box \(K\), there we write the integrand as the divergence of a new field and use the divergence theorem for a box. For short we write \(J = J_\Phi\) and \(\mathrm{div}\,\vek v\) for the divergence of the field \(\vek v\) (definition 4.13). The partial derivatives of the field \(\vek v\) are derivatives with respect to the coordinates of a point of the body, those of the map \(\Phi\) with respect to the coordinates of a point of the box.

1. An open set around the box.

  1. Let \(D'\) be the set of the points \(P\) of \(D\) for which \(\Phi(P)\) lies in \(E\) (figure 4.127). The points \(\Phi(P)\) with \(P \in K\) make up \(V\), which lies in \(E\), so \(D'\) contains \(K\). We need the set \(D'\) because the field \(\vek v\) is given only on \(E\), and \(\vek v(\Phi(P))\) has a meaning only where \(\Phi(P)\) lies in \(E\).
  2. \(D'\) is open. Let \(P \in D'\). The set \(E\) is open, so there is an \(r > 0\) such that every point closer to \(\Phi(P)\) than \(r\) lies in \(E\). We look for a disc around \(P\) whose image stays inside this disc. The components of the map \(\Phi\) are continuously differentiable, hence continuous (lemma 1.92), and there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that for points \(Q \in D\) with \(|PQ| < \delta\) each component of the point \(\Phi(Q)\) differs from the same component of the point \(\Phi(P)\) by less than \(r/2\). By (1.10) the square of the distance between \(\Phi(P)\) and \(\Phi(Q)\) is then less than \(3r^2/4 < r^2\), the distance by lemma 1.29 less than \(r\), and \(\Phi(Q)\) lies in \(E\). Since \(D\) is open, there is also a \(\rho > 0\) such that the points closer to \(P\) than \(\rho\) are in \(D\). All points closer to \(P\) than the smaller of the numbers \(\delta\) and \(\rho\) are therefore in \(D'\).
  3. On \(D'\) let \(\tilde v_{\mathrm{i}}(P) = v_{\mathrm{i}}\big(\Phi(P)\big)\) for \(i = x, y, z\) be the components of the vector \(\tilde{\vek v}(P) = \vek v\big(\Phi(P)\big)\). The map \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable on the open set \(D'\) with values in the open set \(E\), and the \(v_{\mathrm{i}}\) are continuously differentiable on \(E\). By the chain rule (lemma 4.43) the \(\tilde v_{\mathrm{i}}\) are therefore continuously differentiable on \(D'\), and
    \[\frac{\partial\tilde v_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x}(P) = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x}(P) ,\]
    where \(k\) runs over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), and likewise for the derivatives with respect to \(y\) and \(z\).

2. A new field on the box.

  1. On \(D'\) let \(\vek G = (G_{\mathrm{x}}, G_{\mathrm{y}}, G_{\mathrm{z}})\) be the field with the components
    \[G_{\mathrm{x}} = \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{y}} = \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{y}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{z}} = \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} .\]
    In figure 4.127 \(G_{\mathrm{z}}\) on the top face of the box is the scalar product of the field \(\vek v\) and the face vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) at the image of the same point.
  2. The field \(\vek G\) is continuously differentiable on \(D'\). The components of the face vectors \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\) are differences of products of the first partial derivatives of the components of the map \(\Phi\) (definition 2.33), and these have continuous partial derivatives on \(D\) (definition 4.65, item 1). By the rules of differentiation (lemma 1.82, items 1 and 3) the components of the face vectors therefore have partial derivatives that are sums of products of continuous functions and so continuous (corollary 1.70, item 1). The same holds for \(G_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(G_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{z}}\), which are sums of products of the functions \(\tilde v_{\mathrm{i}}\) with components of the face vectors.
  3. By the product rule, applied to each term of the scalar product, \(\partial G_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x = (\partial\tilde{\vek v}/\partial x)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} + \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\), and likewise for \(G_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(G_{\mathrm{z}}\). The sum is
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = {} & \frac{\partial\tilde{\vek v}}{\partial x}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{\partial\tilde{\vek v}}{\partial y}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{y}} + \frac{\partial\tilde{\vek v}}{\partial z}\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}} \\ & + \tilde{\vek v}\cdot\Big(\frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z}\Big) . \end{aligned}\]
  4. By the Piola identity (lemma 4.66) the bracket is the zero vector, and the last term is zero. This is the balance of figure 4.128: the face vectors of a small cell add up to the zero vector, so a constant field carries nothing through the cell.
  5. Into the other three terms we insert the chain rule of step 3 of the first part. The component \(i\) of the vector \(\partial\tilde{\vek v}/\partial x\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}(\Phi)\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x}\). Writing \((\vek N_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{i}}\) for the component \(i\) of the vector \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), we get
    \[\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}}(\Phi)\,\Big( & \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial x}\,(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}})_{\mathrm{i}} + \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial y}\,(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}})_{\mathrm{i}} \\ & + \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{k}}}{\partial z}\,(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}})_{\mathrm{i}} \Big) . \end{aligned}\]
  6. Let \(\mat M\) be the matrix with the rows \(\vek N_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}\). By the theorem 2.76 on the inverse via the determinant \(\mat M/J\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F_\Phi\) of the map \(\Phi\), whose columns are \(\partial\Phi/\partial x\), \(\partial\Phi/\partial y\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial z\). The bracket of step 5 is the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} (\mat F_\Phi)_{\mathrm{kj}}\,M_{\mathrm{ji}}\), that is, the element \(ki\) of the product \(\mat F_\Phi\mat M\) (definition 1.99). By definition 1.110 \(\mat F_\Phi\,(\mat M/J) = \mat I\), so \(\mat F_\Phi\mat M = J\,\mat I\), and the bracket is \(J\) for \(k = i\) and \(0\) for \(k \neq i\).
  7. Of the double sum only the terms with \(k = i\) remain:
    \[\frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial G_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} = J(P)\,\Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\big(\Phi(P)\big)\]
    at every point \(P\) of \(D'\). For a cell this says what we expected: the balance of the field \(\vek G\) on a cell in \(K\) is the balance of the field \(\vek v\) on its image, whose volume is \(J\) times larger.

3. Carrying the integral to the box.

  1. The box \(K\) is a set with volume, and the integral over it is the integral over a box of definition 4.8 (lemma 4.32, item 6). The map \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable and one-to-one on the open set \(D'\), and \(J > 0\). The divergence \(\mathrm{div}\,\vek v\) is continuous on \(V\), because the partial derivatives of the components of the field are continuous on \(E\). Here the second and the third condition of the definition enter. By the change of variables theorem 4.59 \(V = \Phi(K)\) is therefore a set with volume, and since \(|J| = J\),
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \mathrm{div}\,\vek v\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{K}} (\mathrm{div}\,\vek v)\big(\Phi(P)\big)\,J(P)\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  2. By step 7 of the second part the integrand on the right equals the divergence of the field \(\vek G\) at every point of \(K\).
  3. The field \(\vek G\) is continuously differentiable on the open set \(D'\), which contains \(K\). By the divergence theorem 4.14, item 2, applied to the box \(K\) as a body made of boxes with a single cell, the integral of the divergence of the field \(\vek G\) over \(K\) equals the sum of the integrals of the function \(G_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + G_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + G_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\) over the six faces of the box, with the outward normals \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

4. The faces.

  1. On the face \(z = b_3\) of the box \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and the integrand is \(G_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, b_3)\) \(= \vek v\big(\Phi(x, y, b_3)\big)\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{z}}(x, y, b_3)\). The integral over the rectangle is the iterated integral of definition 4.8, that is, (4.38), the flux through the face \(z = b_3\) of the curved box.
  2. On the face \(z = a_3\), the bottom side of the box, we have \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), and the integrand \(-G_{\mathrm{z}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot(-\vek N_{\mathrm{z}})\) gives the flux through the face \(z = a_3\), the bottom face of the body.
  3. On the faces \(x = b_1\) and \(x = a_1\) the integrands are \(\pm G_{\mathrm{x}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot(\pm\vek N_{\mathrm{x}})\), on the faces \(y = b_2\) and \(y = a_2\) they are \(\pm G_{\mathrm{y}} = \vek v(\Phi)\cdot(\pm\vek N_{\mathrm{y}})\), with the face vectors of definition 4.65.
  4. The sum of the six integrals is the flux \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\). Together with the third part this gives (4.40).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7, Theorem 1 (PDF p. 479) states the theorem for closed bounded regions bounded by a surface made of smooth pieces, and proves it for regions that lie between graphs in the direction of all three axes (PDF pp. 480-481). The change of variables is stated in LEBL2 Thm. 10.7.2 (PDF p. 134). The proof by carrying the integral to the box and by the Piola identity is not from the sources.

The proof has shown why the theorem holds for a curved body too. The change of variables carried the integral from the body to the box, where the divergence of the field \(\vek v\) was replaced by the divergence of the field \(\vek G\), whose components are the fluxes of the field \(\vek v\) through the faces per unit area of the faces of the box. Two moves did the work. The chain rule and the inverse matrix turned the derivatives of the field \(\vek v(\Phi)\) with respect to the coordinates of the box into the derivatives of the field \(\vek v\) with respect to the coordinates of the body, multiplied by \(J\), exactly the factor that the change of variables demands. The Piola identity made sure that the derivatives of the face vectors gave no term. The fundamental theorem of calculus worked inside the theorem for a box, once in each direction.

The theorem also says what exactly figure 4.128 means. A constant field \(\vek v = \vek c\) has divergence zero, so the flux of a constant field through the surface of every curved box is zero, in the plane through the four edges of the shape. By the linearity of the iterated integral (lemma 3.54, item 1) the flux through a face is the scalar product of the vector \(\vek c\) with the vector whose components are the integrals of the components of the face vector. Taking \(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\) for \(\vek c\), we find that the integrals of the face vectors over the six faces add up to the zero vector, like the four edge vectors in the figure.

We will cut the ball into a cube, which is a body between two graphs, and into curved boxes. A body made of such pieces is treated by the next corollary, which extends corollary 4.40.

Corollary 4.68 Divergence theorem for a body cut into curved boxes (izrek o divergenci za telo iz ukrivljenih kvadrov)

Let \(V\) be the union of sets \(V_1, \dots, V_{\mathrm{m}}\), each of which is a body between two graphs (definition 4.15) or a curved box (definition 4.65), like the cube and the pieces of the sphere, and let no interior point of any of them lie in another.

  1. \(V\) is a set with volume (definition 4.27), and for every function \(f\) that is continuous on \(V\) the integral over \(V\) is the sum of the integrals over the pieces:
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} f\,\mathrm{d}V = \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{m} \int_{\mathrm{V}_\mathrm{k}} f\,\mathrm{d}V .\]
  2. Let the pieces of the surfaces of these sets (definitions 4.36 and 4.65) be divided into outer and inner ones, and the inner ones into pairs, so that each pair consists of pieces of the surfaces of two different sets (opposite normals) and the flux of every continuous field through one piece is the negative of the flux through the other. Let \(S\) be the union of the outer pieces, the surface of the body \(V\), and \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\) the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces. If the field \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable on an open set \(E\) that contains \(V\), then
    \[\int_{\mathrm{V}} \Big( \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \Big)\,\mathrm{d}V = \int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A . \tag{4.41}\]

The integrals over \(V\) and over the pieces are integrals over sets with volume (definition 4.30).

Proof

We must show both items. The first follows from the additivity of the integral over sets with volume, for the second we add the divergence theorems for the pieces.

1. Volume and integral.

  1. Each piece is a set with volume. A body between two graphs by theorem 4.33, a curved box by theorem 4.67.
  2. By assumption no interior point of any piece lies in another, as for the pieces of the ball in figure 4.129, which meet only in faces. By the additivity of the integral over sets with volume (lemma 4.32, item 4) \(V\) is therefore a set with volume, and the integral of a continuous function over \(V\) is the sum of the integrals over the pieces.

2. The divergence theorem.

  1. Each piece \(V_{\mathrm{k}}\) lies in \(V\), hence in \(E\). If it is a body between two graphs, then by theorem 4.39 the integral of the divergence over it equals the flux through its six pieces of surface, and the integral of definition 4.20 is by theorem 4.33 the integral over a set with volume. If it is a curved box, theorem 4.67 gives the same. On the right of figure 4.129 each piece is drawn by itself, with its own surface.
  2. We add the equalities over \(k\) from \(1\) to \(m\). The divergence is continuous on \(V\), so by the first part the sum of the left sides is the integral of the divergence over \(V\).
  3. The sum of the right sides is the sum of the fluxes through all pieces of the surfaces. The inner pieces come in pairs with opposite fluxes, which cancel, like the pair with opposite normals in figure 4.129. What remains is the sum of the fluxes through the outer pieces, such as the two pieces of the surface of the ball, which is \(\int_{\mathrm{S}} \vek v\cdot\vek n\,\mathrm{d}A\).

Source: KREYSZIG §10.7 (PDF p. 482): for a body that auxiliary surfaces cut into finitely many pieces, the integrals over the auxiliary surfaces cancel in pairs. The proof follows the source.

The proof is the same argument as for corollary 4.40, only with two kinds of pieces, the cube and the curved boxes. The first item came from the additivity of the integral, which knows neither the order of integration nor the shape of the pieces, only that the pieces do not overlap. The condition on the pairs must be checked for every cut, as for the round bar. If we leave it out and some inner piece stays without a partner, its flux stays in the sum, and the right side is no longer the flux through the surface of the body. When two descriptions of the same surface are related by a map with a negative Jacobian, corollary 4.64 gives it.

Let us test all this on a ball. A steel ball of radius \(R = 10\) mm, for instance a ball of a larger rolling bearing, is the set of the points \(P\) with \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\), where \(O\) is its centre and the origin of the coordinate system. We cut it into the cube \(V_0 = [-a, a] \times [-a, a] \times [-a, a]\) with the half edge \(a = 4\) mm in the middle and six pieces, one over each face of the cube (figure 4.129). The figure shows the section \(y = 0\) in the plane with the axes \(x\) and \(z\), in which we see four of the six pieces. On the left they are together: the cube \(V_0\), the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) with a mesh of parameter lines, \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\) and \(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), and on the right each piece is moved outward, so that we see the surface of each one separately. In the section the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) has four sides: a part of the surface of the ball, the side on the cube, which fits the top face of the cube, and the straight right and left cuts. In the same way the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) has a part of the surface of the ball, the side on the cube and the upper and the lower cut.

How do we describe the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) over the top face of the cube as the image of a box? Let us draw it larger (figure 4.130, again the section \(y = 0\) with the axes \(x\) and \(z\), the radius \(R\) and the half edge \(a\)). It is made of the segments from the face \(z = a\) of the cube to the surface of the ball that lie on rays from \(O\). Take one such ray, the one through the point \((s, t, 1)\) at the height \(1\) above the plane \(z = 0\). We describe a point on it by its height \(z\). Since it is a multiple of the vector \((s, t, 1)\), it has the coordinates \((s\,z, t\,z, z)\). The numbers \(s = x/z\) and \(t = y/z\) are ratios of coordinates and say in which direction the ray goes. The ray meets the face \(z = a\) at the point of height \(a\) and the surface of the ball at the point of height \(R/|(s, t, 1)|\), where \(|(s, t, 1)| = \sqrt{1 + s^2 + t^2}\) is the length of the vector \((s, t, 1)\), since the point \(R\,(s, t, 1)/|(s, t, 1)|\) is at the distance \(R\) from \(O\). We divide the height between the two evenly by a number \(\lambda\) between \(0\) and \(1\) and get the point \(\Phi(s, t, \lambda)\) of height \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\):

\[\begin{aligned} \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t, \lambda) &= (1 - \lambda)\,a + \lambda\,\frac{R}{|(s, t, 1)|} , \\ \Phi(s, t, \lambda) &= \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t, \lambda)\,(s, t, 1) , \end{aligned} \tag{4.42}\]

on the box \(K = [-1, 1] \times [-1, 1] \times [0, 1]\). In the figure \(s = 0{,}5\), \(t = 0\) and \(\lambda = 0{,}5\). Then \(|(s, t, 1)| = \sqrt{1{,}25} = 1{,}118\), the ray meets the ball at the height \(10/1{,}118 = 8{,}944\) mm, and the point \(\Phi\) has the height \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} = (4 + 8{,}944)/2 = 6{,}472\) mm and the coordinates \((3{,}236, 0, 6{,}472)\) mm. Here we write the coordinates of a point of the box as \(s\), \(t\), \(\lambda\) instead of the \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) of definition 4.65, so as not to confuse them with the coordinates of points of the ball. The face vectors are therefore \(\vek N_{\mathrm{s}} = \partial\Phi/\partial t\times\partial\Phi/\partial\lambda\), \(\vek N_{\mathrm{t}} = \partial\Phi/\partial\lambda\times\partial\Phi/\partial s\) and \(\vek N_\lambda = \partial\Phi/\partial s\times\partial\Phi/\partial t\).

The face \(\lambda = 0\) is the top face of the cube, the face \(\lambda = 1\) a part of the surface of the ball, and the faces \(s = \pm 1\) and \(t = \pm 1\) are flat, in the planes \(x = \pm z\) and \(y = \pm z\) through \(O\) (figure 4.131). In the figure the piece is lifted above the cube so that we see both whole, the hidden edges are grey and dashed, at the centre of the spherical face is the vector \(\vek N_\lambda\), and the axes \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) are at the bottom left.

Is \(V_{+\mathrm{z}} = \Phi(K)\) a curved box? We must check the three conditions of definition 4.65 on an open set that contains \(K\). The first condition needs the derivatives of the function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|\), which has a root in the denominator. We do not yet have the derivative of a root for functions of several variables in the book. Let us derive it with the same trick of a difference of squares as in lemma 4.16.

The proof will use the same device twice, so let us draw it in advance (figure 4.132). On the number line with zero we mark the value \(p(P)\), which is positive. Around it we take a band of half width \(p(P)/2\), from \(p(P)/2\) to \(3\,p(P)/2\). Since \(p\) is continuous, the value \(p(Q)\) lies in this band for all points \(Q\) close enough to \(P\), because for them the difference \(|p(Q) - p(P)|\) is less than \(p(P)/2\). The whole band lies to the right of \(p(P)/2\), away from zero. So we may divide by \(\sqrt{p(Q)}\) and we have a lower bound for this denominator. At \(p(P) = 4\) the band reaches from \(2\) to \(6\), and \(1/\sqrt{p(Q)} < 1/\sqrt 2 = 0{,}707\).

Lemma 4.69 Derivative of the reciprocal of a square root (odvod obratne vrednosti korena)

Let \(D\) be an open set of points and \(p\) a function that is continuously differentiable on \(D\) (definition 1.91) and positive at every point of \(D\), so the band around the value \(p(P)\) does not reach zero. Then the function \(f\) whose value at the point \(P\) is \(1/\sqrt{p(P)}\) is continuously differentiable on \(D\), and

\[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = -\frac12\,f^3\,\frac{\partial p}{\partial x} , \tag{4.43}\]

and likewise for \(y\) and \(z\).

Proof

We must show that the difference quotient of the function \(f\) converges to the right side of (4.43) and that this is continuous. We remove the root as in lemma 4.16, with a difference of squares. The steps are pure computation with inequalities.

  1. Difference of roots. For positive numbers \(A\) and \(B\) the roots \(\sqrt A\) and \(\sqrt B\) are positive, because the square of the number \(0\) is \(0\) (theorem 1.37). From \((\sqrt B - \sqrt A)(\sqrt B + \sqrt A) = B - A\) we get
    \[\sqrt B - \sqrt A = \frac{B - A}{\sqrt A + \sqrt B} , \qquad |\sqrt B - \sqrt A| \le \frac{|B - A|}{\sqrt A} .\]
  2. Let \(P \in D\). The function \(p\) is continuous (lemma 1.92), so there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|p(Q) - p(P)| < p(P)/2\) for points \(Q \in D\) with \(|PQ| < \delta_1\). For such points \(p(Q)\) lies in the band of figure 4.132, to the right of \(p(P)/2\). So \(p(Q) > p(P)/2\), and by lemma 1.29 \(\sqrt{p(Q)} > \sqrt{p(P)/2}\). Here the condition \(p > 0\) enters: at \(p(P) = 0\) there is no such band, and the function \(1/\sqrt p\) has no value there.
  3. Continuity of the function \(f\) at \(P\). For a point \(Q\) of step 2, with the value \(p(Q)\) in the band, by step 1
    \[\begin{aligned} |f(Q) - f(P)| &= \frac{\big|\sqrt{p(P)} - \sqrt{p(Q)}\big|}{\sqrt{p(P)}\,\sqrt{p(Q)}} \le \frac{|p(Q) - p(P)|}{p(P)\,\sqrt{p(Q)}} \\ &< \frac{\sqrt 2\,|p(Q) - p(P)|}{p(P)\,\sqrt{p(P)}} . \end{aligned}\]
    For \(\eta > 0\) we take the band that the continuity of the function \(p\) at \(P\) gives for the error \(\eta\,p(P)\,\sqrt{p(P)}/\sqrt 2\) and that is not larger than \(\delta_1\). For points \(Q\) closer to \(P\) than this band \(|f(Q) - f(P)| < \eta\), so \(f\) is continuous at \(P\) (definition 1.68).
  4. The difference quotient. The set \(D\) is open, so there is an \(r > 0\) such that the points \(Q_{\mathrm{h}} = P + h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) with \(|h| < r\) are in \(D\). Let \(k(h) = \sqrt{p(Q_{\mathrm{h}})}\). By step 1 with \(A = p(P)\) and \(B = p(Q_{\mathrm{h}})\), for \(0 < |h| < r\)
    \[\frac{f(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) - f(P)}{h} = \frac{k(0) - k(h)}{h\,k(0)\,k(h)} = -\frac{p(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) - p(P)}{h} \cdot \frac{1}{d(h)} ,\]
    where \(d(h) = k(0)\,k(h)\,\big(k(0) + k(h)\big)\).
  5. The function \(k\) is continuous at \(0\): by step 1 \(|k(h) - k(0)| \le |p(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) - p(P)|/\sqrt{p(P)}\), with \(|Q_{\mathrm{h}} P| = |h|\), and \(p\) is continuous at \(P\). By corollary 1.65 \(d\) is therefore continuous at \(0\), with \(d(0) = 2\,p(P)\,\sqrt{p(P)} > 0\).
  6. The function \(1/d\) is continuous at \(0\). There is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|d(h) - d(0)| < d(0)/2\), hence \(d(h) > d(0)/2\), for \(|h| < \delta_2\). This is the same band as in step 2, only around \(d(0)\) instead of around \(p(P)\). For such \(h\)
    \[\Big| \frac{1}{d(h)} - \frac{1}{d(0)} \Big| = \frac{|d(0) - d(h)|}{d(h)\,d(0)} \le \frac{2\,|d(h) - d(0)|}{d(0)^2} ,\]
    which is less than \(\eta\) when \(|d(h) - d(0)| < \eta\,d(0)^2/2\).
  7. As \(h\) tends to \(0\), the value \(p(Q_{\mathrm{h}})\) stays in the band and approaches \(p(P)\). By the definition of the partial derivative 1.26 the quotient \((p(Q_{\mathrm{h}}) - p(P))/h\) converges to \(\partial p/\partial x\,(P)\). By the lemma 1.81 on limit and continuity, item 1, the function that has the value of this quotient for \(h \neq 0\) and the value \(\partial p/\partial x\,(P)\) at \(h = 0\) is continuous at \(0\). Its product with the function \(-1/d\) is continuous at \(0\) by corollary 1.65, and by step 4 it equals the quotient of the function \(f\) for \(h \neq 0\). By item 1 of lemma 1.81, used in the other direction,
    \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(P) = -\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}(P) \cdot \frac{1}{2\,p(P)\,\sqrt{p(P)}} = -\frac12\,f(P)^3\,\frac{\partial p}{\partial x}(P) .\]
  8. Continuity of the derivative. \(f\) (step 3) and \(\partial p/\partial x\) are continuous on \(D\), so by corollary 1.70, item 1, the product \(-\tfrac12\,f\,f\,f\,\partial p/\partial x\) is too. For \(y\) and \(z\) repeat steps 4 to 8 with \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\).

Source: LEBL1 Example 4.1.4 (PDF p. 156) computes the derivative of the function \(\sqrt x\) with the same trick of a difference of squares. The proof is not from the sources.

We apply the lemma to the function \(p = 1 + s^2 + t^2\) of the point \((s, t, \lambda)\), which is a polynomial, positive everywhere (\(p \ge 1\), so the band around \(p(P)\) does not reach zero), with the continuous partial derivatives \(2s\), \(2t\) and \(0\). The function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|\) is therefore continuously differentiable in all of space, with the derivatives

\[\frac{\partial}{\partial s}\,\frac{1}{|(s, t, 1)|} = -\frac{s}{|(s, t, 1)|^3} , \qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,\frac{1}{|(s, t, 1)|} = -\frac{t}{|(s, t, 1)|^3} .\]

The derivatives are products of a polynomial with the third power of the function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|\), so by the product rule (lemma 1.82, item 3) and by the lemma they again have continuous partial derivatives. The derivative of the first with respect to \(s\) is, for instance, \(-1/|(s, t, 1)|^3 + 3s^2/|(s, t, 1)|^5\). The components of the map (4.42) are sums of products of polynomials in \(s\), \(t\), \(\lambda\) and the function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|\), so they have continuous partial derivatives of the first and second order at every point of space. The first condition holds.

The Jacobian. The derivatives of the map are \(\partial\Phi/\partial\lambda = \big(R/|(s, t, 1)| - a\big)\,(s, t, 1)\), \(\partial\Phi/\partial s = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial s}\,(s, t, 1)\) and \(\partial\Phi/\partial t = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}} + \frac{\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial t}\,(s, t, 1)\). The determinant is linear in each column and is zero when two columns are multiples of the same vector (lemma 2.73, items 2 and 3). The terms with the vector \((s, t, 1)\) in the first two columns therefore contribute nothing, and

\[J_\Phi = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2\,\Big( \frac{R}{|(s, t, 1)|} - a \Big)\,\det\big(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}, \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}, (s, t, 1)\big) = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2\,\Big( \frac{R}{|(s, t, 1)|} - a \Big) ,\]

which SymPy has confirmed too. The determinant is positive where \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} > 0\) and \(|(s, t, 1)| < R/a\), that is, where the point on the ball is higher than the point on the cube. On the box \(K\) we have \(|(s, t, 1)| \le \sqrt 3\), so \(a < R/\sqrt 3 = 5{,}774\) mm suffices, which holds for \(a = 4\) mm. At \(a = 5{,}774\) mm the corners of the cube would lie on the surface of the ball. Above a corner the top face of the piece would touch the face of the cube, the segment on the ray through the corner would have length zero, and \(J_\Phi = 0\) there. With a still larger cube the corners would stick out of the ball and the cut would no longer be a cut of the ball. For the open set we take \(D = (-\tfrac54, \tfrac54) \times (-\tfrac54, \tfrac54) \times (-\tfrac14, \tfrac54)\), which contains \(K\). On it \(|(s, t, 1)|^2 < 1 + 2 \cdot \tfrac{25}{16} = 4{,}125\), so \(R/|(s, t, 1)| > 4{,}92\) mm \(> a\). Since \(R/|(s, t, 1)| \le R\), also \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}} > a - \tfrac14\,(R - a) = 2{,}5\) mm. The third condition holds. The smallest value of the Jacobian on \(K\) is \(28{,}38\ \text{mm}^3\) (NumPy), at the corners of the face \(\lambda = 0\), where the piece is thinnest.

The second condition. In figure 4.130 we see it like this: the ray fixes \(s\) and \(t\), and the height on it fixes \(\lambda\). Let \(\Phi(s, t, \lambda) = \Phi(s', t', \lambda')\) for two points of \(D\). The \(z\) component gives \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(s, t, \lambda) = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}(s', t', \lambda')\), a positive number, and the \(x\) and \(y\) components, divided by this number, give \(s = s'\) and \(t = t'\). Then \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) is a linear function of the variable \(\lambda\) with the positive coefficient \(R/|(s, t, 1)| - a\), so the equality gives \(\lambda = \lambda'\). The piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}} = \Phi(K)\) is therefore a curved box.

We get the other five pieces by rotations. The piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) in the direction of the \(x\) axis is the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) turned by a quarter turn about the \(y\) axis, which in figure 4.129 points into the page. It is the image of the same box \(K\) under the map \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}} = (\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{x}})\), where \(\Phi_{\mathrm{x}} = s\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\), \(\Phi_{\mathrm{y}} = t\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the components of the map (4.42). This is \(\Phi\) followed by the map \((x, y, z) \mapsto (z, y, -x)\), this quarter turn, with the matrix with the rows \((0, 0, 1)\), \((0, 1, 0)\), \((-1, 0, 0)\) and the determinant \(1\). The components of the map \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}\) are components of the map \(\Phi\), one of them with the opposite sign, so they have continuous partial derivatives of the first and second order. By corollary 4.44 the Jacobian of the map \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}\) is \(1 \cdot J_\Phi > 0\), and different points again go to different points, because a rotation does not map two different points to the same point. In the same way we get the pieces \(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\) and \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\) with the maps \((-\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{x}})\), \((\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}})\), \((\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, \Phi_{\mathrm{y}})\) and \((\Phi_{\mathrm{x}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{y}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\), all of whose matrices have the determinant \(1\).

The pieces fill the ball and do not overlap. The points of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) are exactly the points \((x, y, z)\) with \(|x| \le z\), \(|y| \le z\), \(z \ge a\) and \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| \le R\): they lie between the cuts \(x = z\) and \(x = -z\), above the face of the cube and below the surface of the ball. Indeed, a point \(\Phi(s, t, \lambda)\) with \((s, t, \lambda) \in K\) has \(z = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) between \(a\) and \(R/|(s, t, 1)|\), \(x = s\,z\) and \(y = t\,z\) with \(|s|, |t| \le 1\), and \(|\overrightarrow{OP}| = z\,|(s, t, 1)| \le R\). Conversely such a point has \(s = x/z\) and \(t = y/z\) in \([-1, 1]\) and \(z \le R/|(s, t, 1)|\), so \(\lambda = (z - a)/\big(R/|(s, t, 1)| - a\big)\) is in \([0, 1]\). Every point of the ball that is not in the cube has a coordinate whose absolute value is larger than \(a\), and it lies in the piece in the direction of the coordinate with the largest absolute value. All pieces lie in the ball, and so does the cube, because by (1.10) each of its points is at most \(\sqrt3\,a = 6{,}93\) mm from \(O\), less than \(R\). The union of the seven pieces is therefore the ball. An interior point of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) has \(|x| < z\), \(|y| < z\) and \(z > a\). If, for instance, \(x = z\) held, the points \((x + h, y, z)\) with a small \(h > 0\) would not be in \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\). It therefore does not lie in the cube, where \(z \le a\), nor in the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), where \(z \le x\), nor in \(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), where \(z \le -x\), nor in \(V_{\pm \mathrm{y}}\), where \(z \le \pm y\), nor in \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), where \(z < 0\). The same holds for the other pieces. An interior point of the cube has all coordinates smaller than \(a\) in absolute value and lies in no piece. The cube is the body between the graphs of the constant functions \(-a\) and \(a\). The ball is therefore made of seven sets that satisfy the condition of corollary 4.68.

Volume. By the change of variables theorem 4.59 with the function \(1\) the volume of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) is the integral of the Jacobian over \(K\). We compute the inner integral over \(\lambda\) with the fundamental theorem of calculus. By the chain rule (lemma 4.43) the function \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^3/3\) has the derivative \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2\,\partial\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}/\partial\lambda = \Phi_{\mathrm{z}}^2\,\big(R/|(s, t, 1)| - a\big) = J_\Phi\) with respect to \(\lambda\), its value at \(\lambda = 1\) is \(R^3/\big(3\,|(s, t, 1)|^3\big)\) and at \(\lambda = 0\) it is \(a^3/3\), so

\[\int_0^1 J_\Phi\,\mathrm{d}\lambda = \frac{1}{3}\,\Big( \frac{R^3}{|(s, t, 1)|^3} - a^3 \Big) .\]

The integral of the function \(1/|(s, t, 1)|^3\) over the square \([-1, 1] \times [-1, 1]\) is \(2\pi/3\), which SymPy has computed, because it needs the arctangent function, which we have not defined. So by the theorem 4.9 on the order of integration the volume of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) is

\[\int_{\mathrm{K}} J_\Phi\,\mathrm{d}V = \frac{R^3}{3} \cdot \frac{2\pi}{3} - \frac{4a^3}{3} = \frac{2\pi R^3}{9} - \frac{4a^3}{3} = 612{,}80\ \text{mm}^3 .\]

By corollary 4.68, item 1, with the function \(1\) the volume of the ball is the sum of the volumes of the pieces, \(8a^3 + 6 \cdot \big(2\pi R^3/9 - 4a^3/3\big) = 4\pi R^3/3 = 4188{,}79\ \text{mm}^3\), the volume of a ball from school geometry. The terms with \(a^3\) cancel: the size of the cube does not change the volume, because for every \(a < R/\sqrt 3\) the six pieces complete it exactly to the ball.

Face vectors. We computed the integrals of the components of the face vectors of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) over its six faces with SymPy and NumPy. In square millimetres they are \((0, 0, 174{,}08)\) for the face \(\lambda = 1\) on the ball, \((0, 0, -64)\) for the face \(\lambda = 0\) on the cube, \((\pm 27{,}52, 0, -27{,}52)\) for the faces \(s = 1\) and \(s = -1\), and \((0, \pm 27{,}52, -27{,}52)\) for the faces \(t = \pm 1\), which lie in front of and behind the plane of the section. The first vector points up like \(\vek N_\lambda\) in figure 4.131, the second down, into the cube, and the other four obliquely down and away from the piece. The sum is the zero vector, \(174{,}08 - 64 - 4 \cdot 27{,}52 = 0\), as the theorem for a constant field demands. On a flat face this integral is the outward normal times the area. The face on the cube is a square with the side \(2a = 8\) mm and the area \(64\ \text{mm}^2\), the face \(s = 1\) has the normal \((1, 0, -1)/\sqrt 2\) and the area \(\sqrt 2 \cdot 27{,}52 = 38{,}92\ \text{mm}^2\).

Fluxes. The field \(\vek v = (x, 0, 0)\), with the coordinate \(x\) in millimetres, points everywhere along the \(x\) axis away from the plane \(x = 0\) and has divergence \(1\), so the integral of the divergence over each piece is its volume. The fluxes through the faces of the pieces \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) and \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) in cubic millimetres, computed with SymPy and NumPy, are:

face \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\)
\(\lambda = 1\), on the ball \(313{,}23\) \(1467{,}93\)
\(\lambda = 0\), on the cube \(0\) \(-256{,}00\)
\(s = 1\) \(149{,}78\) \(-149{,}78\)
\(s = -1\) \(149{,}78\) \(-149{,}78\)
\(t = 1\) \(0\) \(-149{,}78\)
\(t = -1\) \(0\) \(-149{,}78\)
sum of fluxes \(612{,}80\) \(612{,}80\)
volume \(612{,}80\) \(612{,}80\)

For each piece the last two rows are equal, as theorem 4.67 says. We read the signs off figure 4.129. The field points away from the plane \(x = 0\), so through both cuts of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) it flows out of the piece, while through both cuts of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) and through its face on the cube it flows into the piece. On the face of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) on the cube the field is parallel to the face, and the flux is zero. The faces \(t = \pm 1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) lie in the planes \(y = \pm z\), whose normals have no \(x\) component, so \(\vek v\cdot\vek N_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\) there. The face \(s = 1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) and the face \(s = -1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) are the same set of points with opposite fluxes, \(149{,}78\) and \(-149{,}78\). The face \(\lambda = 0\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) is the face \(x = a\) of the cube, through which the cube has the flux \(a \cdot (2a)^2 = 256\ \text{mm}^3\).

That the two fluxes through a shared face are opposite for every field we see as follows. The face \(s = 1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\) and the face \(s = -1\) of the piece \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\) are described by the same function of the variables \(t\) and \(\lambda\), because \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(-1, t, \lambda) = \Phi(1, t, \lambda)\), since \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) depends on \(s\) only through \(s^2\). The vector of the first face is \(\vek N_{\mathrm{s}}\) of this function, the vector of the second \(-\vek N_{\mathrm{s}}\) of the same function, so the fluxes are opposite for every continuous field, as for the cut of the round bar in section 4.2.12.

Neighbouring pieces have twelve shared side faces, one along each edge of the cube. In the section of figure 4.129 we see four of them, the cuts from the corners of the cube to the surface of the ball. The following table covers them all. In it \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{z}} = \Phi\), and \(u\) is the parameter of the face that is not \(\lambda\). In each row the maps of the two pieces give the same point.

piece and face neighbouring piece and face equality
\(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), \(s = 1\) \(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(s = -1\) \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(-1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{z}}(1, u, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), \(s = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(s = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{x}}(1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{z}}(-1, u, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), \(t = 1\) \(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(t = -1\) \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{y}}(u, -1, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{z}}(u, 1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{z}}\), \(t = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\), \(t = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{y}}(u, 1, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{z}}(u, -1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(s = 1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), \(s = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(1, -u, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(t = 1\) \(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(s = 1\) \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{y}}(1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(u, 1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{x}}\), \(t = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\), \(s = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{y}}(1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(-u, -1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(s = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), \(s = -1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(-1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{-\mathrm{x}}(-1, -u, \lambda)\)
\(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(t = 1\) \(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(s = -1\) \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{y}}(-1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{-\mathrm{x}}(-u, 1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{-\mathrm{x}}\), \(t = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\), \(s = -1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{y}}(-1, u, \lambda) = \Phi_{-\mathrm{x}}(u, -1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{+\mathrm{y}}\), \(t = 1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), \(t = -1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(u, -1, \lambda) = \Phi_{+\mathrm{y}}(u, 1, \lambda)\)
\(V_{-\mathrm{y}}\), \(t = -1\) \(V_{-\mathrm{z}}\), \(t = 1\) \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(u, 1, \lambda) = \Phi_{-\mathrm{y}}(u, -1, \lambda)\)

We check each equality by inserting the components. In the fifth row, for instance, \(\Phi_{-\mathrm{z}}(1, u, \lambda) = (\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -u\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\) and \(\Phi_{+\mathrm{x}}(1, -u, \lambda) = (\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -u\,\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}, -\Phi_{\mathrm{z}})\), the first with \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) at the point \((1, u, \lambda)\), the second at the point \((1, -u, \lambda)\). The values are equal, because \(\Phi_{\mathrm{z}}\) depends on \(s\) and \(t\) only through \(s^2 + t^2\).
